abacotthecapofstate.c: ABACOT, the Cap of State, used in old time by our Englijh Kings, wrought up in the Figure of two Crowns.

abactors.c: ABACTORS, the lame with Abigei, such as Steal and Drive away whole flocks of Cattle, or the greatest part of any Herd or Flock; in which the Laywers distinguish them from Eure, who only steal a Sheep or two, ABACUS, sometimes lignifies the A, B, C, some - times a Table of Numbers for calling up Accounts, which was anciently of Brass, and called then, The Table of Pythagoras. It lignifies also, sometimes the Numeral Figures, which used to be drawn on a Table covered with small Sand or Dust, as Persius hints in these Verses, Nec qtti Abaco numeros & sest in pulvere notas Scit rifijfe wafer

abacusinarchitecture.c: ABACUS, in Architecture, is the four square Table that makes the Capital on the Top of a Co - lumn, especially those of the Corinthian Order: and is a Drip or Corona to the Capital. It sup - ports the nether Face of the Architrave and whole Trabeation. In the Corinthian and Comp fit e Or - ders, the Corners of it are called, the Homs, the middle part the Sweep, and the Curvature the Arch; which commonly has a Rose Carved in the mid - die. See Vol. a.

abaftoraft.c: ABAFT, or Aft, a Sea Term, signifying always those Parts which are towards the Stern of the Ship: So they fay. Such a Mast hangs Aft or A - haft, that is, towards the Stern. And because the Matters or Captain ’ s Cabbin is usually in the hin - der part of the Ship under the Quarter Deck, ’ tis common Complement to a Person come on Board a Ship, Sir, will you please to wall Aft.

abalienationaterm.c: ABALIENATION, a Term in the old poman Law, signifying a simple Sale of the Goods of one Citizen to another: These Goods were called, pps tnancupii, or tnancipii; and were Estates either in Slaves or Cattle, and sometimes Land of Inheri - tance i but they must be in Italy

abaptistonorana.c: ABAPTISTON, or Ana - baptifion, an Inftra - ment used by Surgeons, the fame with Modiolm which fee.

abateabatement.c: ABATE, Abatement, lignifies in Law the taking Polfeflion of Land by a Person that hath no right to it, after the Death of the Ancestor, and before the Entry of the right Heir. Also to Abate a Writ; lignifies to destroy it for a time, thro ’ want of good Ground, or other Defed. So to Abate a Ntifance is to destroy it,

abatementofhonour.c: ABATEMENT of Honour, in Heraldry, is an accidental Mark annexed to a Coat of Arms, ' whereby its Dignity is abased by reason of some dilhonourable Quality or Stain in the Bearer, and tis either by adding a Mar of Diminution; or by reversion of the whole Efcutch - on. The Markj of Diminution are, i. A DelfTenn, which is a Square born in the middle of the Field, thus; and belongs to one that hath revoked his Challenge, or eaten his Words. a. A Point Dexter parted Tenn: due to him that is a Braggadocio, or beasts of more than he did, or can do. . A Point in Point Sanguine; thus; due to him that is Lazy and Sloathful in the Wars. . A Point Champ am Tenn. which is due to him that kills his Prisoner after Quarter demanded and his Commanders leave to give it j born thus. B , A Plain Point Sanguine, born thus; due to one that is a Lyar, and tells false Stories to his Sovereign, . A Goar Sinifler Term, born thus; and is due to him that is proved a Coward: But a ( Soar Dexter is not an Abatement. . A Gusset Sanguine, born thus; where are. two Gullets one on each side. The Gusset is an A - batement proper for an Effemi - name, Lascivious Man; and is then born on the right side; but if he be given to too much Wine, the Gusset is on the left side; if to both, he should bear two Gullets, as in this Example. Reversion is two - fold,. When a Man bears in his own Escutcheon another Re - versed, as thus; which is due to a rude and uncivil Treater of Maid or Widdow j or as some fay, for Deflowering her only; and also, for one that runneth a - way from hisSove reign ’ s Banner, av When a Man ’ s own Escutcheon is entirely Reverted, which is due to a Traitor. IV. B. These Abatements are never charged with anything; are always born Angle, and their Colour is never of Metal, but always either Murrey or Tavonej.

abator.c: ABATOR, ( in the common Law ) is he that a - abateth, that is, intrudeth into a House or Land void by the Death of the former Possessor, and not yet entered, or taken up by his Heir.

abbrochment.c: ABBROCHMENT, istheforeftalling of a Mar - ket or Fair, by buying up the Wares before they are exposed to Sale in such Market or Fair, and then vending them again by Retail.

abbuttalls.c: ABBUTTALLS, are the Buttings and Boun - cings of Lands any way, shewing how they lie in refpedl to other places..

abdicationaterm.c: ABDICATION, a Term of the Roman Law, signifying several things; as the Abandoning of a Son, when he was Expell ’ d his Father ’ s House and refuted to be owned as his Child. Abdicare Magi - firatum, or fe Magifiratu, was to abandon or lay down the Office of a Magistrate. We meet there also with Abdicare fe state suo ‘ y which signifies, a Man ’ s renouncing his Condition to become a Slave, and to be degraded from the Priviledges of a Ro - man Citizen.

abdicere.c: ABDICERE, signifies to debar a Man from his Demands or not to allow them: Thus Abdicerevin - dicias was in the Roman Law not to allow a Man the Poffeffionof a thing in Controversie, as Add - zere vindicias is the very contrary. Tho ’ the Word Abdication signifies stri & ly an actual and voluntary Renouncing, yet in a larger Sense, at Common - Law, it may be properly used Where there is only an Implicit Renounciation; as When a Person does such Actions which are incony - distent with the nature of his Trust, he does in con - sequence renounce it; and this was the late fa - mous Case of a certain Prince, where this known and ancient Common - Law - Term was revived tho ’ indeed ‘ tis more generally used amongst the Ci - vilians.. "

abdomen.c: ABDOMEN, the lowermost of the three Venters in an Human Body; properly the Lower Belly: It contains in its Region the Stomach, Gutts, Liver, Spleen, Bladder. within it is covered with a Membrane called the Peritoneum, The lower part of it is called the Hyp ogaflr burn. The fore - moist part is divided into the Epigastrium, the Right and Left Hypocondria's, and the Navel. ’ Tis bounded above by the Cartilago Ensiformis and the Diaphragm, sideways by the sliort or lower Ribs, and behind by the Vertebres of the Loins, the Bones of the Coxendix, Pubis and " Os Sacrum. It hath ten Muscles which both cover it and serve to excrete the Faces and Urine, and to expel the Foe - tus in Women; You will End them under their proper Names.

abductorindicts.c: ABDUCTOR Indicts, is a Muscle of the fore - - Finger, which is not to be seen till the AbduRor Pol - ! licis is raised; by some it is reckoned amongst the Inter offer; it ariles Eleffily from th e Os Metacarpi that sustains the Fore - finger, and defending over the first Internode of the said Finger becomes Ten - dinous, joining with the Tendon of one of the Lumbrical Muscles, and is inferred with it together with the Tendon of the former Muscle. Its Name intimates its Use, in drawing the Fore - finger from the reft.

abductor.c: ABDUCTOR ticuli, a Muscle of the Eye lb called from its Action in retracing or drawing off the Eye from the Nose: It is also called Indigna bundus, because it is made use of in scornful Re - fentments. ' s

ABDUCTOR minimi digits, is a Muscle which appears in some Bodies divided into two or three Muscles, having each a differing Series of Fibres j the first of which fee ms to be a Flexor primi Inter - nodii minimi digiti; the second an AbduEtor of the fame; the third AbduElor Secundi & Tertii In - temodii; but this Division is not constant. It ari - fes fleshly, first, from the Ligamentum Tranfverfate and fourth Bone of the Carpus; Secondly, from the third Bone of the Carpus; and then. Thirdly, ' front the superior parts of the subjacent [ Os Meta - carpi; The two first continue fleshy to their Infer - tions; the former terminating at the superior part of the first Bone of the Little - Finger forwards; the latter ending at the fame part of the said Bone la - terally; the Third becoming Tendinous like the Interojfei, is inserted like them with the Tendon of the Extensor Minimi Digiti at the superior part of the third Bone of the Little - Finger. Its ute is to draw the Little - Finger from the others.

ABDUCTOR PoSicis, is a Muscle of the Thumb, which arises broad and fleshy from the internal part of the Ligamentum Tranfverfale Carpi, whence de - fending it lessens it self, and becomes Tendinous at its Implantation to the superior and external part of the second Bone of the Thumb laterally. This draws the Thumb from the Fingers, from whence it derives its Name.

abductorpollicispedis.c: ABDUCTOR Pollicis Pedis, is a Muscle which ariseth'flefhy from the Os Calcis internally and later - ally, in half its progress becoming Tendinous, it joins with another fleshy beginning, springing from the Os Cuneoforme Majus that sustains the Os Meta - tarif of the Great Toe; both which making one Tendon are inserted to the external part of the Of Sefamoides of the Great Toe laterally. This pulls the Great Toe from the reft, ABLE ’

abductorminimidigitipedis.c: ABDUCTOR Minimi Digiti Pedis, is a Muscle which ariseth outwardly Tendinous but inwardly Fleshy, from the external part of the Os tikis, be - coming Tendinous in half its progress on the out - side of the Foot j it joins with the other fleshy part of this Muscle arising fleshy from the outside of the Os Metatarsi of the Little Toe, and making one Tendon at its Insertion to the upper part of the first Bone of the Little Toe externally and laterally. Its use is to draw off the Little Toe from the reft.

abductores.c: ABDUCTORES, in the general ' are the fame with Abducent Muscles b

abducentmuscles.c: ABDUCENT Muscles, are universally those which serve to open or pull back divers parts of the Body, as the Arms, Legs, Eys, Nostrils, Lips, ( c, these are called also AbduBors, Their Opposite are usually called AdduBors or Adducent Muscles.

abettors.c: ABETTORS, is a Common Law Term, and fig - nifies those that without cause procure others to sue out false Appeals of Murder, or Felony against Men, in order to render them infamous.

abettorsinmurder.c: ABETTORS, in Murder, are those which ad vile or procure a Murder to be commited; in the fame Sense there are Abettors in Felony and Treason; in the last of which they are. W principals, there being no Acceflories in Treason.

abolitionthelicence.c: ABOLITION, the Licence given to a Criminal Accuser, to desist from further Profetution.

abeyanceinlaw.c: ABEYANCE, in Law signifies thing ’ s being in Pojfe only and not in ABu. - Thus suppose a Lease made to A. for, Term of Life, and the Remainder to the right Heir of B. who is living at the time of the Grant; in this case, tho ’ the Remainder pass present - ly from the Grantor, yet it rests not presently, Or takes hold in the Grantee, that is the Heirs of B. but is Indeterminate, in Potentia, in Nubibus, in Abeyance, vi. in consideration of Law: So when the Parson of a Church dies, and the Church is void, the Fee is in Abeyance, because it is not de - terminer who shall succeed him.

abisherising.c: ABISHERISING, and in some Copies, Mijhe - rising, is ( in common - Law being acquitted of A - merceaments, before whomsoever, of Tranfgreifion prov ’ d.

abjuration.c: ABJURATION, formerly was an Oath which a Person who had committed Felony, and who, to avoid the Law, had betaken himself to Sandhiary, took to depart the Kingdom for ever: It was a Law enabled by Edward the Confejfor, but is since changed by the Statutes, H.. c. z.. H.. c... H.. c.. But the Sense of the Word Abjurare originally, in the Roman Language, as it is used by Cicero and other good Writers of that Age, was. To deny a thing upon Oath j to deny that a Man had promised, committed, detained, or did owe any thing, upon his Oath. Thus with him Abjurare Creditum was to forswear a Debt, or to deny on Oath that he ow'd the Debt.

ablactation.c: ABLACTATION, the weaning of a Child that hath sucked its full time. Also a kind of Grafting, when the Cyon remainethon its own Stock, and the Stock you graft it on, together, till such time as they are surely incorporated; then the Cyon is cut from its own, and lives only by the other Stock.

ablaqueation.c: ABLAQUEATION, a laying open or bring the bottom of the Trunk, and Roots of Trees, that so being exposed to the Air, the Sun, and the Rains, they may the better fructify, or bear Fruit the en - suing Year.

ablativecase.c: ABLATIVE Case, is the last of the fix Cafes of Nouns and Participles in Grammar and is so call ed, because it usually takes away one thing front another. Tis called alio the Latin Case, because almost peculiar to the Latin Tongue, and is usually connected with some Propositions - which serve td determine it.

ablutionthepreparation.c: ABLUTION, the Preparation of a Medicine in any Liquor, to Cleanle ir fropi its Impurities.

abluentmedicines.c: ABLUENT Medicines are the lame with Ab ftergent, which fee.

abnodationinagriculture.c: ABNODATION, in Agriculture, signifies the Pruning of Trees, and cutting ofFKnots and Knobs.

abolitioninmetaphyficks.c: ABOLITION, in Metaphyficks, is an utter de - ft ruption of any Being.

abolition.c: ABOLITION of a Law, is the perfedl repeals ing it, or the entire taking of it away, so that it shall never have Force again.

abomasus.c: ABOMASUS, one of the Stomachs of Rumf nant Animals, or such as chew the Cud; of which are reckoned four, the Venter, Reticulum, Omafus, and Abomafw.

aborigines.c: ABORIGINES, are such Nations as the Italians who pretended Anciently to be without Original or Derivation from any other Nation or People.

abortion.c: ABORTION, the bringing forth of a Child ( or Foetus ) before its due time.

abortive.c: ABORTIVE, is spoken of a Foetus brought forth before its time: Hence ’ tis also an Epithet gi - ven tony Design or Purpose that mifcarries.

abrenuncation.c: ABRENUN CATION, is a renouncing or for - saking of any thing entirely.

abreviations.c: ABREVIATIONS, are Contractions in Writing or otherwise, whereby any thing that is written or spoken, is contained in, or takes up much left Room, than it would do if written or delivered at large.

abridgment.c: ABRIDGMENT of a Plaint, in Common - LaW ) is, when one part of the Plaintiffs Demand is left out, and it is pray ’ d that the Defendant may an - fwer to the other.

abrogate.c: ABROGATE, signifies todifanul or repeal: as to Abrogate a Law, is, to lay it aside or to repeal it. So that the

abrogation.c: ABROGATION of a Law, is the repealing it or taking it quite away.

abscisseanulceration.c: ABSCISSE, an Ulceration arising in any Part of the Body after a CrifsiThc fame with Apoftema.

abscisse.c: ABSCISSE, in a Conick Section, or other Cur - vilineal Figure, are the Parts of the Axis cut off by the Ordinates, and accounted downwards from the Vertex of the Section. Thus V r or VR are the Abfcijfe in this Figure. These are called by some Writers, the Intercepted Axes or Intercepted Diamei ters i V

absis.c: ABSIS, the fame With Apsis, which fee;

absolute.c: ABSOLUTE: This Word ( which signifies free trom the Power of another ) is variously used; Sometimes the Terms of a Proposition are laid to be taken Absolutely, that is, without relation to a ny thing else. A Prince isfaid to be Absolute, when he makes his Will his Law, and will in no refpecfi: be restrained or limited by the Laws of his Coun - try. This is otherwise called Arbitrary Power; and arises from an Imperfection both in the Under - ftandingof the Prince, and in the Spirits of the People. But God Almighty is Absolute from the Perfection of his Nature, as containing in himself all poflihle Power, and lying under no Limitations nor Reftraints from any one. Absolute is sometimes taken also in Opposition to Terms or Conditions; thusGod doth not forgive Men their Sins Absolutely, but on Condition of their Repentance and Amend - ment; and a Priest cannot absolve Men from the Guilt of their Sins Absolutely, but only declarative - ly and Ministerially, on the Condition of the Per - fon ’ s Penitence and Refolutions for Amendment. So ( in Law ) an Absolute Estate is one free from all manner of Conditions.

ABSOLUTE ' Number, in an Equation in Algebra, is that which Viet a calls the Homogeneum Compara - tions, and which always possesseth one entire part dr side of the Equation, and is always a known Quantity and the Rectangle or Solid, under the unknown Roots, in Quadraticks and Cubicks. Thus in this Equation aa az z. The Absolute Number is, which is equal to the Product of the two Roots or Values of a, multiplied one into another..,

absoluteequation.c: ABSOLUTE Equation, in Astronomy, is the Aggregate or Sum of the Eccentrick and Optick Equations. See Equation.

absorbents.c: ABSORBENTS, are Medicines that temper and qualify the Acid Juices in the Body, by ambi - bing or drinking them up; Thus Alkali's are said by some to absorb Acids.

abstensioninlaw.c: ABSTENSION, in Law, is a with - holding an Heir from taking Pofleflion of his Land.

abstergentorabjlerftvemedicines.c: ABSTERGENT, or Abjlerftve Medicines, are such as are used to clear the Skin or Superficial Parts of the Body from any Filth, &c. obftru & ing its Pores.

abstersion.c: ABSTERSION, is the Esse & produced by Ab - fterfive Medicines, or in general, any cleansing or wiping away.

abstraction.c: ABSTRACTION, is a Power peculiar to the Mind of Man, in Contradiftin & ion to the Souls of Beasts, and plainly distinguishes Him from Them; whereby he can make his Ideas, arising from par - dicular Things, become general Represent tatives of all of the fame kind. Thus, if ' my Eye represents to me Whiteness in a Wall, I can AbftraEiedly con - sider that Quality of Whiteness, and find it attri - mutable to many other things besides, as to Snow, to Milk, or the like; and this Quality, whatever it be, thus considered apart from the Concrete, or the Subject in which it inheres, is said to be taken in the AbJlraEl.

abstract.c: ABSTRACT, is frequently used also forafmall Draught or Epitome of any greater Work.

abstractnumbers.c: ABSTRACT Numbers, are those which are con - fidered as Pure Numbers, without being applied to any Subject; and so AbftraEied Mathematicks, is used in opposition to Mixt Mathematicks the for - mer signifying pure Geometry or Algebra; and the latter Opticks, Dialling, Navigation, ( c. where PhyficalConfiderations are connected with the Ma - thematical.

abundantnumbers.c: ABUNDANT Numbers, are those whose Parts added together, make more than the. whole Num - ber which they are Parts of as v, g, Twelve, whose Parts being,,,, and. these all ad - ded together make Sixteen: Thus also the Parts of zo make, ( c.

abyss.c: ABYSS, is any vast deep Place, which either hath no Bottom, or else hath none discernible, or ac least is supposed to have none. The Learned Dr. Woodward, in his Natural Hi - story of the Earth, P.. tells us. That there is a mighty Colledtion of Waters inclosed in the Bow -; els of the Earth, constituting an huge Orb in the Interiour or Central Parts of it; and over the Sur - face of this Water, he luppofesthe Terrestrial Star - ta to be expanded: This is what Moves calls the Great Deep, and what many Authors call the Abyss. And that there is such a vast Collection of Waters lodged in the Bowels of the Earth, is confirmed by, abundance of Observations. The Water of this vast Abyss the Dr. asserts / doth communicate with that of the Ocean by means of certain Holes, Hiatus ’ s or Chasms, palling betwixt it and the Bottom of the Ocean: And this and the Abyss he supposes to have one com - mon Centre, around which the Water of both of them is placed; but so, that the ordinary Surface of the Abyss is not level with that of the Ocean / nor at so great a distance from the Centre as that is, it being for the m oft part restrained and depress - fed by the Strata of Earth lying upon it; but where - ever those Stata s are broken, ors lax and prose that Water can pervade them, there the Water of the Abyss doth ascend, fills up ail the Clefts or Fijfures whereinto it can get admittance or en - trance, and saturated ail thelnterftices and Pores of the Earth, Stone, or other Matter, all around the Globe, quite up to the Level of the Ocean.

academy.c: ACADEMY, is a kind of higher School or U - diversity, where young Men are instructed in the Liberal Arts and Sciences. ’ Twas so called at first from Academia, the Name of a Place near Athens, and built, fay some, by Cadmus the Phoenician; o - thers, by one Academus, whence it had its Name: ’ Twas planted with Trees; and here Plato taught his Dilciples Philosophy, who from hence are call - ed Academicks. Cicero alls call ’ d one of his Coun - try Seats by this Name, where he had fine Groves, and pleasant Walks for the Entertainment of his Philosophical Friends; and here he wrote his. Books, D. Nat. Deorum and De Amicitia, and his ' Offices, which therefore he called his Academical Treatises.

academicks.c: ACADEMICKS; so the Followers of Plato were anciently - called,, because they studied in the Academia. Afterward it became the Name of a Sect of Sceptical Philosophers, who maintained. That all things were uncertain, and that Reason and Truth were changeable, so thar Men ought to doubt of every thing, and believe nothing.

acantabolus.c: ACANTABOLUS, the fame with Vo sella ( ex - cepting that the Volsella is crooked ) a Surgeon ’ s Instrument to take out any thing that shall happen to stick in the Oesophagus or Gullet; tis something like a Pair of Plyers, and may be reckoned as a kind of Forceps.

acantha.c: ACANTHA, is with some Anatomists the most backward Protuberance of the Vertebres of the Back; and is otherwise called, Spina Dorsi.

acatalectickverse.c: ACATALECTICK Verse, is ' one exa & Iy per - sect, where not so much as one Syllable is either redundant or deficient, ACCEDAS

accedasadcuriamawrit.c: ACCEDAS ad Curiam a Writ made out of the Chancery, and Returnable in the Kings Bench or Common Pleas, and directed to the Sheriff, requir - ing him to go to the Court of some Lord, or Franchise, ( ' where a Plaint is sued for taking of Cat - tle as a Distress, or any false Judgment supposed to be made in any Suit in such a Court, which is not a Court of Record, ) and there make a Record of the said Suit, in presence ef the Suitors of the said Court, and also of four other Knights of the fame County and to certifie it into the King ’ s Court, at the Day limited in the Writ.

accedasadvicecomitem.c: ACCEDAS ad Vice Comitem, is a Writ directed to the Coroner, requiring him to deliver a Writ to the Sheriff, who having a Pone delivered to him, fuppreftes it.

That the Mutati - on of Motion it always proportionable to the Force im - pressed, and always it according to that fame Line of Di - section, th. tRea. ion of the Acceleration of the Descent of heavy Bodies, will be very clear andinteHigible. Since the Space in the first part of Time is, in the second, in the third, &c, if you confider the Space run through in the. second Par - ticle of Time separately, it will be as; and if from, the Space described in the third part of Time, you take, the Space before described in the d Moment, there will remain, &c. where - fore supposing the Moments or Parts of Time e - qual, the Spaces described by the Descent of an heavy Body beginning from Reft, in each Mo - ment considered separately, will be as the natural odd Numbers, T,,,,, n,,,, . And since the Velocities acquired in falling, are as the Times, the Spaces run through will be also as the Squares of the Velocities; and both Times and Velocities will be in subduplicate JQ - tio of the Spaces described by any falling Body.

accentingrammar.c: ACCENT in Grammar, is a Mark placed over a Syllable, to shew ' tis pronounced with a strong - er or weaker Voice. The Greeks, who were the greatest observer of Accents, distinguish them into th c Acute one mark ’ d thus, ( ' ), the Grave one thus ' ) and the Circumflex thus, ( ). But of late one Hennin a Dutch - man hath written a Book to prove the Accents were not Ancient among the Greeks, and that that Language ought not to be pronounce - ed according to them: He pretends no Accents are be found in any MSS. above oo / Years old, and takes them to be an Invention of the Arabs - about the time of Mahomet ’ s Death. He says, the Mas - sorites of Tiberias brought them into the Bible a - soot the Sixth Century, and that they were per - seated by Pabbi Judah Pen David Chiug, born in Sep, about the Eleventh Century.

accentsingrammar.c: ACCENTS, in Grammar, hew how to judge of the Measure of Time, in which each Letter, Syllable, Word, or Expression is pronounced - the Elevations and Deprelfions of the Voice, the Si - hence or Repose of the Voice at the End of Words or Sentences, These Accents may be very, numerous: There are in the Hebrew Grammars more than Thirty of them, and Servius Honor am reckons Eight in the Latin. The Acute ccent shews when the Voice is to be raised, and is expressed thus ( ). The Grave Accent hows when the Voice is to be depressed, and is figured thus, ( ' ). The Circumflex Accent is compos ’ d of both the Acute and the Grave, and is expressed thus, ( A ). The Long Accent shews that the Voice is to flop upon the Vowel that has that Mark, and it is ex - pressed thus, ( ). The Short Account shews that the time of Pronun -, cation ought to be short, and is marked thus, ( ): Hyphen, is an Accent in Grammar, that implies two Words are to be joyned, as male - Janus. Diafiole, is an Accent in Grammar, which shews that those Words or Sentences to which it is ad - joyned are to be separated, its mark is (, ). Apofirophe, is an Accent in Grammar, Flowing there is a Vowel to be rejected, and is expressed thus, ( ’ ) and placed over the Head of the Letter. ’

accident.c: ACCIDENT: This Word is used by Logici - ans in three Senses. i. In opposition to the Essence of any Thing, whatever doth not essentially belong to it may ( tho ’ a Substance it self ) yet be an Accident or Ad - junct to that Thing, or belong to it only accident - tally, as the Clothes a Man hath on the Money in his Purse, &c. These indeed are more proper - ly called Adjuncts; and by the School - men are di - ftinguifhed by the Name of Verbal Accidents. Z. In Contradiftindlion to the Essential Proper - ties of any Subject, many Qualities are called Ac - cidents; because they are there not EJJentially but Accidentally. This in the Schools is called Accident VradidabiUs, and implies a Common Quality, which may or may not be in any Subject, as any particular Colour, &c. . In opposition to Substance, a Thing is called an Accident, when it is its Essence or Nature to In - here or subsist in some Substance, and cannot be alone: And thus it is with all Qualities whatsoever. This is called Accident Predicamentale, and the nine last Predicaments are in this sense Accidents. In reference to its Cause also, or at least as to our Knowledge of it, a Thing is frequently stile an Accident, by which we mean an EfFedb either ca - usually produced, or which to us appears to have been so.

While an Animal is capable of Accretion, and the Particlesof which the solid Parts consist are not entirely united at their Extremities, but are capable of receding one from another, both end - ways and laterally the Spirits ad upon the Nutritious Particles ( which are of a Viscous Nature ) by their Rotary Morion by which they carry them to the Sides of the Fibres and Bony Strings, driving some against the sides of their Parts, and forcing them out laterally: Others they drive into the Interstices between the Extre - mities, thereby lengthening every Series of them ” ' where they are placed and fix ’ d, and thus the Pat - of an Animal Body increase both in Thicknrffand Longitude. acids.c: ACIDS, whose Particles are supposed to be long - ilh, flexible, penetrating, and attenuating; and which have their Points sharp and piercing. You may easily know whether any Liquor contain in it any Acid Salt or not, by dropping some of it on a little Syrup of Violets spread on white Paper; or in a Solution of Blue - bottle Flowers, ( c. for then the Blue will be immediately turned into a Red or reddish purple Colour; whereas if it turn Green, tis a lign the Liquor abounds with Salts of an Uri - nous or Lixiviate Nature; which how to distil - gttilh, fee those PVords: The Acidity of any Liquor may also be concluded by its being able to destroy the Blueness of a Tindture of Lignum Nephriticum: ( See Colours, and the ways of producing sudden changes of them ) AClDULiE, any Medicinal Waters that are not hot, like those at the Bath, which are called Tbernia.

adepsorpinguedo.c: ADEPS or Pinguedo, Fat, is a similar part of the Body: But Adept and Pinguedo differ in this, ' that Adept is a thicker, harder, and more earthy, Substance than Pinguedo the Fat which is particularly meant by Adept flows from the Blood thro peculiar Vessels into Bags or Bladders appropriate thereunto, as is plain from the Observation of MaP plghius.

adeptistsoradepts.c: ADEPTISTS, or Adepts, are such Alchymists as pretend to have gain ’ d the Secret ol the Tranfmu tation of Metals, or to make the Philosophers Stoned Of these Myftical Invisible Gentlemen ( they fay ) there are always in being; which are kept sup ’ ply ’ d by new ones when any of the Fraternity pleat eth to die, or to translate himself to some place where he can make use of his Gold, for in this wicked World it will not procure them Shirts.

adequate.c: ADEQUATE; a thing is said to be adequate to, or adequately to agree with another, when ’ tis every way equal to it in Extent, Capacity, Pow - er, ( c. and all other Properties; and neither ex - ceeds it, nor falls short of it in any helped. And thus when the Notions or Ideas that we have of a - ny thing, take in all the Properties of that thing, and that we omit conceiving nothing which be - longs to it, we then fay we have Adequate Ideas of such things.

adequateideas.c: ADEQUATE IDEAS, are those Ideas which perfectly represent the Architypes or Images which the Mind supposes them to be taken from; which it intends them to stand for, and to which it refers them.

adiaphorousorneutral.c: ADIAPHOROUS, or Neutral, i. e. indifferent: So Mr. Boyle Calls a kind of Spirit which he distil - led from Tartar and some other Vegetable Bodies; which was neither Acid, Vinous, nor Urinous. Tis made thus; First, Shavings of Box, Guajacum, or any other ponderous Wood are distilled per fe ip a Retort; and then the sourish Liquor is redifi - ed to free it from the Phlegm: After this a Quanti - ty of Powder of Coral, ( c. was thrown into the sowre Spirit, which it readily dissolved; and the Acid Parts of the Menstruum did so associate themselves with the Coral, as to leave a part of Liquor that was by no means of an Acid Nature, but which when gently drawn off the Coral, was of a strong smell, yet without any Acidity, and in many relpeds ofa different Nature from almost any other common Spirit, A. adjectives.c: ADJECTIVES ( in Grammar ) are such Words as describe the manner only of the Being of a thing, and have no natural subsistence of their own ? but do subsist by Noun Substantives, to which they are joyned.

adinquirendum.c: AD INQUIRENDUM; a Writ in Law com - minding an Enquiry to be made ( for the better Execution of Justice ) about the Merits of a Cause depending in the King ’ s Court.

adjoiningangles.c: ADJOINING ANGLES, in Geometry i See Angles, of Contiguous.

adjournment.c: ADJOURNMENT, is the putting off of any Court or Meeting, and appointing it to be kept at another Plate or Time.

adiposamembrana.c: ADIPOSA MEMBRANA, is the Basts of the CelluU'AdifoJce, is double, and may be divided in - to two Parts; the one is External throughout which there are a number of little Cells, full of Fat; the other is Internal, which Anatomists have mistaken for the Membrana Cdrnofa, because it has a greater number of Blood Vessels.

adiposavena.c: ADIPOSA VENA, or Penalis, a Vein arising from the descending Trunk of the Cava; which spreads its self on the Coat, and Fat, that covers the Kidneys.

adiposiductus.c: ADIPOSI DUCTUS, call ’ d also Sacculi, Vefi - cut Adifcfie or Lobuli, are Vessels which convey the Adepscr Fat Into the Interstices of the Muscles, or to the Parts between the Flesh and the Skin.

adit.c: ADIT, is the shaft, or Entrance into any Mine.

adjudge.c: ADJUDGE, when a determinate Sentence is past in the behalf of another, the Case is said to be Adjudged for him

adjunct.c: ADJUNCT: Whatever comes to any Being from without, is called an AdjunB to that Being; as being not naturally and essentially belonging to it, but adjoined or superadded to it.

adjuraregis.c: AD JURA REGIS, is a Writ that lies for the Kings Clerk against him that fought to ejeCt him, to the Prejudice of the Kings Title in Right of his Crown,

admeasurementofdower.c: ADMEASUREMENT of Dower, is a Writ that lies where a Woman is endowed by an Infant, or by a Guardian, of more than she ought to have.

admeasurementofpajlure.c: ADMEASUREMENT of Pajlure, is a Writ that lies against such, as having Common of Pa - fture appendant to their Free - holds, do surcharge it with more Cattle than they ought to do.

administration.c: ADMINISTRATION, ( in Law ) is the difpo - sing of a Man ’ s Goods or Estate that died intestate, or without any Will, with an Intent to give an Ac - count thereof.

administrator.c: ADMINISTRATOR, he that has the Goods of a Man dying intestate, committed to his Charge by the Ordinary, and is accountable for the fame. If the Person be a Woman, she is called an Admini - firatix.

admittendoclerico.c: ADMITTENDO CLERICO, is a Writ grant - ed to him that hath recovered his Right of Present - tarin against the Bishop, in the Common Bench.

admittendoinsocium.c: ADMITTENDO in Socium, is a Writ for the Association of certain Persons to Justices of Assize before appointed.

adnatatunica.c: ADNATA TUNICA, is the common Mem - brane of the Eye, called ConjunElive, it springs from the Skull, grows to the Exterior part of the Tunica Cornea; and that the visible Specie's may pals there, leaves a round Cavity forward, to which is annexed another Tunic, without any particular Name, made up of the Tendons of thole Muscles which move the Eye by reason of its Whitnefs, ’ tis called Albuginea.

adocto.c: AD OCTO, among feme of the Ancient PhU lofophers, is a Term signifying the Highest or Su - perlative Degree; because they reckoned no De - gree above the Eighth, in their way of distinguish - ing of Qualities.

adonick.c: ADONICK, a fort of a sliort Verse, confuting of a Daily le and a Spondee as Bara juventus ’ tis usually placed at the end of each Stanza of Sa thick Verles. So called from Adonis, in whole praise they were first made.

adquoddamnum.c: AD QUOD DAMNUM, is a Writ which ' ought to bellied before the King grant certain Li - berries, as a Fair, Marker, ( c. to the Prejudice of others. There is also anotherWrit of Ad quod. Damnum if any one will turn a Common High - way, and lay out another as beneficial.

adterminum.c: AD TERMINUM qui prateriit, is a Writ of Entry, that lies where a Man having leafed Lands or Tenements for Life or Years, and after the Term expired, is held from them by the Tenant, or o - ther Stranger that occupieth the fame, and defer - eth the Leffior: In such case this Writ lieth for the Lessor and his Heirs.

advanceditch.c: ADVANCE DITCH, in Fortification, is a Ditch dug all along the Glacis beyond the Count erfcarft and usually filled with Water.

advanceguard.c: ADVANCE GUARD, is the first Line or DU vision of an Army, ranged or marching in Battle - aray; or that part which is next to the Enemy, or which marches first towards them. The whole Body of any Army consists of the Advance Guard j the Arriere Guard, and the Main Body, Sometime also a Party of i or Horse com - mended by a Lieutenant beyond, but within fight of the Main Guard, is called an Advance Guard j and is designed for the greater Security of the Camp.

advent.c: ADVENT, in the Sacred Calender, is the Time from the Sunday that falls either upon St. Andrew ’ s Day, or next to it, till Christmas - which time was wont anciently to be spent in a pious Prepara - tion for the Advent, or coming on of the Feast of our Saviour ’ s Nativity.

adventitiabona.c: ADVENTITIA BONA, were anciently such as came to a Man unexpectedly; Windfalls, as we call them now: Hence the Word Adventitious comes to be used by Philofophick Writers, and to signify such Matter as doth not properly belong to any mix ’ d Body, but comes to it from some other Place. Thus, tis a Question, whether in the Freezing of Water, there do notenter in some Frigorifick. Particles, which are Adventitious to the Water, from the Air, or the Freezing Mixture.

advocates.c: ADVOCATES, in. the Ecclesiastical Court, were either Advocate of the Causes and Interest of the Church, retain ’ d as a Counsellor and Pleader, to maintain the Properties and Rights: Or, Ad - vacate or Patron of the Presentation and Advow - fon, Both these Offices did formerly belong to the fame Founder of a Church or Covent, and his Heirs, Vho were bound to proted and defend the Church, as well as to nominate or present to it. But when the Patrons grew negligent, or were jMcn of no Interest or Ability in the Courts of Ju - stice, then the Religious began to retain a Law Ad - vacate, to follicite and prosecute their Controverfi - al Causes. Advowson is of two forts; First, Advowson hi Gross, that is, some or principal, not belonging to any Mannor, as a Parcel of its right: Secondly, Advowson Happen - dant, which depends upon a Mannor, as appurte - nant to it; and this may be fold by it self, and then it is in Gross: And while it is dependant to the Mannor, tis by Kitchen called, an Inch - dent.. r.,

agist.c: AGIST ( a Term in Law ) signifies to take in, and feed the Cattle of Strangers in the King ’ s So - reft, and to gather Money due for the fame to the King ’ s use. The Officers doing it are called, AGtSTERS; and theffOffice is called, AGISTMENT.

agitation.c: AGITATION, in general, signifies Motion of ACtion; but ’ tis mostly used in a Philofophlcal Sense for the brisk Intestine Motion of the final ! Corpuscles of any Natural Body. Thus Fire or Heat agitates the small Particles of dll Bodies,, and puts them into a Rapid Motion.

agnation.c: AGNATION, in the Civil Law, is the Term for that Line of Cor. sanguinity which is between Males descended from the fame Father; as Cogna - tion is the Line of Parentage between Males and Females, both descended from the fame Father. The Use of both these Words is derived from the old Pyman Law.

agriculture.c: AGRICULTURE, is the Art of Tilling, Ma - during, and Cultivating the Earth, in order to render it fertile, and to make it bear Plants, Trees and Fruits.

agrypnocoma.c: AGRYPNOCOMA, the fame with Coma Vi - AIDE DE CAMP; in an ' Army, is an Officer always following one of time Generals, i. e. the General, Lieutenant General, or Major General, to receive and carry their Orders as Occasion re - quires. Aides Majors as it cpmains Battallions, When the Battalion is drawn up / ' the Aide Majors Poll: is on the Left beyond all the Captains; and behind the Lieutenant Colonel.

air.c: AIR. The Atmofpherical Air in which we breath is a Diaphanous, Compressible and Dilatable Fluid Body, covering the Earth and Sea to a great Height above the highest Mountains and differs fromthe JEther ( among other things ) in this, that it Refra & s the Rays of the Moon and other rem - ter Luminaries. This Air seems to consist of three differing Kinds of Corpufc'es, or small Bodies: . Such as are carried up into it in the Form of Exhalations or Vapours from the Earth, Sea, and all Animal, Vegetable and Mineral Bodies, by means of the Suns, or the Subterraneal Heat.. . There are yet a more subtle fort of Particles in the Air, ' which we may reckon emitted into it from the Heavenly Bodies; and also the Magne - tick Steams of this Globe of Earth and Water. But . There is also a Third kind of Par tides, which perhaps do molt properly merit the Name of Acre - al, as being the proper and distinguishing Parts of Air taken in the ftriefteft Sense; and these are Cor - muscles which are constantly Elajlical or Springy. For Elallicity is an Essential Property of Air, and ‘ tis thought no other Fluid hath any thing of it, but only so far as it participates of Air, or hath Air contained in its Pores. So that our Air probably doth either consist of, or abound with Parts of such a Nature, that in case they be bent or compressed by the Weight of the incumbent part of that - mosphere, or of any other Body, they do ended - vour to free themselves from that pressure, by bear - ing against the Bodies that keep them bent and as soon as these Bodies are removed to give them way, they unbend themselves, either quite, ors far forth as the Bodies that resell; them will permit, and thereby expand the whole parcel of Air, these Elastical Bodies compose. Dr. Hook, in his Micrograph, p.. seems to think the Air to be nothing else but a kind of Tin - j dture or Solution of Terrestrial and Aqueous Par deles dissolved in, and agitated by the iEtherj and these Particles he supposes to - be of a saline nature Mr. Boyle found, that one and the fame portion of Air, may take up times the Spaceiit doth at another time. See Trads about the admirable RarefaElion of the Air. And in the said Discourse he tells us, That he found by undoubted Expert -; ments, that the fame quantity of Air, by only ) having the Pressure of the Atmolphere taken off iri the Pnemmatick Engine, and without any Adventi - tious Heat to encrease its Spring, would possess a - above times its natural Space or Dimensions, Dr. Gregory in his Ajlron. p., ffiewS, that if Air expand it self according to Mr. Boyles observed Law, v / p. That the Spaces into vhich it may be com prcjfed, eye always reciprocally proportional to the corner easing weight: Then a Globe of Air of the Diameter of one Inch, if rarefied so, as ( accords ing to that Rule ) itmuft be at the distances the. Earth ’ s Semi - diameter ( from the Earth ) will fill all the Planetary Regions as far as, and much beyond, the Sphere of Saturn. And the great Dilatation and Corripxeffion of Air may be easily enough conceived, without the Inter - mention of any subtile Matter, if we imagine each proper elastick Particle of Air to be like a little Spring of a Watch coiled up round, or wound up like a Piece of Ribband: For, if you allow fur - ther, that these Particles have, also a Circular, Motion round their o wn Axis, the Parts of each ’ Roll, Coil, or Lamina will endeavour to recede from the Axis of its Motion, and this more op less, according to the Velocity of their Motion by which means they will acquire a Springiness outward like a Watch Spring, and will ended - vour to fly or unwind themselves out to their full length, but that they are hindered by other such Particles on every side: And therefore these E - elastick Particles in the lower Parts of the Atmo -. sphere, will always be kept bent or wound up, by, the weight of the whole of the Air j but if at any time they can get rid of this weight and external pressure, they will readily, by their natural Spring,, evolve themselves, and extend their Roll, or Cir - cles to vastly large Dimensions. And this may be the reason of the Tumefcence of a Bladder not apparently blown out, in the exhausted Receiver of a full - blown one ( if dry ) breaking there, and of the breaking of square figured Vials, when stop ’ d Well, and the Air throughly drawn off from them. And ’ tis equally easy to conceive, that a great; Dilatation or Rarefaction of Air may be produced by Heat for the Rapid Motion of the Calorifick Particles must needs so move the Aereal ones, and by that means may make them more ended - vour to recede from the Axis of their Motion, and consequently more unwind or unroll themselves; wherefore they must take up more space, and must more thrust, by this encreased Spring, all other Bodies from them, and separate themselves from one another. Mr. Boyle, in his Discourse against Linus, strews, that the Strength required to compress Air, are in Reciprocal Proportion ( nearly ) to the Spaces compare - hending the fame Portion of Air.

AIR, The admirable Sir Isaac Newton, in the Ob - fervations mention ’ d in the d Book of his Opticks by considering the Colour ’ d Rings made by Corn - pressing tWo Prisms, or two Object Glasses of large Telescopes together, comes to a Calculation of the thickness of the Air contain ’ d between the Prisms and Object Glasses in such a State of Compression and at last he seems ( he faith ) to gather this Rule That the thicknels'of the Air is proportionable to the Secant of an Angle, whose Sine is a certain ' mean Proportional between the Sines of Incidence and Refradiom And that mean Proportional, so far as by the Measure he took could be determin'd, he found was the first of Arithmetical Mean Proportionals between those Sines accounted from thegreaterof the Sines ( /. e. ) from the Sine of Re - franion, when the Refraction is made out of the Glass into the Plate of Air or from the Sine of Incidence, when the Refraction is made out of the Plate of Air into Glass. And in Observation Page. He faith that the Thickness of the Air be - tween the Glasses there, where the Rings are suc - ceflively made blithe Limits of the Colours, Red, Orange, Yellow, Green, Blue, Indico and Violet, in order are to one another as the Cube Roots of A I R the Squares of the eight Lengths of a Musical Chord which Sound the Notes in an Eighth, Sol, la, fa, Sol, la, mi, fa, Sol: That is as the Cube Roots of the Squares of the Numbers i,,, i., - j j S X - j " And according to his most accurate Observati - ons the Thickness of the Thinned Air, which be - tween two Glasses exhibited the most Luminous Parts of the first fix Rings of Colours, were s ' g ' T ooo t i o o o I " P ttt j of UU Inch;,.., ’ ’ Tis highly probable that True and Permanent Air is made by Fermentation, ( faith the fame Au - thor ) and Rarefradtion of Bodies that are of a ve - ry fixt Nature: Those Particles flying and avoid - ing one another with the greatest Force at a di fiance, which when very near, attrap and adhere to one another with the greatest Violencei The Particles therefore of True and Perma - next Air, being Extracted from the Denfeft and most fixt Bodies will be Denser and Craffer than those of Vapour; and from hence, its likely, may be Heavier also than those, and that the Parts of a Humid Atmosphere may be Lighter than those of & dry one, as in Fact it appears to be; by the ri - ling of the Mercury in dry Weather, and by Clouds and Vapours riling in and floating in bur Atmo - spherical Air. And he very justly thinks that the Rarefracftion and Condensation of the Air cannot be accounted far from the Spring or Elastick Forms of the Particles, without a Supposition that they are endued with some Centrifugal Force or Power, by which they Fly and, avoid one another, and the Dense Bodies from whence they are Extracted. See AttraBion. And that this spelling Force, which is the Cause of Filtration and of the Ascent of Water in small Capillary Tubes to much greater Heights than the Surface of the Water in the open Vessel, in which they are placed. The Air within the Tubes being much rare than in more open Spaces, and by that means not pressing so much on the Surface of the Water within the Tubes as without. And this Account Dr. Hoo ) had hinted at long ago; Sir If. did his admirable Prin. Philo. Mathemat. Prop.. P.. long ago Demonstrate, That Particles en - devouring to Recede from or avoid one another with Forces reciprocally Proportional to the Distance between their Centers, will Compose an Fdafiiclg Fluid whose Density shall be Proportionable to its Compression, and from such a Property all the appearances of our Air may be very well accounted for. And I think much better than from the Supposition of its Par - titles being Spires contorted into Spheres, through whose Interstices the Rays of Light may freely ? ass, &c. tho this be very ingenious: But I think can never solve the Prodigious Rarefradiion of this most useful Fluid.

Also, that a Lamb ’ s Bladder being counterpoi - zed in a nice Pair of Scales in the Receiver, on the Air ’ s being drawn out, did manifestly prepon - delate; but when the External Air was let in again, the Scales returned to their former Equilibrium. An iEolopile well heated, and then having its little Hole stop ’ d, was cooled, and weighed; after which the Hole being opened, the Air was heard plainly to tush in with a whistling Noise, and then the iEolopile being weigh ’ d again, it was ma - nifeftly heavier than it was before. The Magdehurgick Engine being weighed when full of Air, and afterwards being again weighed when Was well exhausted, was found to weigh an entire Ounce and T - less than it did before. And Mr. Boyle found by accurate Experiments, that a small Receiver weigh ’ d Grains more when full of Air, than after it was exhausted. He found also that A Glass Bubble as big as an Hen ’ s Egg, having as much Air as could be driven out by Heat, had then its Stem nimbly sealed up, and then being left leisurely to cool ( for there is great Danger of its breaking ) was put into a nice Balance, and then the Scales were equipoized: After, the sealed End being warily broken off, the Air was heard to rush in with a whistling Noise, and then the Scale in which the Bubble was, did manifestly pre - ponderate by near of a Grain. And after this, filling it with Water, it was found to hold Grains of that Liquor; so that allowing for of the Cavity of the Bubble ’ s being filled with Air, which perhaps might weigh about a Grain, the Proportion of Water to Air appears in weight to be about to one, and roundly it may be sup - posed as to one, because ’ tis not possible but that some Air must remain in the Bubble more than is now accounted for, Mr. Boyle found by repeated Experiments, that the weight of Air to Water is as to. airpump.c: AIR PUMP, an Instrument to exhaust the Air out of proper Vessels. Mr. Boyle oWnshe had the first hint of it from Schott us, who had published to the World, but Mr. Beyle had not seen the Book ) that one Otto Gerick, Consul of Magdehurgh, had found out a way of evacuating Glass Vessels, by sucking out the Air at the Mouth of the Vessel, plunged under Water. But this Engine was de - sectile in two respects:. That in order to eva - curate the Vessel, there was required the continual Labour of two strong Men for two Hours.. The Receiver and Engine being all of one Piece, there was no way to get things in and out of ir, in order to try any Experiment upon them. To re - med which, and to supply those Imperfections which Mr. Boyle had heard the Otto Gerick Engine laboured under, he directed one Mr, G. and Dr. Hook, to contrive a never and better Air Pump which Dr. Hook. effeCted in the following Form, which I will describe, because it was the first of the kind made here. This Air Pump consists of two Parts; a Glass - Vessel; and a Pump to draw the Air out of it. The Glalsis expreffedby the Fig.. A. having a Hole at the Top with a Cover fitted to ir, and also a Stop - Cock fattened to the Extremity of its Neck below; its Cavity being large enough to contain about do lb. of Water. The Diameter [ BC ) of the Hole at the Top of the Vessel ( A ) is about four Inches, the Orifice whereof isencom - passed with a Lip of about an Inch in height, whose use is for the Cover to reft on; which Cover is described in the Second Figure, where ( D E ) denotes a Brazen Ring, which is to cover, and to be closely cemented on the Lip ( BC ) of the first Figure. To the internal tapering Orifice of this Ring, is fitted a Brass Stopple ( EG ) so exaCt, as to prevent any considerable access of External Air: In the midst of this Cover there is a Hole ( H I ) of about half an Inch Diameter encompass ’ d with a Ring or Socket of Brass, to which is likewise fitted a Stopple ( AL ) of the fame Metal, so exquisitely adapted to it, that it pay be turned round, without admitting in the least Air, and yet may be put in or taken out at pleasure: Through the lower end of it there is a lirrle Hole ( ) made for passage of a String, (,, ) which is likewise to pass through a small Brazen Ring ( Lj fixed to the Bottom of the Stopple ( F G ); the use of which String is to move what is contained in the exhausted Vessel, without unstopping it. That the Stop Cock ( S ) ( in the first Figure ) might be better fattened, to the Neck of the Receiver, and cement - ed on with Pitch, Rosin and Wood - ashes well in - corporated together, and poured hot into the Cava - ty of the Plate; and to prevent the Cement from running into the Orifice ( ) of the Shank ( X ) it was stop ’ d with a Cork, having a String fixed to it, that it might be drawn out at the upper Orifice of the Receiver, and then the Glass Neck of the Receiver being well warmed, and thrust into the Cement, Ht'diiIed the Interstices betwixt the Tin Plate and the Receiver, as also between the inter - nal Superficies of the Receiver, and the Shank of tfie Cock The lower Parr is the Sucking Pump or Air Pump, supported by a Frame of Wood, with three Legs, ( III ) so contrived, so r the freer Motion of the Hand, that one side of it may stand perpend - cular; across the Midst of the Frame is nailed a Board ( ) to which the Pump is fattened. The Pump is made up of four Parts, vi. An ex - atst and strong Cylinder of Brafsof about In - ches in length, with a Cavity of about Inches Di - ameter; to which is fixed a Sucker made up of two Parts; the one ( ) somewhat less in Dia - meter than the Cavity of the Cylinder; on which a thick Piece of tann'd Leather is nailed, whereby it closes so exactly to the Cylinder, that the Air cannot insinuate it self between them: The other Part being a thick and narrow Plate of Iron ( ) Is firmly joyned to the Middle of the former Part ( ) it is somewhat longer than the Cylinder; one Edge of it being smooth, but the other indented ( as in the Figure ) with a row of Teeth; to the In - terfaces of which are fitted the Teeth of a small Iron Nut ( L B ) which is fastened by two Staples ( ). to the under side of the cross Board ( a ) on which the Cylinder rests, and is turned to and fro by the Manubrium or Handle ( ). Thelaft Part of the Pump is the Valve ( R ) being a Hole at the Top of the Cylinder, a little taper towards the Cavity; to this Hole is fitted a Brass Pegg, to be put in or taken tout upon occ - sion. Having thus described the Engine, it will be requisite for the better exclusion of the outward Air, and the more easie moving of the Sucker, Stop - cock and Key S, as also the Valve, that they should be well oyled with Sallad Oyl; but sometimes Oyl and Water together prove more esse & ual: Also, that the Ingress of Air betwixt the Brass Cover and the Ring may be likewise pre - vented, the Edges of both must with the former Cement, be carefully plastered, and fpreadon with a hot Iron, that it may run the better, and fill the little Cavities. Things being thus fitted, and the lower Shank ( O ) of the Stop - cock being put into the upper O - xifi. ee of the Cylinder, then the Handle being turned till the Sucker riles to the top of it, and shutting the Valve with the Plug, and turning the other way, the Sucker is drawn down to the Bot - tom; by which means the Air is driven out of the Cylinder, and a Succession from without be - ing prevented, the Cavity of the Cylinder must be emptied of Air; then if the Turn - cock be turned, so as to afford a Passage betwixt the Receiver and Cylinder, part of the Air contained in the Receiver, will descend into the Cylinder, and by turning back the Key, that may be prevented from flying back into the Receiver, and may also, by opening the Valve, and winding up the Suck - er, be forced into the open Air; and so by rite - rated Exfudions of the Air out of the Receiver, and Expulfions of it again out of the Cylinder, it may be exhausted as the Nature of the Experiment requires. When this Engine is seton work, these Pheno - mena are observed (. ) That the Sucker being wound up, and upon flopping the Valve, and turning the Key, drawn down again; the Air in both Vessels will be brought to an equal measure of Dilation; and upon returning the Key, and Opening the Valve, near a Cylinder full of Air will be expelled; but the Receiver by reiterated Exfudions, being more and more exhausted, less proportionably is forced out; so that at lead, before you need to open the Valve, the Sucker may be forced up almost to the Top of the Cy - hinder; and if, when it is so exhausted, you let go the Pump, the Valve being stopped, the Suck - er meerly by the Protrusion of the External Air, overpowering that more rarified Air within, will be forced up to the top of the Cylinder; where - by Vis observed, That as the Sucker is prefsd higher by the External Air, it shews the Receiver to be more or less exhausted; the Air in the Cy - hinder being accordingly more or less able to resist the External, as it varies in quantity. ’ Tis also observed. That whilst the Receiver retains any, considerable quantity of Air, there is a brisk noise immediately produced upon the turning of the Key. . Also, that when the Receiver is well ex - haunted, the Brass Key ( that is a Stopple to the Brass Cover ) cannot be lifted up without some di - fficulty, for it feels as if some great Weight were fastened to the Bottom of it: The Caule of this Phenomenon seems to be, That the Air in the Receiver being very much dilated, its Spring must be proportionably weakened, and coni equently the lower End of the Stopple is accordingly press ’ d up, whereas the Spring of the external Air is not at all weakened; so that a Strength to lift up the Stop - ple, must support a Pressure equal to the Difpro - portion betwixt the Force of the internal expanded Air, and that of the Atmofpbere incumbent upon the upper part of the Stopple: But ) if the Air be let into the Receiver by Degrees / the Weight that is fuppofedto keep the Stopple down, may be felt to decrease more and more, the internal Air by this recruit approaching more to an / Equilibrium with the External, till at last the Receiver being fill ’ d with Air again, the Stopple may be easily lifted up. Mr. Boyle, after some Years Experience, found it convenient to alter a little the Form of his first Air Pump into that which the annexed Figures represent: And the advantagious Differences be - tween this and the former Engine are as follow - eth. ( Vil Plate I. ) . The Cylinder is contrived to be placed with - in a Frame of Wood which is filled with Water, so that the Cylinder is always kept quite covered with it; by which means the Sucker is always kept Turgid and Plump, and the Water also fills up all the little Intervals or Spaces between the Sucker and the Bartel,, and by that means the Air is much more exactly excluded than in the former Engine. But here great Care must be taken in turning the Stop - cock, or else the Water will get into the Receiver, and spoil the Experiment. . Because in this Engine the Sucker is to be al - ways under Water. There is a Perforation P, ( See Plate II. ) which passes perpendicularly thro " it, and, together with the Stick RS, serves for a Valve, and is to bestow ’ d at the Bottom of the Cy - hinder NO, when it is full of Water; wherefore the Stick RS must be of a considerable length, as of or Foot. . The chief thing in this reformed Engine is ) that the Pipe A B ( Plate II. ) whose End B turns upwards, is made to lie in a Groove or Gutter hol - lowed purposely for it in the Board C D E F, on which the Receivers are to reft. This Board was covered covered with good Cement, and then on it was ap - plied a strong Plate of Iron of the bigness of the Board, having only a Hole in the Middle for the Mouth of the Pipe B to pass through; and this Plate he added, because he found that the Weight of the Atmolphefe would sometimes force the Air to penetrate through a thick Board, tho its Pores were also designedly filled with Oyl. The Edges of this Plate should be a little turned upward, to hold a little Water, which now and then will be apt to get into the Receiver. The Stop - cock, G HI R tho it may be soder - ed into the Cylinder at I, yet had better go on. with a Screw for then it may be more easily mended if it should hot prove right or stanch, and also will not be so apt to break off. Tis conve - tient also to have a little Cover of Tin, &c. to cutover the Nose of the Pipe B, to hinder things from falling into it, or injuring it, and to keep the cement out of it, when very small Receivers are used.., n There is this considerable Advantage m this Hat Board on which the Receiver is placed; that the Receiver needs no Stop - cock of its own, but is u - fualiy one entire piece of Glass in the form of aBell, or Cucurbit, f c. which will much better keep out the Air than if it were perforated, tho the Stop - cock should be never so good. Care must be taken to get a good Cement to fatten the Receivers to the Plate: That which the Honourable Mr. Boy / u fed was a well wrought mix - ture of equal parts of Bees - wax and Turpentine; tho in the Winter he found it best, to use little more of the Turpentine, and in the Summer a greater portion of Bees - wax. Here tis observable, That this double Engine is upon many occasions to be prefer ’ d before a single me ( that ’ s mov ’ d with the Foot ) for it doth not on - ly produce a double etfed, but performs it much more easily; for in these Engines, which are fur - ni & ed but with one Tube, whilst the Plugg is drawn out to evacuate the Pump, the whole Pillar of the Air, incumbent on the Plugg, is to be ele - vated by force; and again, when the Plugg returns back, it is also by force to be restrained, left it Should be too swiftly impel ’ d by the Air, and so break the Bottom of the Engine; but in thei zldouble Enginet, the Plyer of them is in a manner wholly free from that toil. For the Pluggs are easily lifted tip, in the first fu & ion; because the Air, immedi - ately derived from the Receiver R into the Pumps, jprefles the Pluggs downwards, almost as strongly as the external Air incumbent on the opposite Parts; and when the quantity of the internal Air is di - minish ’ d, it comes to pass, that the Plugg to be de - press ’ d, tends downward with so much the greater force, and so by means of the Cord GGG corn - calling the Pulley, draws the other Plugg upwards, and at the fame time hinders it from too much Velocity of descent; so that by this means both Pluggs at one and the fame time will be helpful to him that exercifeth the Pumps. This Engine is of great use in order to those Ex - periments which cannot be very well made but with velocity and Ipeed; seeing the Pluggs make but a small resistance, a Man may easily judge, that the two Pumps of this Engine may be plyed with greater ease and more Ipeed, than one Pump in a single Engine can. aisteterium.c: AISTETERIUM, the common Sensory, which Cartes would have placed in the Glandula Pinea - Ivs, but is now generally supposed to be about the beginning of the Medulla Oblongata in the Corpus Striatum.

ajutage.c: AJUTAGE, is the Spout for a Jets d'eau in a - ny Fountain: Mr. Marriott asserts, That an even polished round Hole in the End of the Pipe, will - give an higher Jet than either a Cylindrical or a Conick Adjutage; but of those the latter is the best.

alainbotany.c: ALA, in Botany, lignifies the Angle ( which ge - nerally is acute, and never greater than a Right one on the Fee ? Stalks of Plants, and is always tending upwards ) that either the Leaves or the Foot Stalks of Leaves make with the Stalk, or with any Branch of the Plant. Sometimes also tis taken for a little Branch, making an Angle after that manner with the Stalk.

alabastra.c: ALABASTRA, in a Plant, are those little green Leaves which compass in the Bottom of the Flower.

albafirma.c: ALBA FIRMA, in Land, is an Annual Rent in Money, payable to the Chief or Lord of any Hun - dred; and Spelman faith, ’ Tis called Alba because it is not paid according to the Custom f old Times in Corn ( which was call ’ d Blackmail ) but in Silver, or as they fay now in feme Parts of England, in White Money. There are Tenures of this Nature in Wefimorland, Part Inftitut. Sol..

albugineaoculi.c: ALBUGINEA OCULI, is a very thin white Coat or Tunic of the Eye, adhering to the Cornecr extending it felt beyond the Selerotick, even to the Circle of the Iris, but leaves a Hole forward for the opening of the Apple of the Eye. See Tu - nica Adnata: Tis by some Writers call ’ d Tunic A Conjunftiva.

albugineatestis.c: ALBUGINEA TESTIS, is the White Mem - brane immediately involving the Telle or Testi - cles

albugothepinandweb.c: ALBUGO, the Pin and Web, is a white Speck in the Horney Tunicleof the Eye, which hinders the Sight, and usually follows an Infkmation, Wound or Ulcer of that Part. Sometimes it ’ s taken for the Album Oculi, or White of the Eye; being that part where the Tunica Adnata or Albuginea adheres to the Sclerotica.

albumoculi.c: ALBUM OCULI, sometimes is taken for the fame with Albugo: But by Galen and Hippocrates is used for that Tunick of the Eye which is usually call ’ d, the Tunica Adnata; and by some Writers / - buginea Oculi: Which fee under those Words.

alcaicks.c: ALCAICKS, are a fort of Verles confiding of two Dactyls and two Trochees, as some will have it - but Fabricius faith, they consist of Feet, of which the first is a Spondee or Iambickjhe. second an Iambick ? the third a long Syllable, the fourth a Daftlye, the fifth a Da ft lye or Amphimacer; as these of Horace Vides ut altd fiat nive candidum Sorafte, neejamfufiineant onus.

alchymist.c: ALCHYMIST, is one that studies Alchymy; that is, that Sublimer Part of Chymijlry which teaches the Transmutation of Metals and the Philofoper ’ s Stone; according to the Cant of the Adeptists, who amuse the Ignorant and Unthinking with hard Words and Non - sense: For were it not for the Arabick. Particle Al, which they will needs have to be of wonderful vertue here, the word would fig - nisi no more then Chymijlry. Whose Derivation fee under that Word. This Study of Alchymy hath been rightly defined to be, Arsfme Arte, cujus principium eft mentire, medium labor are, & finis mendicare; That is, an Art without an Art, which begins with Lying, is continued with Toil and Labour, and at last end in Beggery. And so poor Penotus found ir, who after he had spent his whole Life and Fortune in this vain Study, died at last in an Alms - House at Tver don in Switzerland; and used to fay, he would recommend the Study of Alchymy to & mortal Enemy, whom he did not dare openly to attack.

alcoholaterm.c: ALCOHOL, a Term used by the Chymifts both for a very fine or impalpable Powder; and also for a very pure Spirit well edify ’ d or dephlegmated. Thus the highest edify ’ d Spirit of Wine is called Alcohol Vini. Hence to Alcoholize any thing, with them lignifies to subtilize; as when any thing is beaten to a very fine Powder, & V. How to make a tolerable true Alcohol or pure Spirit of Wine, see in Alcali ate Spirit of Wine.

alcoveinarchitecture.c: ALCOVE, in Architecture is a part of a Cham - ber separated by an Efirade or Partition made by Columns and other corresponding Ornaments, in which is placed a Bed of State, or sometimes Seats to entertain Company.

algebra.c: ALGEBRA; the wonderful Analytic k Art, or the Art of Equation. In Arabickfs called Al - giabr W ’ al - mokabala, from the former of which Words we call it Algebra; and it may be render ’ d, either the Art of Befit ut ion and Comparison, or the Art of Befolution and Equation. Lucas de Burgoi the most Ancient European Writer of Algebra we have, de - fines it Beftaurationis & Oppoftionis fcgula. The Italians gave it the Name of Bpgula Rci & Census; that is, the R le of the Boot and the Square, because they call the Root Rer, and the Square Census; and from Cofa in the, Italian Language, for Bps or the Root, comes the Word Cojfick,: For some Writers call the Powers of Numbers, as the Boot, the Square, Cube, &c, Cojfek. Numbers. Cardan calls it, and that very justly, Ars magna, J The great Art; following therein Lucas de Burgo, who stiles it in Italian, L ' Arte Maggiore. It was certainly of Old in use amongst the Greci - ans, but purposely concealed as a very great Se - cret. We have some Examples of it in Euclide, or at least in Then upon Euclide, who tells us, it was first communicated by Plato: There are also In - stances of this Art in Pappus; and we find the Ef - sects of it plainly in Archimedes, Apollonius, and some others, tho ’ studiously covered and disguised. The first Books among the Greeks, and, I believe, the only one that treats profeffedly of Algebra, is that of Diophanm: Published at first in Latin by Xy ladder, afterwards in Greeks and Latin by Bachet, with some things added of his own; and since him by Mr. Fermat, with some Additions of his likewise. But it certainly was in use among the Arabs more anciently than among the Greeks and they are fu poied to have had it from the Persons, and the Persons from the Indians. Thence, that is, from the Arabs, the Moors and Saracens brought it into Spain, from whence it came into England; and that before we knew any thing of Diophantus. The Use of the Numeral Figures, Mathematick Learning, and all our old Astronomy, came to uS likewifethe fame way from the fame Original, and about the fame time.... The first European Writer of Algebra ( as was hinted above ) is Lucas Pacciolus of Lucas de Burgo a Minorite Frier: His Book is in Italian, printed at Venice.. He makes mention of oneLeo - nardus P if anus aud leveral others, from whom he learn ’ d it, but we have none of their Writings, He says, this Aft came originally to us from the A - tabs, and makes no mention of Diophantus, who therefore ’ tis probable was not yet known here. His Algebra goes nb farther than Quadratick Equations, Next came out Stiphelius a good Author, but he also went not beyond Quadraticks. Blit Scipio Ferreus, Cardan, Tartctlea, and some others, proceeded to give a Solution of some Cu - back Equations. After this Bombelli went a little farther, and ( hew - ed how to resolve a Biquadratick Equation into two Quadratick ones, by the means of a Cubick. Then, in the Iaft Century, appeared Nonniui ( ' Nunne in Spanijh ) Bytmus, Schonerus, Saliguacus, Clavius, cc. who wrote on this Subject in various ways, but generally went ho farther than Quadratick Equations. About this time out came Diophantus, whole Method differs much from that of the Arabs, which others had hitherto followed. All this while, the known Quantities in any E equation, were designed only by the Numeral Let - ters, and there were no Symbols nor Marks but for those that were unknown of fought. But then came Vieta, A. D., nd introdu ced what he called his Specious Arithmetic k.; which is a way of giving Marks or Symbols to all the Quantities, both known and unknown; whereby a very short and conspicuous way of Notation was gained, the whole Operation exposed always to the Eye in a short Synopsis, and many Discoveries were made in Algebra, not before taken notice of. Vieta also introduced the Numeral Exegefs of adfeded Equations, l'hewing how to extract their Roots in Numbers. And in the Denomination of the Powers of Numbers, he follows Ditphantus, and not the Arabian manner used by others. The Incomparable Mr. Oughtred followed, and mightily improved the Specious Algebra of Vieta., in his Clavis Mathematica, first published: He also affeding Brevity, ( which indeed lie was a versed Master of, being short but not bfeure ) in - vented maii Compendious Characters or Ligatures to note the Sums, Differences, BpClangles, Squares GubeSj and theif Sum, Difference, cc, by which, means his little Book contains more excellent and useful Geometry, than many other large Volumes, Oughtred in his Clavis usually contents himself with the Solution of Quadraticks, rarely proceeding to those of higher Powers, because he designed it a an Introduction to Algebra only. The Famous Mr Harriott was Contemporary with Oughtred, but died before him; he left many good things behind him, of which nothing is yet published but his Analytice or Algebra, which Mr, Warner printed A. D.. From this great Man did Des Cartes borrow, not to fay steal, all the fa - mous things in his Geometry, which are purely Al - gebraical, as any one may fee, that will compare their Methods together: For ’ tis impossible but one must be copied after the other: But the Geo - metre of Des Cartes was not published in French till , the AJ. G - she Year, and not in Latin till the Year: Therefore he must have seen and copied Harriotts Book. Mr. Harriott did wonderfully improve ( in this Treatise ) that which is purely Algebra, in the sol - lowing Refpeds, and many others which I might mention. i. He brought in small Letters instead of the Capitals ufedby Viet a and Oughtred. x. He waved the Uncouth Terms of Quadrato - Cube, Sursolid, &c. explaining the Power plainly to the Eye, by only repeating the Root as often as the Index of the Power. . He hewed the true Original and Constitute - on of all Equations, by putting all the Equation o - yer to one side; and thereby making the whole equal to nothing; whereby also he determined the Number of Roots, which he hews are in Number, such as the Index of the highest Powers in the E - equation. . He discovers the true Conftru & ion of the Ab - solute Number ( the Homogeneum Comparationis ) in a Quadratick or Superiour Equation; hewing it to be the Product of the continual Multiplication of all the Roots. . The fame he doth also by the Co - efficients. . He shews the way to multiply the unknown Roots of an Equation according to any Proportion assigned, thereby freeing the Co - efficients from Fradions and Surds. . He hews howto reduce the adfeded Qua - dfaticks, to simple Equations, and all adfeded Cubicks to a Form easily solvable, by the means of destroying the second Term in such Equations: . He hews the Method ( and a very good one Vis / of solving all Adfeded Quadraticks by corn - pleading the Square. . He mightily also improves the Exegesis Na - tter of a, invented by Viet a. All these vast Improvements, and many more ( which, to avoid Prolixity, I omit ) did Des Cartes take from Harriott, without ever so much as na - king him, and publish them as his own. Tis true, in his Geometry there are abundance of excellent things about the accommodation of Algebra to Ge - metrical Proportions, and many very fine Geometrical EffeCtions andConfirudions; but this was not Harriott ’ s Business, who kept himself to pure Al - zebra only. As to which Des Caries hath added but one single Rule ( and even that is plainly deducible from Harriotts Principles ) over and above what is in Harriott; and that is, the Method of dissolving a Biquadratick Equation, whose second Term is wanting, into two Quadraticks, by means of a Cubick Equation of a plain Root; and this, after all, both Bombell and Vi eta had done before him. And thus leaving the French Plagiary, I come next to another of Our Country Algebraifts, Dr. Pell, who revised and altered a Piece of Algebra first publiflied in High Dutch, A, D., at Zorich; and after Translated into Englijh by Mr. Thomas Brancher, and printed Ah D., and called. An IntroduElion to Algebra: In which Dr. Pell gives us a peculiar Method of his own for applying Algebra to Problems of divers forts; and introduces a way of keeping a Begifter of the whole Process in the Margin. He Drews us also there how to judge whether a Problem be fully determined or not; which is by this Rule ( as Dr. Wallis interprets him ). If the Number of the Data, or things given in any pucjiion, be independent of each other ) sewer than the things fought, the Question is not fully determined, but is capable of innumerable Answers or Solutions. But if the Number of both Data and Quaefita be the fame, the Question is then determined to either tofome one, ortofome certain number of Solutions. And when the Data are more in number than the Quas ta, so many as exceed are always superfluous, and sometimes, it may be, are contrary to, or in - consistent with others, and consequently render the thing impossible. Dr. Pell also, besides the former Characters, in - produced this Mark - for Involution, and this cut for Evolution, as he calls it, i. e. for Squarings Cub - ing, &c. of any Quantity, and for Extracting the Square, Cube, &c. Roots out of any Quantity. He makes also the Mark - - to stand for Division, and Registers the several Steps of the whole Process by Numeral Figures in their Order in the little Co - lumn in the middle; keeping an account also in Symbols of the several Operations in the Column towards the Left Hand, that so you may fee how any Quantity or Equation in the large Column to - ’ wards the Right Hand is produced. In which ve - ry good Method he is follow ’ d by Mr. Ward, in his, small Treatise of Algebra.. Algebra is well enough divided into . Numeral or Vulgar; which was that of the Ancients, and served only to find the Solution o Arithmetical Problems, without any Demonftrati - on; such as those given us by Diophantus, cc. . Specious or New, called sometimes Logiftica Speciofa, and often Species alone; which since Vi eta hath been perform ’ d by the Letters of the Alphabet: And this way of Notation is very pleasing to the Mind, afllfting to the Imagination, and easy to the Memory. This also is no ways limited, like the former Algebra to any one certain kind of Problems, but serves equally for the Xnveftigation and Demon - station of all Theorems; especially if to those two you add the new Methods of . Fluxions; a large Account of which you will have under that Word. And the several Operations of Algebra, such as Addition, Subflr action, Multiplication, Division, Ex - traction of Boots, Fractions, Equations, & c. you will find Dire & ions how to perform under those several, Words.

alienasubject.c: ALIEN, a Subject born in a Foreign Country, who ( by our Common Law ) is not capable to in - merit Lands in England till Naturaliz d by Ad: of Parliament.

aliformesmusculi.c: ALIFORMES MUSCULI, Alares, Pterygoides, are Muscles arising from the Pterygoide Bones ( the Process of the Os Cuneiforme, partly with a Ner - vous Beginning, and partly Fleshy j and ending in the Neck of the lower Jaw, and towards the in - ternal Seat of the Head.

aliment.c: ALIMENT, is whatever serves to nourish, sup - ply the Decays of, and to recruit an Animal or Vegetable Body.
