This was recoverable in the Spiritual Court, but now only in Chancery. ALIQUOT PART of a Number, is such an one as will exactly measure it without any Remainder. But ah ALIQUANT PART, is that which cannot measure any Number exactly, but that some Re - mainder will be left. Thus is an Aliquot Part of a, because being taken times it will just mea - sure it; but is an Aliquant Part of ia, for being taken twice it falls ihort, and when taken three times it exceeds a.

alkahest.c: ALKAHEST; one of th, e Canting Terms of the Alchymijls, by which they intend an Universal Menjlruum that will dissolve all manner of Bodies; and by which they pretend to extract the Sulphur of Metals. Some Chymifts have given this mighty. Name to the TinBure, or Liquor of Flints, which is a Solution of them made ( after Calcination ) by the means of Salt of Tartar; and ' others to the Liquor of Fixt Nitre, which is Nitre calcined and fixed, by burning powder ’ d Coals with it, and at last run into a Deliquium, by being fet in a cool Cellar, as Oil of Tartar per Deliquium is made. Van Helmont calls this Liquor sometimes Ignis Ge - senna: He pretends to be Master of it himself, and Mr. Boyle is inclined to believe him. Helmont faith, it would dissolve all Bodies, without leaving any Caput Mortuum, and was as fit for a new Opera - tion after it had dissolved one kind of Body as at first; it would dissolve Metals, Marchafites, Stones, and even Glass it self when finely powdered. Tis found that the common Menjlruums, such as AquaFortis, Spirit of Nitre, See. when they have once dissolved any Metal, are render ’ d uncapable by it of any further service, having the Points or Edges of their Acids so broken, that they can hard - ly dissolve anymore of the the fame, or any other Metal. Therefore this Immortal Alkaefi had in this respect a wonderful Preheminence, if what they relate of it be true. And to shew that some - thing of this nature is possible, Mr. Boyle says, That he distill ’ d a Spirit from Verdigreafe, which would serve more than once as a Menjlruum to dissolve Bo - dies, or to draw Tinctures, and being drawn off was ready for the fame Operation anew. ALKALISATE SPIRIT OF WINE so Mr; Boyle calls a Spirit of that Liquor distill ’ d from Salt of Tartar, or Tartar calcined to Whiteness: And by so drawing off Spirit of Wine from that Salt, you may get easily a pure and rich dephlegmated Spi - rit ( vi. one that shall burn all away, and fire Gun - powder, ) after this manner; Put about an Inch thick of Tartar calcined white, into a Glass as long and slender as you can procure, and then put upon it Spirit of Wine that hath been once rectified, to a Fingers height above the Tartar, and fitting on a Head, draw the Spi - rit off in a very gentle Heat; or at least, lb much of it as you conclude, or find will come pure, and it will answer your Expectation at the first Diftilla - tion. The Tartar being dried and new calcined will serve again for a new Operation, If you can - not procure Tartar, Quick - lime, or the Salt of Pot - Ashes will do tolerably well, EjfayofVnfuc cefsfulnefs of Experiments.

alkaliachymicalword.c: ALKALI, a Chymical Word signifying the fixt Salt of any Plant and is so call ’ d, because the Herb called Kali, which is a kind of Sea - Blite t Glass - wort, or Sait - xvort, yields such a Salt in a great quantity. This fixt Salt of Plants ( which is made by burning the Plant, making a Lixivium or Lee of its Allies j and after filtrating the Lee, e - evaporating the Moisture over a gentle Heat, that the fixt Salt may remain at the bottom of the Ves - sel ) being render ’ d very Porous by the Fire s pass sing so often thro ’ it in its Calcination, and it ma be fixing there some of its Essential Salt: And be - cause very many of the fiery Particles do also stick in those Pores, it makes a very great Ebullition or Effervescence when any Acid Liquor is mingled with it, and from thence all Bodies that do, or are sup - pofedto ferment with Acids, are now always call a Alkalies or Alkalisate Bodies; not because they, must always contain any Hidden Alkali in them which some Chymifts assert as necessary to the Cause of Fermentation; but because they are of the Nature of Alkalies themselves, and have their Pores naturally so form ’ d, in such a proportion, as that they are fitted to be penetrated and put into a violent Motion by the Points of the Acid poured upon them. These fixt Salts of Plants are called Fixt Alkalies; but the Volatile Salts of Vegetables; because they will ferment with Acids, are calied Volatile Alkalies,

N.. hath obliged the World with a more perfect Discovery of the Human Allantois; and assign ’ d the Reasons why those who believed its Existence had not be - fore Fore fully found it out giving alfoan Answer to ? to the Objections of thole, who even still, deny its Reality.

alligation.c: ALLIGATION, is a Rule in Arithmetick ( so called from the Numbers being bound or connect - ed together by Circular Lines ) relating to the mix - ture of Merchandizes; as Corn, Wine, Metals, Medicines, &c. one with another; and to the Proportion of the Ingredients in any Quantity of, and the Price of such a Mixture. ' Tis distinguish ’ d into two kinds, vi. Alligation Medial and Alter - mate. Alligation Medial teaches how to find a Mean in the Price, Quantity or Quality between the Ex - treats; and all Cafes in it may be solved by these Propositions and Rules; . Having the Quantity of the Ingredients, and the particular Prices, to find the Price or Value of some part of the Mixture. Rule; Multiply the Ingredients severally by their own Prices, and Divide the Sum of those Produ & s by the Sum of the Ingredients, and the Quotient answers the Question. . Having the particular Prices of the Ingredi - ents, and the Sum paid or received for a Mixture bought or fold; to find what Quantity of each was bought or fold. Rule j Divide the Sum paid or received for the Mixture bought or fold, by the Sum of the parti - cular Prices, the Quotient gives what was requir - ed. I . Knowing the Ingredients of a Mixture, to augment or diminish the Mixture propordnally. Rule; Sum up the Ingredients; then fay, As that Sum is to the Augmentation or Diminution, so is the Quantity of each Parcel of the Mixture to she Quantity of the Mixture desired. . Knowing the Nature, Quality, or Fineness of she several Ingredients of a Mixture, to find the resulting Temperament or Fineness of the whole. / e Place the several Quantities of the Mix - ture in Rows, against which place orderly their several Qualities of Fineness, and multiply each Quantity by its own Quality or Degree office - siss, then as the Sum of all the Quantities is to the Produ & s of all the Quantities, so is Unity to the Qualitity or Fineness of Mixture. Example; There are melted and mixed toge - ther two kinds of Silver, one worth s. and the other worth. an Ounce, and there were Ounces of the former, and of the latter; what h ihe value of an Ounce of the Mixture ? Oun. /. Silva L : J. dj ’ ( . Knowing the Quantities of a Mixture, to find the particular Quantities of any Ingredient in any part of the Mixture. If the Mixture be compounded of but two things, then fay. As the Total of the Ingredients in the Composition, is to the part of the Mixture proposed: So is the Quantity of the Ingredient propofedin the whole Composition, to the Quanti - ty of the Ingredient in the Part desired. But if the Mixture be decompounded, then you must repeat your Work upon every Mix - ture. ' i " . Knowing the Total of a Mixture, with the Total Value, and the Values of the several Ingre - dents mixed, to find the several Quantities mixed, though unequally. Rule. Multiply the Total of the Mixture by the least Value; fubftradl the Product from the Total Value, and the Remainder is the first Dividends Then take the said least Value from the greatest valued Ingredient, and the Remainder is the first Divisor. The Quotient of this Division shews the Quantity of the highest Priz ’ d Ingredient, the o - ther is the Complement to the Whole: And when more Ingredients than two are in the Composition, the Divilors are the several Remains of the least Value taken from the other,, The Dividends are the Remains left upon the Divisions, till re - main there; which will be one fort f the number of Ingredients, and this defective Ingredient is to be supplied as a Complement; and in Division no more must be taken in every Quotient, than that there may remain enough for the other Divisors, and the last to leave nothing remaining. II. Alligation Alternate, ( hews the due proportion of every Ingredient entring the Mixture, anti counter - changes the Places of such Excesses or Differences as fall out between the Mean Price and the Extreames, ascribing it to the greater Extream which proceeds from the Lesser, and the contrary. Rule. Let every greater Extream be linked with one Lesser. . When either of the Extreams be single, and the other Extreams be plural, the single Extream must be linked to all the reft. . If both greater and lesser Extreams are not single, then they may be linked so diversly, that sundry Differences may be taken, and Diversities of Answers to the Question, yet all true: But if one of the Extreams be single, there can be but one Answer. . The Numbers being linked, take the Diffe - rence of each Number from the Mean or common Price, and place this Difference against the Number it is linked to alternately. . Every Number linked with more than one must have all the Differences of the Numbers it is linked to fet against it. . Those Differences relolve the Question, when the Price of every of the Ingredients is given with - out their Quantities, and the Demand be to mix them so as to fell a certain Quantity at a mean rate. . But when the Quantity of one, with the Price of all the Ingredients, is given, and the De - and All a LT and is to know the Quantities of the other In - gredients, then the Rule of Three is to be used. . And when the Price of every Ingredient is gi - ven, without any of their Quantities, and the De - and be to make up a certain Quantity to be fold at a mean Rate, then all the Differences added to - gether, shall be the first Number in the Rule of Three the whole Quantity to be mixed shall be the second Number; and each Difference apart the several third Numbers: And so many forts mix ’ d, so many Operations of the Rule of Three. . allioththename.c: ALLIOTH, the Name of a Star in the Tail of the great Bear, whose Observation is much used at Sea. The Elevation of the Pole or the Latitude may thus be easily found by this Star. Observe when AUiotfs comes to the Meridian un - der the Pole, then take the Height of the Pole - Star with a Quadrant, and out of that substract.. the Distance of the Pole - Star from the Pole, the Re - mainder is the Pole's Height, or the Latitude.

alliteration.c: ALLITERATION ( a Figure in Rhetoriek ) is a repeating and playing on the fame Letter.

allocationefacienda.c: ALLOCATIONE FACIENDA, is a Writ di - erected to the Lord Treasurer and Barons of the Exchequer, upon complaint of some Accountant, commanding them to allow him such Summs as he hath by vertue of his Office lawfully and rea - sorably expended.

allocationinlaw.c: ALLOCATION, in Law, is an Allowance made upon an Accompt.

allodiallmdsare.c: ALLODIAL Lmdsare those, for which noRents Fines, nor Services are due. Such as FreeLand.

allodiumalaw.c: ALLODIUM, a Law - term, signifying, every Man ’ s own Land, &c. which he possesseth meer - ly in his own Right, without acknowledgment of any Services, or payment of any Rent to another, which is a Property in the highest degree.

alloeticks.c: ALLOETICKS, are Medicines confiding chief - fly of Aloes.

allogotrophy.c: ALLOGOTROPHY, with some Writers, is a Disproportionate Nutrition of the Body; whenone part ( as in the Rickets ) is nourished more than the other,

alloy.c: ALLOY, is the Proportion of a Baser Metal min - gled with a Finer or Purer; as the Quantity of of Copper that is mingled with Gold to make it of a due hardness to be coined into; Money, is called its Allay: And Gold that hath more of this than it ought to have, is said to be of a Courser or Great - ter Alley. The Proportion of Alloy for Gold used in our Mints is about a th part.

almacantersstaff.c: ALMACANTERS STAFF, is an Instrument usually made of Pear - Tree or Box, with an Arch only of degrees, to take Observations of the Sun, about the times of its Riling and Setting, in order to find the Amplitude, and consequently the Variation of the Compass.

almonds.c: ALMONDS of the Throat or the Tonfillce a Glandulous Substance representing two Kernels placed on each side of the Vvula, at the Root of the Tongue. They are covered with the common Tunic of the Mouth, and have Veins and Arteries from the Carotides and Jugulars They are of a lax and spongy Substance, having several Sinus's within them, in which they contain theLiquor of the Saliva, which they receive from the Brain, and by. dispersing it to the Larynx, Jaws, Tongue, and Oe - fopagus, do moisten and lubricate those Parts. When these are swelled and inflamed by a Cold / &c ‘ they very much straiten the Passage of the Throat, and render Swallowing painful and di - fficult, and help to make what we call a fore Throat, and as the Country People fay, the coming down of the Almonds of the Ears.

alopecy.c: ALOPECY, is a shedding of the Hair, occ - signed by the Pox, or other wife: So called from a Fox ur & jts, whose, Urine is said to make places bald, and barren for a Year, as the Scholiast oa Callimachus observes; or from a Disease peculiar, to a Fox. It is called like wife osiacn -, from the Figure, because that the parts smooth and destitute of Hair, look winding like a Serpent, in Greek Its common to both these Distempers that the Hair fall of Areatim, i. e. by shedding, whence in general this Disease is called Area. Blanchard.

alphus.c: ALPHUS, is a Cuteaneous Distemper, in which the Skin is rough, and looks here and there as if there were Drops of a white Colour upon it: Some pall it Morpheve; it differs from the Leuce, in that it penetrates not so deep as the Leuce doth.

alramechastar.c: ALRAMECH, a Star ’ s Arabic f ' Name, which is the fame with Ar Slums.

alterage.c: ALTERAGE, or ALTARAGIUM, is a Word which includes not only the. Offerings made upon the Altar, but also the Frofit that arises to the Priest by reason of the Altar.

alteration.c: ALTERATION, is, in a Physical Sense, that Motion by which a Body is varied or changed in some Circumstances from what it really was be - fore, though as to Sense, its Nature and Bulk ap - pear to continue still the fame; so that it consists in the Body s acquiring orlofingfuch Qualities, as whether present or absent, do not essentially change the Subject: And herein it differs from Generation and Corruption, which Terms express the Acquifi - tion or Loss of the Essential Qualities of any Bo - dy. Or otherwise, i ALTERATION, is an Accidental and Partial Change made in any Body, without proceeding so far as to make the Subject be quite unknown, or to take anew Name or Denomination upon it: Or it may be called the Acquisition or Loss of such Qua - lities as are not Essential to the Form of any Body ALTERING REMEDIES; such Medicines as serve to purify and restore the due Mixture of Blood, and other circulating Humours, E ALTER; ALTERNATE PROPORTION: See the Word Proportion, N.. L ALTERNATE ALLIGATION: See Alliga - tion Alternate.

alternbase.c: ALTERN BASE, a Term in Trigonometry, di - ftinguifhed from the True Base, thus; In Oblique Triangles the True Base is always either the Sum of the Sides, ( and then the Difference of the Sides is called the A Item Be ) or the True Base is the Difference, and then the Sum of the Sides is call - ed the Altern Base.

alternation.c: ALTERNATION, is a Word ufedby Dr. Wal - lis, and others for the different Changes or Altera - tions of Order in any Number of things proposed. Of this that learned Mathematician hath a peculi - ar Discourse at the end of his Algebra. This Al - vernation is easily found, by only continual Multi - plication of all the Numbers beginning at Unity. Thus, if it were required to know how many Changes can be rung on fix Bells, you need only write down i,,,,,, and then multiply all those Numbers continually one into another, and the last Product gives the Number of Changes, which is Changes.

alto.c: ALTO & BASSO, for in Alto, & in Bajfo in Law signifies the absolute Submission of all Dis - ferences, small and great, high and low, to a Judge or Arbitrator.

alvearium.c: ALVEARIUM, is the Cavity of the inward Ear, near the Passage which - Conveys the Sound, where that yellow and bitter excrementitious Stuff is bred, call ’ d EarTVax.

amain.c: AMAIN; a word used at Sea when a Man of War giveth Defiance to another Ship, or biddeth her fir ike her Topfails or yield for to bid a Ship Strike Amain, is to order her to let fall her Top - fails.

amalgamateachymicalterm.c: AMALGAMATE, a Chymical Term signify - ing the mixing Quicksilver with some melted Me - tal: The Design of which is either to render the Metal fit to be extended on some Works, as in Gilding, I c. or else to reduce the Metal into a very subtile Powder. The Amalgama af Gold is thus made; Take a Dram of the Regule of Gold, beat it into very thin little Places, which heat in a Crucible Red hot in a strong Fire, then pour on it an Ounce of pure Quicksilver; stir the Matter with an Iron Rod, and when you find it beginning to raise a Fume, which will soon happen, cast it into an Earthen Pan filled with Water; it will co - agulate and be - come tradable. Wash it often to take away its Blackness, and pressing from it with your Fingers and in a Linen Cloth, that Mercury that remains ununited with the Gold. The Gold will retain a - bout thrice its weight of the Mercury. If you would reduce the Gold into Powder, put this Amalgam into a Crucible over a gentle Fire, and the March A MN ty will evaporate into the Air, and leave the Gold at the bottom in an impalpable Powder, which you may melt into its Form again; and if it should re - tain any Blackness from the Mercury, Oil of Tartar per Deliquium will fetch it oft. For Experiment fake, you may make a Lumi - nous Amalgama after this manner. Put into a long Vial i o. Grains of the Phosphorus made from Urine, and pour on it two Drachms of Oil of Afpike: The Glass must be large enough for two Thirds at Ieaft to remain empty. Heat it a little with a Candle, and the Phosphorus will dis - solve with an Ebullition: Whilst this Dissolution is making, pour into it half a Drachm of pure Quicksilver, shaking the Glass that the Matter may be Hir ’ d and mix ’ d. Yon will have an Amal - gam which will appear all of a Fire in the Dark; but it must, like the Phosphorus, be kept close Hop ’ d from Air, else it will soon be spoiled. If the Amalgam of Gold be design ’ d to be so hard, as to be fit to be powder ’ d, you must use three parts of the Metal, and z of Mercury; but if you would have it to soft as to spread, you must use parts of. Mercury to one of the other Metal.

amanses.c: AMANSES, abarbarous factitious Word which some of the canting Chymifts use for counterfeit Gems, and precious Stones.

amaurosis.c: AMAUROSIS, is a dimness of Sight, whether the ObjeCt be placed near or at distance; but so that no external Fault appear in the Eye, if you inspect it never so narrowly; the DefeCt consists in the Obstruction of the Optic Nerve: It is called also Gutta Serena. Blanchard.

ambages.c: AMBAGES, an idle Circumlocution, or vain connecting together of farfetch ’ d Words or Sayings, remote from the true'purpofe of the Speaker.

ambe.c: AMBE, is a superficial jutting out of the Bones: Also a Chyrurgeon ’ s Instrument, with which dis - jointed Bones are fet again.

ambidexter.c: AMBIDEXTER ( in Law ) signifies that Juror or Embraceor that takes Monies of both Parties for giving of his VerdiCt, for which he forfeits ten times as much as he taketh. And ordinarily, Ambidexter denotes that Man that can equally use both his Hands,

ambient.c: AMBIENT, encompassing round about: Thus the Bodies which happen to be placed round any other Body are called the Ambient, and often the Circum - Ambient Bodies; and the whole Body of the Air, because it encompasses all things on the Face of the Earth, is often by Physical Writers called, by way of Eminence, The Ambient.

ambit.c: AMBIT, of any Figure in Geometry, is the Perimeter, Circumference or Sum of all the Bound - ing or Encompassing Lines that include it.

ambligonialingeometry.c: AMBLIGONIAL, in Geometry, signifies Obtu - angular, or that the Sides of any Plane Figure make an Obtuse Angle one with another. Thus an Ambligonial Triangle is that which hath one Ob - use Angle.

amblyopia.c: AMBLYOPIA, is a dullness or dimness of Sight when the Object is not clearly discern ’ d at what distance soever placed, and proceeds from an im - perfeCt Obstruction of the Optick Nerves, a light Suffusion, want of Spirits, or groflhefs of the fame, &c. Some reckon kinds of Ambliopi a, Viz, My - pia, Presbytia, Nyttalopia, and Amaurosis: Which fee under those Words. Blanchard.

amblotigkmedicines.c: AMBLOTIGK Medicines, are such as Cause A - bortiom

ambuscadeaplace.c: AMBUSCADE, a Place where Soldiers hide themselves to surprise the Enemy.

amendment.c: AMENDMENT ( a Common - Law Term ) fig - nifying the Correction of an Error committed in a Process, and efpied before Judgment, but maybe amended by the Justices after Judgment; and if there be Error in giving Judgment, they may not amend it, but the Party is to put in his Writ of Error.

amercement.c: AMERCEMENT, ( a Term in Law ) is a Pe - nasty assess ’ d by the Peers, or Equals of the Party amerced, for an Offence done.

AMERCEMENT, Dr. Kennet, in the Glossary at the End of his Parochial Antiquities, strews that Amerciamentum is a Pecuniary Punishment impos ’ d upon Offenders a la mercie, at the Mercy of the Court; and therefore in our Law is frequently tail ’ d Miferi cordia, and there is this stated dise - rence between Fines and Amercements; Fines are Punishments certain and determin ’ d by some Sta - tute but Amercements are Arbitrary Impofitions proportion'd to the Fault, at the Discretion of the Court.

amercementroyal.c: AMERCEMENT ROYAL, is when a Sheriff, Coroner, or other such Officer of the King is a merced by the Justices for Abuse in his Office. ( Blunt makes this Difference between Amerce -, ments and Tines; that the latter, as taken for Pu nifhments, are Punishments certain, which grow expressly from some Statute; and Amercements are arbitrarily, imposed by Ajfeerors.

amethistinheraldry.c: AMETHIST, in Heraldry, is the Term for the Purple Colour in the Coat of a Nobleman; which in all Gentlemen ’ s Escutcheons below that Degree is called Purpure, and in those of Sovereign Prin - cos ' Mcycuyv

amitterelegemterr.c: AMITTERE LEGEM TERR, a Law Term, signifying to lose the Liberty of swearing in any Court, to become Infamous; the Puniffiment of a Champion overcome or yielding in a Fight, or in Battel, and the Jurors found Guilty in a Writ of Ataint, and of a Person outlawed.

amnesty.c: AMNESTY, is an A Cl of Oblivion j such as was granted at King Charles Restauration.

amnion.c: AMNION or AMNIOS, is the innermost Mem - brane with which the Kem in the Womb is most immediately covered, and with which the reft of the Secundines, the Chorion, and Allantois is eject - ed after the Birth; it is whiter and thinner than the Chorion '. It contains not only the Foetus, but the Nutritious Humour, whence the Fcetus by the Mouth and Throat fucks its Nourishment. It is outwardly cloathed with the Urinary Membrane and the Chorion, which sometimes stick so close to one another, that they can scarce be separate'd: Though it is not knit to the Chorion in any Place, save where the Umbilical Vessels pass through them both into the Placenta. It hath Vessels from the fame Origin as the Chorion. Before the Ovum is impregnated, this Membrane ( Contains a Limpid Liquor, out of which, after Impregnation, the Embryo is formed. In it ( says Gibson ) resides the Plaftick Power, and the Matter also out of which the first Lineamants of the Em - bro are drawn; but because its Liquor is so very little, there Tranfudes through this Membrane the Amnion, a part of the Nutritious Albugineous Humour which is contained in the Chorion, which it had imbibed out of the Vterus, and by the Juxta - Position or Addition of its Humour to und - fcernible Rudiments of the Embryo, it receives its Encrease, But though the Amnion have its additi - oval Nutritious Liquor at first only by Tranfudati - on, yet when the VmbilicalHeJfds and the Placenta are formed, it recedes it after another manner for then its Liquor at first being separated from the Mpther ’ s Arteries by the Placenta, and imbibed by the Umbilical Vein of the Foetus, it passes directly to its Heart, from whence, being driven out by the Aorta, it is set forth again, in good part, by the Umbilical Arteries, out of whose Cavities, be - ing plentifully dispersed through the Amnion, it if - A MU I xa & j. in i war nr ri, mir, TT nr n ww wmme EECTg ) t mca ai ats fuesintd its Cavity; just as the Juices which are far more gross and viscid than this, do sometimes critically, and often on taking a Purge, ouzes into the Intestines out of the Small Mouths of the Ar - teries: Indeed, here the Intervention of the Glands assists this Matter; but xis hoped some curious Person one time or other will discover, that there are such also in the Amnion.

amortise.c: AMORTISE ( a Term in Law ) is to alien Land or Tenements to any Coporation, Guild or Fraternity, and their Successors, which cannot be done without Licence of the King, and the Lord of the Mannor.

ampelite.c: AMPELITE ( in Agriculture ) is a kind of Black or Bituminous Earth, used about Vines, to make them thrive the better.

amphibologyagrammaticalfigure.c: AMPHIBOLOGY, a Grammatical Figure, when our Expredions seem to look one way, and are intended another.

amphiblestroides.c: AMPHIBLESTROIDES, or the Tunica Reti - na or H etiformis of the Eye, is a soft, white and slimy Substance; which is so named, because that being thrown in the Water it resembles a Net it shoots from the very Center of the Optick Nerve, and consists of the. Medullar Substance of it, and expanding it self over the Vitreous Humour, is ex - tended as far as the Ligamentum Ciliare, or the Ligaments of the Eye - lids: This Tunic, in that it is whitifti and of a marrowy Substance, seems to proceed from the very marrowy and fibrous Sub - stance of the Optick Nerve; so that it is, as it were, an Expansion of Nervous Fibres, which are there gathered in to one Bundle, into a Contexture made like a Net; and indeed if the whole Eye were ta - ken for a Flower, growing, as it were, to the Brain by the Stalk of the Optick Nerve, the Tunica Retina would be the very Flower it self, and the two other Tunicles, the Sclerotica and Choroides, be only in the nature of a Stem. This Tunick seems to be the principal Organ of Sight, & receives the visible Species within the Bed of the Eye much after the fame manner as a whited Wall, or apiece of white Paper in a darkened Chamber, receives and represents the visible Species which are intro - mitted through a little Hole. See Camera Obscura.

amphibrachys.c: AMPHIBRACHYS, is the Foot of a Latin Verse consisting of three Syllables, where the two Ex - treats are ihort, and the Middle long, as Amare.

amphibranchia.c: AMPHIBRANCHIA, are places about the Glandules in the Jaws, which moisten the Afepera Arteria and Stomach.

amphibious.c: AMPHIBIOUS, is used for an Animal that lives both on Land and in the Water, as an Otter, Beaver, Sec.

amphimacer.c: AMPHIMACER, is he Foot of a Latin Verse, consisting of three Syllables; the two Extreams long, and the Middle Ihort j as Caflitas. AMPHIDiEUM, with fame Writers is the Sum - mit or Top of the Mouth of the Womb. Blan - chard,

amphiprostyleaterminarchitecture.c: AMPHIPROSTYLE, a Term in Architecture for a kind of Temple of the Ancients, which had four Columns in the Front, and as many in the Face behind.

amphiscii.c: AMPHISCII; so the Inhabitants of the Tor id One are called in reSpetft of their Shadows; be - cause their Shadows fall both ways, vi. to the South ( as ours always do to the Northward ) when the Sun is beyond them in Northern Signs, and to the North when the Sun is to the Southward of them in Southern Signs.

amphismela.c: AMPHISMELA, is an Anatomical Instrument used in the Diffecftion of Bones.

amphitheater.c: AMPHITHEATER, is a place built for Adfcing; and seeing of publick Spectacles and Stage - Plays s The Common Theatre was but semicircular, but this was built entirely round, or in form of a per - sect Circle. '

ampliation.c: AMPLIATION ( in Law ) signifies a defferingof Judgment till the CaufeTe further examined.

amputation.c: AMPUTATION, is the Surgeon ’ s Term for the cutting off any Member of the Body.

AMUNITION - BREAD, in an Army, is that which is provided for and distributed to the Soul - diers.

amy.c: AMY ( is a Law Term ) Signifying the next to be trusted for an Orphan or Infant.

amygdalateinpharmacy.c: AMYGDALATE, in Pharmacy, is an Artifici - al Milk, or Emulsion made of blanch ’ d Almonds, &c. AMYGDALAE: See Tonfill.

analysisapcfolution.c: ANALYSIS, a Pcfolution of any thing into its component Principles: Thus a Chymist is said to Analyse Bodies, when he diffolves them by the Fire, and endeavours to find out their Constituent Farts: And Algebra is sometimes called the Ana - lytick Art, because it teaches us to solve Quefti - ons, and to demonstrate Theorems, by enquiring into the Bottom, into the Fundamental Constitute - on and Nature of the Thing, which is, as it were, resolved into its Parts taken all to Pieces, and then put together again, that so we may fee into the Reason and Nature of it. And in this Sense Analytical Demonstrations are opposed to Synthetical ones, which fee. The Ancients had some Knowledge of this Art, but kept it concealed; whose Invention The ascribes to Plato, and he de - fined it ( according as Vi eta renders it ) Ajfumpti Qucejiti tanquam co ? iccJJi, per conftequentia ad verum concejjum; a taking of that as granted, or cones - fed which is enquired after, and thence going back by Confcquences to wh t is confessedly true.

Our famous Butler makes his Impertinent Heroeand Scholar Hudibras be profoundcdly skill'd in Anaiytick. anarchy.c: ANARCHY, wants all Government in a And tion where there is no Supreme Authority lodged m either Prince or Rulers; but the People live without any Rule or Government at all, and all things are in the utrnoft Confusion,

anasarcha.c: ANASARCHA, is a white, soft, yielding Tu mourof rhe whole outward Body, or of some of its Parts, which dents in by compressing the Flesh - it is caused by the Blood upon a double account; first, when it doth not rightly sanguify or affimi - late the Chyle; and again, when it is not right - ' ly accended in the Lungs; the Blood thus pervert - ed, pours forth the Serum at the Extremities of the ’ Arteries in greater quantities than it can receive and reduce by the Veins and Lymphedu & s, or ex - pell by the Veins and Pores, and other Passages that fend it forth. If the Humours be too vifeous, it is called Leucophlegmatia. Blanchard.

anastomapique.c: ANASTOMA PIQUE, ( Medicines ) are such as open and dilate the Orifices of the Vessels, and by that means help to make the Blood circulate freely, and pass easily out of the Arteries into the Veins.

anastomosis.c: ANASTOMOSIS, is an Effluxion of the Blood, the Lympha or Chyle, at the meeting of Vessels that close not narrowly: It is also taken for the mutual opening of Veins and Arteries into one another;

anatocism.c: ANATOCISM, is the annual Increase or Inte - real of Money, whether Simple or Compound. And under it, they also comprehend the Valuation of Annuities. See I interest '.

anatomy.c: ANATOMY, is an artificial DifTedion of an Animal, especially Man, whereby the Parts are leverally discovered and explained, for the use of Physick and Natural Philosophy; and he that is skilful in this Art, is called an Anatomifl.

anchile.c: ANCHILE, is the back part of the Knee; alto the Contradion of a Joint, especially of the Ham.

(. ) The Stock., a Piece of Wood fa - ttened unto the Beam near the Ring, serving to guide the Fluke, so that it may fall right, and fix in the Ground. They fay an Anchor is foul, when by the turning about of the Ship, the Cable is hitched about the Fluke. The Shank of an Anchor is to be times the length of one of its Flukes; and a Ship of Tun hath her Sheet Anchor of Weight; and so proportionably for others sailer or greater.

anchoringoranchorage.c: ANCHORING, or Anchorage, is Ground fit - ting to hold a Ship ’ s Anchor, that so Hie may ride k out safely: The belt Anchoring Ground is stiff Clay or hard Sand; and the best riding at an An - chor, is when a Ship is Landlockj, and out of ihe Tide.

anchorage.c: ANCHORAGE, fin Law ) is a Duty taken of Ships for the Pool of the Haven where they call Anchor; for no Man can let any Anchor fall on ‘ the King ’ s Ground in any Port, without paying for it to the King ’ s Officer appointed by Patent.

ancient.c: ANCIENT, is the Flag or Streamer in the Stern of a Ship.

ancon.c: ANCON, is the Top or Point of the Elbow, and is taken also sometimes for the backward and larger hooting forth of the Vim.

aneurism.c: ANEURISM, is a Disease which is a kind of Dilatation or bursting of the Arteries, always beating, and swelling sometimes to the bigness of an Egg, which yields if you compress it, but re - coils presently. The moll Accurate and Learned Dr. Tyfon found in his Anatomy of theTajacu or Afer Me xicanus, several AneUrifmata in the Aorta or great Artery, which it seems were natural, and which he never saw before in the Arteries of any other Animal: Though Malpighius, as he observes, took notice of such in the Aorta of Silk - worms.

angariaaterminlaw.c: ANGARIA, a Term in Law, signifying any troublesome or vexatious Duty or Service paid by the Tenant to the Lord.

angleingeometry.c: ANGLE, in Geometry, is either Plane or Solid. A Plane Angle is the Inclination, Aperture or Distance between two Lines meeting in a Point, and Which, when the Lines forming it ( which are F call AN G tailed its Legs ) are Right or Strait tones, is called a Right Lined or Rectilineal Angle, as B; but when the Legs are crooked Lines, tis called a Curvilineal Angle, as A; and when one Leg is ( trait and the other crooked, ns called a Mi xt An - gle, as C. An Angle is usually marked with Letters ( efpe - cially if there be more Angles than one at the fame Point ) whereof the middle Letter, which is al - ways placed at the Angular Point where the Lines meet, denotes the Angle. The Quantity, i. e. the Greatness or Smallness of an Angle, is by no means measured by the Length of its Legs, but by their Distance from, or In - clination to each other. Thus the Angle B is less than A, though the Legs of B are much longer than those of A, but then those of B are more inclined to each other, than the Legs of the An - gle A. Which, to conceive the better, imagine ' the Angle A to be laid upon B, as the prick ’ d Lines about B do represent; then ’ tis plain, the Angle B will easily be contained within A; and therefore is less than A, because its Legs come nearer, or are more inclined towards each other, than those of A; and consequently A will be a greater Angle than B, because its Legs are farther distant from each other than the Legs of B. If you imagine the Legs to open and fliut like those of a Joint Rule, or a Pair of Compasses, the thing Will be very plain. The Quantity of any Angle is measured by the Number of Degrees of the Ark of a Circle inter - cepted between the Legs of the Angle, whose Center is the Angular Point. Thus the Ark a b is the Measure of the Angle a e b; and if that Ark contain Degrees, the Angle is laid to be an An - gle of Degrees. A RECTILINEAL ANGLE is of forts. . Right, when one Leg of the Angle Hands exa & ly upright, or perpendicularly on the other, as pc doth on cb and enclines no more one way than it doth another. antartickcircles.c: ANTARTICK CIRCLES: See Polar Circle s. ANTARTHRITIC MEDICINES, are such as are used against the Gout.

antasthmatickmedicines.c: ANTASTHMATICK MEDICINES, are such as are used against the Ajlhma. antecedent.c: ANTECEDENT, fin Logick ) is the first of the two Propositions in an Enthymema, as the lat - ter is called the Consequent.

antecedentinmathematicks.c: ANTECEDENT, in Mathematicks, is the former of twoTermsin Proportion, or that which is compared with the other; thus, if the Proper - tion were of A to B, A is said to be the Ante - cement.

antesinarchitecture.c: ANTES, in Architecture, are Square Pilasters which the Ancients used to place at the Corners of the Walls of their Temples.

antestature.c: ANTESTATURE, is a small Retrenchment made of Pallifadoes, or Sacks of Earth fet up ia haste to dispute with the Enemy the remainder of a Piece - ANT - Piece of Ground, part whereof hath been already

anthelix.c: ANTHELIX, ' is the Protuberance of the Ear, or the inward Brink of the outward Ear, being a Semicircle within the Helix, and almost parallel to it.

anthelminticks.c: ANTHELMINTICKS, are such Medicines as destroy Worms.

antherje.c: ANTHERJE, are those little Tops or Knobs which grow on the Tops of the Stamina ol Flow - ers, and are oftner called Apices: Which fee. Mr. Ray Englifties them Chives,.

anthology.c: ANTHOLOGY, is a Discourse or a Treatise of Flowers, or the Art of a true Florist. ANTHRACOSEs OCULI, isacorrofivefcaly Ulcer in the Eye, attended with a general Tumour, cfpeeially of the Parts about the Eye.

anthraxcarho.c: ANTHRAX, Carho, Prune, or Carhunculus, is defined to be a Tumour that arises in several Pla - ces, surrounded with hot, fiery, and most sharp Pimples, accompanied with acute Pains, but with - out ever being separated; and when it spreads it self farther, it burns the Flefli, throws off Lobes when it is rotten, and leaves an Ulcer behind it, as if it had been burnt in with an Iron, Blan - chard...

antias.c: ANTIAS, in the plural Antiades, are the Glands called the T onfills or the Bimonds of the Ears. ANTIAPHRODIlICKS, are Medicines that lay Lust.

antiasiaticks.c: ANTI ASIATIC KS, Remedies against short - ness of Breath.

antibachius.c: ANTIBACHIUS, isa Latin Verse whose Foot con lilts of three Syllables, the two first long, and. the last Ihort.,...

antcardium.c: ANT CARDIUM, the fame with Scrohiculus Cordis. AN TICTHONES, the fame with Antipodes.

antcks.c: ANT CKS, in Architecture, are certain carv - ed Works representing divers odd Shapes of Men, Beasts, Birds, Fifties, Flowers, c. which being rudely determin ’ d and form ’ d one out of another, serve as an Ornament to the whole Fabriek, and afford a grateful variety to the Eye of the Behold - er.

antidiluvian.c: ANTIDILUVIAN, is whatever was before Noah's Flood: Thus those Generations from Adam which were before the Flood, are called the Antidiluvians, as those finee descended from Noah are called the Pott Diluvians. The Earth that then was before it was destroyed by the Flood, and which the Ingenious and Learned Dr. Tho. Burnet conceives to have been very different from ours in Form, Constitution, Figure and Situation, is call - ed the Antidiluvian Earth. But Dr. Woodward in his Natural History of the Earth, undertakes to prove from a Series of Ob - fervations carefully made, i. That the Face of the Earth before the Deluge was not as the Theorist imagines, Smooth, Even, and Uniform, but as it is now. Unequal distil - guifhed into Mountains, Valleys and Plains; as al - io having a Sea, Lakes and Rivers. x. That this Sea was Salt as. ours is, agitated hy Tides, replenished with Fishes of all kinds, and that the Ocean then was nearly of the fame Extent, and possess ’ d an equal ftiare of the Globe with the present one. . That the Antidiluvian Earth was fleck ’ d with Vegetables and Animals on all sides and in all Parts of it quite round the Globe had both Me - tals and Minerals in it; had the fame Position in respect ot the Sun which ours now hath, its Axis being not parallel, but incline ’ d as at present, to the Plane of the Ecliptick; and consequently there were then the fame Succeilion of Heat and Cold, Wet and Dry, and the fame Vicissitudes of Sea - sons, Spring, Summer, Autumn and Winter, a there, are now.,

antidoteamedicine.c: ANTIDOTE, a Medicine against deadly Pol - fon.

antepilepticks.c: ANT EPILEPTICKS, are Remedies against the Falling - sickness.

ant.c: ANT I - HECTICUM POTERII, or Jupiter ’ s Diaphoretic k., is a Chymical Medicine made by the mixture of T in, the Martial Regulus of Antimts - ny, and fixed by Salt - Peter. See the Operation in Letnrkery s Chym. iil. ry, Iaft Edit. P.. AN - TIHYPNOTICKS, Medicines that drive away Sleep., -

anti.c: ANTI - HYPOCHONDRlACKS, are Medicines used against the HypochondriacI Melancholly
ANTI - LOGARITHM, the Complement of the Logarithm of any Sine, Tangent, or Secunt to Deg.
ANTI - LOGY; is a Contradiction between any Words or Passages in any Author.

ANTI - ME i RICAL, is whatever, is, contrary to the Nature and Order of Metre or Verse ANTIMONIUM DIAPHORETICUM, is made of one part of Antimony and of Salt - Peter, powdered and mixed together, and thrown Spoon - ful by Spoonful into a Red hot Crucible, a Deto - nation will follow each Spoonful; when all is put in, continue a great Fire about the Crucible so about two Hours; then throw the white Matter into an Earthen Vessel of fair Water, and leave it steeping warm for about two Hours, that all the Salt - Peter may be dissolved; then pour off the Li - quor gently, and wash several times the white Powder at the Bottom; which is the Calx of Anti - many, or AntimoniumDiaphoreticum. Some use it as a Diaphoretic but Lemery faith, he could never find it would, raise a Sweat., - ANTIMONIUM MEDICAMENTOSUM; is a Preparation. confiding of Ounces of Antimo ny, Ounce of Salt of Tartar, and Ounces of Salt - Peter fluxed together into a Regulus, which is afterwards powdered and wash ’ d;,, ANTIMONIUM RESUSCITATUM, is made of equal Parts of Antimony and Sal Armoni - aci sublimed together three times; then the Subli - mate is waste ’ d with distill ’ d Vinegar warm to get out the Salts.,

ANTI - iECI, are such Inhabitants of the Earth as dwell one against another in the fame Semi - circle of the fame Meridian, and in the fame De - r gtee gree of Latitude, but one North, the other South. These have Noon and Midnight at the fame time, but the Seasons of the Year are contrary; as when the Northern Anti act have their Summer, the Southern have Winter, cc. In one Word, they live under the fame Meridian, but opposite Parallels.

antinephritic.c: ANTINEPHRITIC, is a Medicine good, a - gainst the Stone.

antinomasy.c: ANTINOMASY; is a Figure in Grammar, or rather Rhetorick, whereby an Appellative is used instead of a proper Name; as the Philosopher in - Head cf Aristotle, cc. and whatever is thus deli - vered or spoken, is said to be To delivered or so - ken Ant onomaflic ally. /

antinomy.c: ANTINOMY, is a Contradiction between two ' Laws.

antepagments.c: ANTEPAGMENTS, ( in Architecture ) are the Garnifliing of Polls or Pillars.

antipasis.c: ANTIPASIS, the fame with the Revulsion of a Disease, when the Humours flowing into some one Part, are turned back again, and forced to take some other Course

antiperistasis.c: ANTIPERISTASIS, according to the Peripa - teticks, is a certain Invigoration of the Internal Heat of any Body, by its being environed all round with Cold. They instance in Lime grow - ing hot on the EiFufion of cold Water, ( c.

antipfristaltick.c: ANTIPFRISTALTICK, is a Motion by which the Excrements of the Guts are carded upwards instead of downwards, which is the usual and na - tural Peristaltick. Motion. See that Word.

antipharmacum.c: ANTIPHARMACUM, the fame with Anti - dote, is a Medicine that expels Poison. ANTIPHRASlS, a figurative Speech, having a contrary meaning to what it carries in appear - ranCe.

antipilepticks.c: ANTIPILEPTICKS, are Medicines against the Falling - Sickness.

antipodes.c: ANTIPODES, are such Inhabitants of the Earth as live diametrically opposite to one another, that is, in Parallels of Latitude equally distant from the Equator, but one North, the other South; and under the fame Meridian, though i o. or just half of that Meridian distant from one ano - ther.

antipraedicamentsinlogick.c: ANTIPRAEDICAMENTS, in Logick, are such Notions as are previously necessary to under - stand the Do & rine of the Predicaments; such as the Definitions of Univocal, Equivocal, and De - nominative Terms, ( c.

antiptosisafigureingrammar.c: ANTIPTOSIS, a Figure in Grammar, wherein one Case is put for another. AN TISCII, is a Term in Geography, signify - ing such Inhabitants of the Earth as live in two Places opposite to one another, one on the North, the other On the South Side of the / Equator; so that their Shadows at Noon fall different ways, one direCtly opposite to the other.

antistrophe.c: ANTISTROPHE, is a Figure in Grammar, whereby two Terms of things which are mutual - ly independant one upon another, or reciprocally converted; as if one should fay, the Mailer of the Servant, and the Servant of the Mailer.

antithenar.c: ANTITHENAR, one of the Muscles that ex - tends the Thumb.

antithesisinrhetorick.c: ANTITHESIS, in Rhetorick, is a setting two things by way of Opposition one against another, that so the Excellence of one, and the Evil and the Folly of the other may the better appear.

antitragus.c: ANTITRAGUS, a little Prominence at the lower end of ' the Antihelix, feared opposite to the Tragus, whence it has its Name.

antaeci.c: ANTAECI, the fame with Anticeci, which fee.

antonomasia.c: ANTONOMASIA, ( a Trope in Rhetorick ) is when the proper Name of one thing is applied to several others; or on the contrary, the Name of leveral things to one. By this T rope we call any Voluptuous Person a Sardanapalus, and any Cruel Person a Nero, for the one was a Voluptuous King, and the other a Cruel Emperour: Or when we fay, the Philofo - her has prov ’ d it in his Metaphyficky; The Orator gives this Precept in his Rjpetorick,; we mean Ari - stote and Cicero.

anus.c: ANUS, is the Extremity of the Intejlinum Re - ft um; it consists of three Muscles, two called the Levatores, which distend and open the Anus in or - der to discharge the Excrements; and one called the SphMfter, which Ihuts stand keeps its. There is alfcf a Cavity in the Brain called Anus, which arises from the four Trunks of the Spinal Marrow; and by some the Skin which goes over the Navel,, in aged Persons becoming wrinkled, is called Anus.

aorta.c: AORTA, or great Artery, so called because it is the greatest Artery in the whole Body, from which all others ( except the Pulmonary ) are derived: It rises immediately out of the left Ventricle of the Heart, and at its rife hath three Valves, which have the fame Use and Figure as the Semilunares in the Artena Pulmonaria. As soon as the Aorta comes out of the Heart, it ascends a little upwards, and then turns downwards to form the descending Trunk, because the Blood might offend the brain, if it ran With that impetuosity with which it ’ s thrown out of the Heart; and from the upper side of this turning, the Cervical and Axillary Vessels do arise: By this Artifice, as the Blood collides against the sides of the Aorta, its force is broken, ' part of it is taken in by the Mouth of the ascend - ing Branches, but its greatest part is dire & ed down - wards. At the rife of the Coronaria out of the Aorta, there is a Valve placed that permits the Blood to flow out of the great Artery into them, but hinders its reflux. When it has pierced the Pericardium and bended a little Arch - ways back - wards, it is divided into two Trunks, whereof the one is called Truncus Afcendens, the other Be - feendens. The Aorta hath four Tunicas, a Nervous, a Glan - dulous, a Muscular, and a Membranous one, which is the Internal. See Arteries. m APAGOGICAL DEMONSTRATIONS are such as do not prove the thing diredlly; but shew the impossibility and absurdity which arises from denying it; and therefore ’ tis usually called l ed - tio ad impojfibile, vel ad Abfurdum.

apathy.c: APATHY, is an utter want of Pafilon.

apepsie.c: APEPSIE, bad Digestion or rawness of Sto mach, when there is no good Concodlion of the Aliments.

aperienspalpebramrectus.c: APERIENS PALPEBRAM RECTUS, is a Muscle so called from its streight Progress and Use. It arises harp and fleftiy from the profoundeft Part of the Orbit, near the Place where the Optick Nerve is transmitted,. passing diredlly over the Musculus Attollens, it becomes Tendinous as it marches over the Bulb of the Eye, whence growing still broader and thinner, till it is insert - ed to the whole superiour part of the upper Eye - lid.

aperitivemedicines.c: APERITIVE MEDICINES, orfuch as open the obftrudled Passages in the small Vessels, Glands or Pores, and by that means promote a due Circu - lation of the contained Juices.

aperturafeudi.c: APERTURA FEUDI, a Term in the Civil - Law, signifying the loss of a Feudal Tenure by Default Feud was Default of Iffiie of him to whom the soft granted or given.

aperture.c: APERTURE, in some Writers of Geometry is the Inclination of one Right Line to another which meet in a Point and form an Angle. And - ns lo called, because the Angle is the opening of the Legs of the Angle, like those of a Joint Rule.

apertureinopticks.c: APERTURE, in Opticks, is the Hole next to the Obied Glass of a Telescope or Microscope, through which the Light and Image of the Object comes into the Tube, and thence is carried to the Bye Mr. Au out faith, he found that the Aper - tures of Telescopes, ought to be nearly in a Sub - duplicate Proportion of their Lengths. The visible Area of an Object, is not encreased or diminished by the greater or lesser Aperture of the Object Glass; all that is effeded thereby, is the admittance of more or leis Rays, and cone - quently the more bright or obscure appearance of the Object. When you look at Venus through a Telescope, you mu ft use a much less Aperture ? than for the Moon, Jupiter or Saturn, because her Light is so vivid and glaring.

apetalousflowersorplants.c: APETALOUS Flowers or Plants, are by the Botanists accounted such as want: the fine coloured Leaved of Flowers which they call Pet la: Thele Flowers are otherwise called Stamineous, and are justly reckoned ImperfeEl.

apex.c: APEX, is the top, point, uppermost or lharpeit part of anything. APHiERESIS, in Grammar, is that Figure which takes away a Letter or a Syllable from the beginning of a Word. In Surgery, is that part which teaches to take a - way Superfluities.

apheliumoraphelion.c: APHELIUM, or Aphelion, or Auge in the Co - pernican Hypothefu, is that point or the Earth s, or any other Planet's Orbit, in which it is thefartheft distant from the Sun that it can ever be; and when tis at its nearest distance, it is said to be in its Pe - rihelion.. Sr. Isaac Newton proves the Aphelia of the planets well as the Nodes to be at reft, Prop.. Bool. In Philof. Trans. N.. is a Arid Geometrical Method for finding the Aphelia of the Planets by Mr. Halley.

aphorism.c: APHORISM, is in a general Rule, or eminent but short Observation, experienced for a Truth in any Art, or relating to Practice.

apices.c: APICES, of a Flower, are those little Knobs that grow on the Tops of the Stamina, jin the middle of the Flower: They are commonly of a dark purplish Colour. By the Microscope they have been discovered to be, as it were, a fort of Capsul a Seminales or Seed Vessels containing in them small Globular, and often Oval Particles, of various Colours, and esequifitely formed, as I have often with Admiration observed my self: In the Plant called Germanium pobertianum or Herb Pp - heroi these Apices are of a deep purple Colour, and the Pulvifcular Matter within of a glorious Yellow j they are exquisitely Spherical, and af - ford a very plealant Profped in the Glass. What the Use of these so finely elaborated Par - titles is, is not yet, that I know of, discovered Some have guessed it to be a kind of Male - Sperm t which falling down into the Flower,. they will have to help, fecundate and ripen the Seed j but this I rake to be a meer Fancy,

apnoeaadepravationanddiminution.c: APNOEA, a Depravation and Diminution, or an entire Suppression of. Breathing,: at least to Sense, as it happens in Swoonings, Fits of the Mother, and strong Apoplexies.

apochylisma.c: APOCHYLISMA, is any Juice boiled and thickened with Honey or Sugar into a kind of hard Confidence. This is called also Pp. pubabv and Sue cage.

apocopeafigureingrammar.c: APOCOPE, a Figure in Grammar, wherein the last Letter of a Word or Syllable is cut off. . APOCROUSTICKSj are ( ' according to some Physicians ) such Medicines as hinder the Influx of the Humours to any particular part of the Bo - dy, and reject those which are beginning to flow thither.

apodicticalargumentorsyllogism.c: APODICTICAL Argument or Syllogism, figni - fies a plain Proof or Demonstration of a thing.

apodioxisafigureinrhetorick.c: APODIOXIS, a Figure in Rhetorick, wherein any Argument or Objection is with Indignation rejected as absurd.

apogee.c: APOGEE or APOGiEUM, in Astronomy, is the farthest distance that any Planet can be at from the Earth in its whole Revolution as Peri - gaum is its nearest distance. How to find both Apogaum and Perigaum see the Geometrical Method of Caffini, with some Considerations upon it by Mr. Mercator, in Philof Trans. N..

APOGEE of the Ejuant, is. the farthest di - stance of it from the Earth, or that Point where the Circumference of the Equant is interfered by the Linea Apfidum in the remotest part of the Dia - meter as the Perigee of the Equant is the oppo site Point of the nearest part of the Diameters The Mean
APOGEE of the Epicicle, is a Point where the Epicicle is cut above by a Right Line drawn from its Center to the Center of the Equant, or the Point of the Epicicle most remote from the Earth.

apologetical.c: APOLOGETICAL, is what is said or written by way of Excuse or Apology for any Adfion.

apologue.c: APOLOGUE, is an instructive Fable, like those of Also.

apomecometrie.c: APOMECOMETRIE, is an Art teaching the Pradtifer how to measure things at a Distance, vi how far they are off from Him.

aponeurosis.c: APONEUROSIS, is ( with Anatomists ) ' the spreading or extension of a Nerve, or a Tendon out in Breadth, in the manner of a Membrane: Also the cutting off a Nerve or Tendon is so called.

aporeinmathematicks.c: APORE, in Mathematicks, is a Problem which though it be not impossible, yer is very difficult to be resolved j and hath not yet actually been so Thus the Quadrature of the Circle may be called an Apbre, because there is yet no Way or Path di - severed to lead us into it.

apophlegmaticalmedicines.c: APOPHLEGMATICAL Medicines, are such as are endowed with the Faculty of drawing cold G ' pituixous pituitous Humours from the Head, and discharge - ing them by the Nose or Mouth.

apophygeinarchitecture.c: APOPHYGE, in Architecture, signifies that part of a Column where it seems to fly out of its Base, like the Process of a Bone in a Man ’ s Leg, and begins to ( hoot upward. But this Apephyge is really no more than the Rings or Ferrils thereto - fore fattened at the Extremities of wooden Pil - lars to keep them from splitting, and afterward imitated in Stone Work.

apophysis.c: APOPHYSIS, is a Protuberance made by the Fibres of a Bone produced above its Superficies, and is ordinarily upon the Extremity of the Bones.

apoplexyattonitusstupor.c: APOPLEXY, Attonitus Stupor, Sy deratio, and Morbus attonitus, is a profound Sleep, wherein the Patient being either vehemently shaken, tossed or pricked, yet perceives nothing, nor affords any sign of Action, accompanied with a difficulty of Respiration for the most part, and sometimes with none at all. Blanchard. APORRHEiE, are Vapours and Sulphureous Effluviums which exhale through the Pores of the Body

aporrheasaword.c: APORRHEAS, a Word used by Mr. Boyle for Effluviums; of the fame Sense with the former.

aposiopesis.c: APOSIOPESIS, ( a Figure in Rhetorick ) is when on a sudden a Perion changes his Passion, cutting oft ' his Discourse so that the Hearer can - not easily imagine what it is he intends: As it is very common upon occasion of threatening, to fay, If &c. But, &c.

apostareleges.c: APOSTARE LEGES, and Apoflatare Leges, signifies willfully to break or transgress the Laws.

apostatacapiendo.c: APOSTATA CAPIENDO, is a Writ direct - ed to the Sheriff, for to take the Body of one, who having enter ’ d into, and professed feme Or - der of Religion, leaves it and departs from his House, and wanders about the Country.

apostrophe.c: APOSTROPHE, is a Figure in Rhetorick, when the Speaker is in an extraordinary Commo - tion, turns himself on all Sides, and addresser him - self to all Beings, whether sensible or insensible; whom he, for the present, supposes to be equally capable of hearing his Complaint, and of return - ing an Answer to his Demands.
APOSTROPHE, also, is an Accent in Gram - mar, ( hewing there is a Vowel to be rejected, and is expressed thus ( ’ ) and placed over the Head of the Letter. Vofflus writes it Apoftrophus.

apothegm.c: APOTHEGM, is a short pithy instructive Sen - tence spoken by some grave and considerable Man; or else made in Imitation of such. As the Apo - thegms of Plutarch, or those of the Ancients col - elected by Lycoftkenes. APOfOME, in Mathematicks, is an Irratio - nal Remainder, or Residual Root; when from a national Line, as suppose a, you cut off a part as h, which is only commensurable in Power to the whole Line. Then ’ tis exprest thus a b, and is called Apotome, because it signifies a Remainder left by cutting off b.

apotomeinmusick.c: APOTOME, in Musick, is the difference be - tween the greater and the lesser Semitone.

apozeme.c: APOZEME, is a Decoction of Roots, Woods, Barks, Herbs, Flowers, Fruits, Seeds, & c. which is boy led down commonly to Twelve, Fifteen or Twenty Ounces. It is either Purging, Loosening, Altering or Drying, Cephalidi, Stomachick., Diu. reticle, Spleneiick, or Hepaticl, according as the Indications of the Disease direct. . APPARENT CONJUNCTION: See Con - jun'cli on Apparent.

apparentplace.c: APPARENT Place of a Star, is a Point de - terminer by a Line drawn from the Eye through the Center of the Star j whereas the True or Real Place is determined by a Line drawn from the Center of the Earth to the Star or Planet.

APPARENT PLACE of any ObjeEl in Opticks is that ( " different from the real one ) in which it appears when seen through one or more Glasses. For when by Refraction through Glasses, that parcel of Rays which fall on the Pupil of the Eye from each Point of any near Object, is made to flow as close together as that which comes from a distant one; or when by the fame way, the Rays coming from distant Objects are made to Diverge as much as if they flowed from nigh ones, then the Eye must necessarily fee. the Place of the Object changed which Change is its apparent Place. If an Object be placed nearer to a Convex Glass than is the Distance of its Focus, its Appa - rent Place may be determined - as Mr. Molyneux in Dioptr. p.. shews. But if the Object be in the Focus of the Glass, ' the Locus Apparens of the Object cannot be deter - mined; only, as Dr. Barrow faith, it will appear vastly remote. Nor can the Locus Apparens be determined, if the Object be beyond the Focus of a Convex Glass. But if an Object be more distant from a Convex Glass, then its Focus and the Eye lie beyond the difiinB Base, the apparent Place of the Object will be in th e dijlinB Base.

appealofmayhem.c: APPEAL of Mayhem, ( in Law ) is an accusing of one that hath maimed another: But that being no Felony, the Appeal is but a kind of Action of Trespass, because there is nothing recovered but Damages.

appeal.c: APPEAL, ( in Law ) is a removing of a Cause from an Inferiour Judge to a Superiour: Also a private Accusation of a Murtherer, by one who had Interest in the furthered Party; or of any Felon, by one of his Complices in the Fact.
APPEAL of wrong imprisonment, a Term in Law, is by some used for an Action of wrong lm - prisonment.

appellant.c: APPELLANT, is he that brings an Appeal.

appellativeatermingrammar.c: APPELLATIVE, a Term in Grammar, fignx - lying a Name in oppofidon to Proper, and which belongs to a whole Species or Kind, as Man Chy - mijl, & c.

appellororappellant.c: APPELLOR or Appellant, the fame with Ap prover.

appendantandappurtenant.c: APPENDANT and Appurtenant ( in Law ) are things that by time off prescription have belonged, appertained, and are joyned to another principal, thing, by which they pass and go as accessary to the fame special thing, as Lands, Commons, ?. to a Mannor; Courts, Ways, &c. to a House, Of - sice, or such others.

appendiculavermiformis.c: APPENDICULA VERMIFORMIS, so some Anatomists call the Inteflinum Caecum or Blind Gut, from its Figure and manner of Situation, which in some Animals hangs pendulous like a Worm, and is not filled with Excrement, as it is in others. HAPPEN - APPENDIX, the fame with Epiphysis.

appensa.c: APPENSA, the fame with Periapt a, such things as are hung about the Necks of diseased Persons, to free them from some Distempers which they labour under such as a dried Toad to Hop Bieeding, Peony Roots tor Convulsions, &c.

appertinances.c: APPERTINANCES, lignify, in the Common - Law, things both Corporeal, belonging to ano - ther thing, as the more principal; as Hamlets to a chief Mannor, Common of Pasture, Turpary, Piscary, and such like; and Incorporeal, as Li berries and Servicesof Tenants.

applicateingeometry.c: APPLICATE, in Geometry, is a Right Line, otherwise called the Ordinate or Semi - ordinate in a Conick, Section: See the Word Ordinate, or any Treatise of Conick, Selilions.

application.c: APPLICATION, is sometimes the Geometry - cal Term for Division, the Reason of which see in Geometrical Division. But Application all fig - nifies the fitting or applying one Quantity to ano - ther, whole rea ’ s, but not Figures, are the fame. Thus Euclid, Book. Prop. teaches how to a Right Line given, to apply a Parallelogram equal to a Rectilineal Figure given.

applicateordinate.c: APPLICATE ORDINATE, ( a Term in Geo - merry ) eeOidinate. It signifies a Right - line ap - plied at Right - angles to the Axis of any Conick Sedhon, and terminated by the Curve.

applyaterm.c: APPLY, a Term used by Geometricians in three Senles. . It signifies to transfer a Line given into a Circle ( most usually ) or into any other Figure, so that it shall be there fitted or Accomodated, ( which is alio another Word they use for the fame thing ) according to its proper length. Tis also used to express Division in Geometry, especially by the Latin Writers, who, as they fay, Due in, when they would have multi - ply ’ d by; so they fay, Applica ad, when they would have divided by. See Division Geometrical, or in Lines, where the Reason of this way of speaking is explained. . It signifies alio to fit Quantities whose Area ’ s are equal, but Figures different, so that they shall conform to one another; as when Euclid in his lixth Book, teaches how, on a Line given, to apply Parallelogram equal to a Rectilineal Figure given.

apportionment.c: APPORTIONMENT, is a dividing into Parts a Rent which is dividable, and not entire or whole; and forasmuch as the thing out of which it was to be paid is separated and divided, the Rent also ( hall be divided, having respect to the Parts.

apportuminlaw.c: APPORTUM, in Law, signifies Revenue, Gain or Profit, which a thing brings to its Owner.

apposale.c: APPOSALE ) Sheriffs, is the charging them with Money received upon their account in the Exchequer.

appositioningrammar.c: APPOSITION, in Grammar, is the putting of two or more Substantives together in the fame Case.

apprendreinlaw.c: APPRENDRE, in Law, signifies a Fee or Pro - fit to be taken or received.

apprehension.c: APPREHENSION, is the simple Contempla - tion of things that present themselves to the Mind, as when we confider the Sun, the Earth, a Tree, Rotundity, a Square, Cogitation, Entity, pro enouncing nothing expressly concerning them; and the Forms under which they are considered are called Ideas.

approachesinfortification.c: APPROACHES, in Fortification, are Works call up on both sides j so called because the Be - sieges by that means may draw near a Fortrels without fear of being discovered by the Enemy. Or Approaches are all forts of Advantages by the help of which an Advancement may be made to - ward a place besieged.

appropriarecommunam.c: APPROPRIARE COMMUNAM, todifeom - mon, that is, to separate and enclose any parcel of Land that was before open Common.

appropriation.c: APPROPRIATION, is when the Advoyyfon of a Parsonage is given, or belongs to any Biffio - prick, Religious House, College, &c And to their Succdfors, so that the House or Body is both Patron or Parson, and some one of the Mem - bers officiates as Vicar. ’ Tis called Appropriation, because the Profits of the Living are appropriate to the use of the Patrons.

APPROPRIATION, is the Granting a Part - chial Church, or the great Tithes and better Pro - fits, adProprios ufus, to the proper use of some Re - ligious House, to enjoy for ever: Whence it was call ’ d Perpetuum Beneficium.

appropriare.c: APPROPRIARE ad HONOREM, a Term in Law, signifying to bring a Man not within die extent or liber cy of such an Honour.

approvement.c: APPROVEMENT, is where a Man hath Com - mon within the Lord ’ s waste Ground, and the Lord encloses part of the Waste for himfeif, hav - ing nevertheless sufficient Common, with Egress and Regress for the Commoners. This Inclosing is called Approvement, APPkOVuR, ( in Law ) is he who hath com - mitted some Felony, which he confeffes; and to save himfeif, impeaches his Accomplice or Ac - complices and he is so called, because he must Prove that which he hath alledged in his Appeal.

approvers.c: APPROVERS of the King, are those that have the letting of the King ’ s Demeans in small Man - nors for the King ’ s greater Advantage.

appurtenances.c: APPURTENANCES, in the Common Law are the fame with Appendant e; Which fee.

apsisinastronomy.c: APSIS, in Astronomy is used as well for thd highed part of an Orbit, to which when a Planet comes, it is at the greatest distance from the Earthy and is called the Apogaum ' as the lovoeji part of that Orbit, when the Planet is in his nearest di - stance to the Earth, which is called the Perigaunt of that Planer.

aptitude.c: APTITUDE, is the natural Disposition that any thing hath to be fitting for such or subst i Pftf - Purpose. Thus Oil hath an Aptitude sto burn and Water to extinguish Fire.

aptote.c: APTOTE ( in Grammar ) is a Noun Indecli - table, or which is without the variation of Case.

apyrexy.c: APYREXY, is an Intermission, Cooling, or A - bating of a Fever the Cause of it is, that all the Morbifick Matter is spent in one Fit, and so it in - termits till new come, and begins to swell and fer - ments as the other. Blanchard.

aquasductus.c: AQUAS DUCTUS, ( in Anatomy ) is the Bony Passage of the Tympanum of the Ear reaching in - to the Palate of the Mouth. . AQUA FORTIS, is made by distilling in a close Reverberatory Furnace a Mixture of equal Parts of Purified Nitre, Vitriol calcined white, and Potter ’ s Earth or Clay dried and powdered. A small Fire is used at first to warm the Retort, and to draw off the Phlegm but as loon as the Spirits begin to appear in the Receiver in Red Clouds, the fire is raised to the moll intense degree, and kept so till white Fumes begin to come forth then unlute the Yelfels, and you have the Aqua Fortis in the Receiver. ' Tis used to dilfole Men - tals,

aqualiculus.c: AQUALICULUS, the lowest part of the Belly, being the fame with Hypogastrium.

aquariusaconstellation.c: AQUARIUS, a Constellation in the Heavens, being the Eleventh Sign in the Zpdiac it is com - monly marked with this Character zz, and con - . AQUATICK or AQUATILE, is that which belongs to, or lives mostly in the Water: Thus those Animals or Plants that live or grow usually In Water, are called Aquatic ! Animals and Plants..

aqueduct.c: AQUEDUCT, is the Term in Architecture for a Conduit or Work to convey Water ( without force of Engines ) to any Place.

aqueoushumour.c: AQUEOUS HUMOUR, or the watery Hu - mour of the Eye, is the utmost being transparent, and of no Colour it fills up the Space which lie between the Cornea Tunicle and the Chryfialline Humour:

aquilaalba.c: AQUILA ALBA, or the white Eagle, the fame with Mercuritts Dulcis, which fee.

aquilaorvulgarvolans.c: AQUILA, or Vulgar Volans, a Constellation in the Northern Hemisphere, consisting of a Stars.

arathealtar.c: ARA, the Altar, a Southern Constellation con - gaining Stars.

aracnoides.c: ARACNOIDES, is the Chrijlalline Tunic of the Eye; by some called also

araneatunica.c: ARANEA TUNICA, or Chryflallina and is that which surrounds and contains the Chryfialline Humour by reason of its light thin Contexture, like that of the Web of a Spider, it has the Name of Aranea. This Coat, by means of the Ciliary Processes, helps to move the Chrystalline Humour of the Eye nearer to or farther from the Retina, and perhaps also to fender its Figure more or less Convex.

areostyleinarchitecture.c: AREOSTYLE, in Architecture, - is a fort of Edifice where the Pillars are fetat a great distance one from another.

arbitrator.c: ARBITRATOR, is an extraordinary Judge in one or more Causes between Party and Party, cholen by their mutual Confents. The Civilians distinguish between Arbiter, who is to proceed and judge according to Law and Equity mingled, and Arbitrator, who is permitted wholly to use his own Discretion, without Solemnity of Process or Course of Judgment, to hear and determine the Controversie committed unto him.

arbitrement.c: ARBITREMENT, is a Power given by two or more contending Parties, to some Person or Per sons to determine the Matter in Dilpute between them j and to pronounce the fame, to which they bind themselves under a Penalty to stand: And the Determination thus made is called an Award or the Relult of an Arbitration.

arbormaris.c: ARBOR MARIS, a Name by some Chymists given unto C oral, because it grows like a Tree or Plant under the Water of the Sea.

arboreous.c: ARBOREOUS, is by the Botanists used for luch Fungi or Mufci which grow upon Trees whereas others grow on the Ground. Thus A ? a r / c is a Fungus Arbor eus, because it always grows on the Larix. But the Fungus Pulverulentus is Terre - Prial, always growing on the Ground.

arborist.c: ARBORIST, is one that hath good Skill in the several Kinds and Natures of Trees and knows how to propagate and preserve them well for their leveral Uses.

arcanumcoralinum.c: ARCANUM CORALINUM, is the red Precipitate of Mercury, on which hath been burnt fix times, well edify ’ d Spirit of Wine in order to burn oft ’ some of the Acids, and to sweet - en the Precipitate so as that it may be fit to be tak - en inwardly,

arcanumduplum.c: ARCANUM DUPLUM, is a kind of a Salt gain d by walking the Caput Mortuum remaining after the Distillation of double Aqua Forth with warm Water which Water is afterwards filtrated and evaporated, and the Salt remains at the Bot - tom of the Glass.

arcanumjovis.c: ARCANUM JO VIS, is an Amalgaima made o equal Parts of Tin and Mercury, powder ’ d and digested with good Spirit of Nitre and from it the Spirit being drawn in a Retort, the dry Mass is powdered again, and then digested with Spirit of Wine till the Powder be insipid.

arch.c: ARCH or ARC, in Geometry, is any part of the Circumference of a Circle.

ARCH - DEACON, being only a Person chose out of those Deacons which were originally the Attendants on, and Servants to the Bishop in Spi - ritual Affairs, at first was a person employ ’ d by the Bishop in more servile Uses, and he always was in Syp - fervience to the Vrbans or Ifural Deans of Chriftianity, to whom Arch - Deacons were as much inferior as their Order of Deacon was to that of Priest. Till by the Advantages of a Per - synal Attendance on the Bishop, and a delegation to examine and report some Causes, and a Com - mission to visit some remoter parts of a Diocese, their Power and Dignity was advance ’ d above the Arch - Presbyter or Down. Dr. Kjnnets Glofiary. ’ Tis now allow ’ d that Arch - deacons have a Power, not only to Visit, but to Suspend, Excommunicate, and in many places to Prove Wills, and, in some to InftitutC to Benefices. ’ Tis one part of thearchy - Dea - con ’ s Office to InduCt all Clerks into their Benefi - ces within his Jurisdiction, and by the ACt of Uniformity he is now obliged to be in Priests Or - ders.
ARCH - PRESBYTER, the fame with Ifural Deans.

archaisms.c: ARCHAISMS, are obsolete Expfeffions now out of use, and to be found only in ancient Au - thors.

arches.c: ARCHES, for the Court of the Arches ) is the chief and most ancient Consistory belonging to the Archbishop of Canterbury, and it is so called from the Arches of the Church where the Court is kept, namely, Bow - Church in London. ARCHAiUS, with the Paraceljians, is the Prin - cipe of Life, Health and Vigour in any Animal Body.

ARCHES, are part of the inward support of any SuperftruCture, and they are either Circular, Ecliptical or Screight. Of the Circular Arches some are exactly Semi - circular, as the Arches of Bridges, &c. some are such as the Work - men call Seen or Scheme, which are flatter Arches, less than a Semi - circle. Some Circular Arches are such a those in our Gothicf Buildings, di Tarqo & di quar - to acute, as the Italians call them, or as we fay of the third and fourth Point. Because they consist of two Arches of a Circle ( meeting in an Angle at the Top ) and drawn from the Division of a Chord into three or four, or more Parts at pleasure. El - liptical Arches were formerly much us ’ d instead of Mantle Trees in Chimneys: They had a Ffeyffione, and Cbaptrels or Impajls, and consisted of two Hanfes and a Scheme. Strait A rchesatz us ’ d over Windows and Doors, &c. having plain strait Edges both upper and under; these Edges are parallel, but both the Ends and Joints do all point towards a certain Center. They are now usually about a Brick and a half thick, which when rubbed is about Inches. The Work - men call the Le - selling End of this Arch the Skew - back -, and the level Joints between the Courses of Bricks in the Arch, they call the Sommering.

archipelagusingeography.c: ARCHIPELAGUS, in Geography, is ' a pare of the Sea containing many small Ifiands One near another, and consequently several little Seas deno - minated from those Illands as the Grecian Archie pelagi or FEgean Sea.

architectonics.c: ARCHITECTONICS, is that which builds a thing up regularly according to the Nature and Properties of it. Thus that elastick ' Nature, Power, Spirit, or whatever it be called, which hatches the Ova of Females into living Creatures of the fame Species, is by some called the Archie tccltonick Spirit.

That it hath Volute or Scrolls like the lonick, when the Corinthian hath curled Stalks; and therefore ’ tis called Composite because composed of the lonick and Corinthian together. : MV ' V V ‘ ifae best way to fortify Cities, Camps, Sea - Ports, or any other Places of Strength. The Ancients at several Times, and on several Occasions, establish'd Orders of Architecture, that is, forts of Pillars, the Tufean, the Do - rick, the lonickt the Corinthian, and the Composite or Roman Order, ( which fee under those Words ). The Difference between which Orders consists in the Column, with its Base and Capital, and the En - tablature, that is, the Architrave, Frife and Cornice for these are the Parts which constitute the Order, and each one hath its proper and peculiar Mea - fures. Besides these Ancient Orders, some Authors mention two more, as that of the Caryatides and the Perfick, ( which fee ). The Rules of ArchiteBure require, That in a well - built Fabrick there should be Solidity, Con - venience and Beauty; to which some Writers add, Order, Disposition, Proportion, Decorum and Oecono - my: And these Eight, they fay, make the neceffa - ry Parts of Architecture. Solidity, implies the Choice of a good Foundation, and good found Materials to work with. Convenience consists in so ordering and disposing the Parts of an Edifice, that they may not hinder or embarrass one another. Beauty is that agreeable Form and pleasing Appear - rance which it exhibits to the Eye of the Spectator. Order ( they say gives each Part of the Building a convenient Bigness, whether we confider them apart, or with Relation to the Whole. And Di - fpofttion they make the due Ranging and agreeable Union of all the Parts. Proportion, is the Relation that all the Work hath to its Parts, and which every one separately hath to the Idea of the Whole: For among Works that are perfect, from any particular Part we may make a certain Judgment of the Greatness of the whole Work: v. gr. the Diameter of a Pillar, or the Length of a Triglyph, gives us a right Idea of the Whole to which they belong. And to ex - press the Relation that many things have to one a - other, as to their Greatness, and the different number of their Parts, Vitruvius indifferently uses those three Words; Proportion, Eurithmy and Symmetry; the two last of which are of much the fame Sense with the first. Decorum or Decency comes next to be considered, which consists in making the whole Afped of the Fabrick so correB, that nothing shall appear but what is founded upon, and approved by some Au - thority: And they fay, Decorum teaches you to have a Regard to these things, Design, Custom and ' Nature. The Regard to Design makes us choose ( for Instance ) other Dispositions and Pro - portions for a Palace than a Church. The Re - sped we pay to Custom, makes us adorn the Por - ches and Entries into such Houses as are within Rich and Magnificent. And the Regard we have to the Nature of the Places, makes us pitch upon different Profpeds for different Parts of a Build - ing: As for Example, we expose Bed - Chambers and Libraries to the Morning Sun: Winter Apart - ments to the Weft, and Clofets of Pictures, to the North, because they require an equal Light. Oeconomy teaches the Architect ( they fay ) to have regard to the Expences that are to be made, and the Quality of the Materials, near the Places where he builds, and to take his Measures rightly for the Order and Disposition; vi, to give the Fabrick a convenient Form and Magnitude
