area.c: AREA, of any Figure in Geometry, is its Inter nal Capacity or Superficial Content reckoned m the Square Parts of any Measure as if a Field be in the Form of a Square, and its Side be Yards in length, its Area or Superficial Content will be square Yards: Or will contain little Squares, each of which is a Yard every way. Problems. To find the Area of all forts of Plane Figures. . For a Square or Re ( dangle, multiply one Side found in any known Measure by another; The Product is the true Area. The Reafori of which you have under Multipltcdtion in Geometry: which fee. . For all Parallelograms, multiply the Perpen dicular let fall from any side, by. the side it falls upon; and the Product is the Area. Because all such Figures are equal to Rectangles of the fame or equal Base and Altitude., . For all Plane Triangles, multiply half the Per pedicular let fall from an Angle, by the opposite side, or half that side by the Perpendicular, and the Product is the true Area; because Triangles are the Halves of Parallelograms of the lame of equal Safes and Altitudes. . For a Trapezium, where two Sides are Pa - parallel, multiply the Sum of the Parallel Sides ( b and d ) by half ( p ) the Perpendicular. i . For any other Trapezium, or any Multangular Flaw Figure, resolve it Diagonally into Triangles; and add the Areas of those Triangles ( found by the d Problem ) into one Sum j which will be the true Area of the whole. Thus, suppose a Trape - zium whose Sides are not parallel, divide it into two Triangles by a Diagonal, and let f a Perpendicular from the other Angles thereto; then multiply the whole Base by half the Sum for half the Base by the whole Sum ) of the Perpen - diculars, the Product is the Area Base, its half Sum of the Perpend, ir, its half, si ) Area. ' . For all Regular Figures or Polygons, multiply the half Sum of all the Sides by the length of a Line drawn from the Center to the Middle of any one Side, the Product gives the Area. Because that Line will be equal to the height of each Triangle in the Polygon, and their Bases will be also equal, because they are Sides of a Regular Polygon. Thus in a Hexagon, whose Side is Yards and the Distance from the Center to the Middle of any of the Sides i o Yards. The Sum of the Sides is x -, whose half is, which multiplied by, produces Yards, the Area of the Hexagon . For aH Csrclesf multiply half the Circumfe - rence by the Radius, because every Circle is equal to a Rectangle A, one of whose Legs is the Peri - sphery, and the other the Radius, as Archimedes hath demonstrated. For Practice, measure the Semi - diameter, then fay. As: zz S is the Semi - diameter: To the Circumference s which found, multiply by half the Diameter ( os Radius ) the Product is the Area. . For a SeBor of a Circle f multiply the Radius or one of its Legs by half the Arch ( or half the Radius by the whole Arch ) the Product gives the Content. : For all Segments of Circles, find the Area of the SeBor instilling on the Arl, and also the Area of the Triangle, and subtract that of the Triangle from that of the SeBor, the Remainder is the Area of the Segment. o. For an Ellipsis, multiply the longest Diame - ter by the shortest, and exrrad the Square Root: of the Product, it gives the Diameter of a Circle, whose Area is equal to the Area of the Ellipsis be - cause the Diameter of such a Circle is a mean Proportional between the Diameters of the Ellipsis . For a Parabola, multiply the entire Ordi - name by the Abscissa or intercepted Ax; then dou - ble that Product, and divide the whole by; the Quotient is the Area.

areometer.c: AREOMETER, is an Instru - ment to measure the Gravity of Liquor. ’ Tis usually made of a thin fine Glass of this Figure, and sealed at the Top, there be - ing first as much running Mer - cury put into it, as will serve to keep it swimming in an ereft Position. The Stem is divided into Degrees, and by the depth of its descent into any Liquor, its Lightness is concluded; for that Fluid or Liquor in which it finks least, must be heaviest, and that in which it finks lowest, will be lighted:.

AREOMETER, besides that mention'd in Vol. I. Mr. Homberg of Paris hath invented a New Instrument of this Kind, which is describ'd in Phil. Trans N. z z. artery.c: ARTERY: There are three kinds of Dudts in an Animal Body which bear the Name of Ar - tery, the Afperia Arteria or trachea, the Arteria, Pulmonark or Vena Arteriosa; both which fees And most properly, the Aorta or great Artery, which carries the Spirituous Blood from the left l Ventricle of the Heart by its Branches, to all j Parts of the Body; This, and its Ramifications, j are the only true Arteries. The Word Artery, some j fay, is derived from a Ito tS a ) par, because ’ tis continually riling or moving with a Pulse like Mo - tion; and may be defined to be an Organical and Similar Part, oblong and round, appointed to con - very Spirituous Blood to all Parts of the Body. The greatest Aorta in the whole Body is the A - orta, for thatReafon often called the Arteria mag - na i and from it all the Arteries in the whole Body are derived, except the Arteria Pulmonark. A brief Account of which, and how they spring froth the Aorta, I shall here fubjoift. Before it comes out of the Pericardium, it fends out sometimes one, but oftner two small Arteries on each side one, which compass the Basis of the Heart like a Garland in their Circuit, fending down divers Twigs lengthways on the Hearts and these are called the Arterice Coronaries. When ’ these two small Arteries have encompassed the Ba - sis and meet, they inosculate one with another, but not with the Veins: At their rife out of the Aorta, there is a Valve to hinder the Reflux of the Blood into the Aorta. These Coronary Arteries Dr. Buyfch observes, fend Branches to the Auricles i ? and to the very Substance of the Heart it self, and to the Root of the Trunk of the Aorta. The ascending Trunk then running up under the Vena Cava, lies upon the Wind - pipe, and pre - gently fendeth forth two large Branches, where - of one passeth to the Right, the other to the Left Arm: They are called Rami fubclavii, because they march under the Calvicu ’ a;; and as soon as they are gone out of the Breast, are called Axil - lares. The Right is the larger, and rising higher, goes a more direct way towards the Right Arm j the Left is less, and rising lower, ascends more obliquely towards the Left Arm. They fend our I cut several Branches both from their lower and upper. side. From - the Lower proceeds the Superiour Inter - nal, which runs along the Ihterftices or Inter - vals of the four uppermost Ribs, and fends Slips to the neighbouring Muscles and spinal Marrow. These sometimes are propagated from the Cer - vical Arteries coming out through the Holes of the Vertebrce. From the upper side of each Subclavian springs first the Mammari, which descends towards the Breast through the Muscles that fill up the Inter - ftices of the Cartilages of the true Ribs; and a considerable Branch of each descending out of the Thorax by the Sides of the Cartilage enfifor - mis, run down the Abdomen under the Mufculi Petli, spreading there into many Twigs, which are laid to inosculate with the Extremities of the like Twigs of the Epigastrick Artery ascending. But that Opinion is so opposite to the Circulation of the Blood, that it is impossible to be true; for no Blood can ascend by the Mammari ce, nor de - ascend by these ascending Twigs of the Epiga - Jlrix. The next is Cervicalis ( other wife called Vette - Iralis ) which fendeth Slips to the Vertebra and Muscles of the Neck, at whose seventh Vertebra it enters in by the Holes of the transverse Pre - cedes, and pierceth the Membrane that in - rests the Spinal Marrow, bellowing Twigs both on the Membrane and Marrow, and runs up therewith in at the great Hole of the Occiput, and being enter ’ d the Skull, both Branches ( the Right and Left ) join under the Medulla Oblong - gata, and then are divided into innumerable ttioft small Twigs, which make wonderful Net - like Plexus in the Pia Mater about the Cerebel - lum, and run into the Substance of the Cerebel - lum it self; and some of them being united with those of the Carotides, make part of the very Pete mirable. The third Artery that rifeth out of the upper side of the Subclavianis Mufcula, which is spent on the Muscles of the Neck, and sometimes alio on some of the Arm. After the Subclavians have had all these Pairs of Arteries going out of them, they pass out of the Thorax, and begin to be called Axillar. At the fame Place, or very near, where the a - sending Trunk of the Aorta fends out the Subcla - viand sideways, the remainder of it is divided in - to two, called Carotides, which ascend diredlly upwards ( though the Right sometimes arise from the right Subclavian ). These, at their rife, are sustained by the Thymus; and having bellowed Twigs on the Larynx, Tongue, the Muscles of the OsHyoides, and the neighbouring Gland, pass up on each Side by the sides of the Wind - pipe to the Jaws, with the Internal Jugular Vein, and there are each subdivided into the External and Internal Branches. The External is smaller, and is dispersed into all the Muscles of the Checks, Fore - head, Temples, Lips, and, in general, through all the outer Parts of thf Head and Face. The Internal, which is larger, fends forth some more Twigs to the Larynx, Tongue &c. as also to the Glands behind the Ears, and the spongy Parts of the Palate and Nose. Then it entreth the upper Jaw, and bellows a small Slip on the Root of each Tooth ( as the External did on the i Roots of the Teeth of the lower Jaw ) whereby Harp Humours flowing in upon them, sometimes caiife a very painful Tooth - ach. The remainder of it climbs upon the Skull, being abotit the Ba fu divided into two Branches: The less and hin - der whereof having sent ode Slip to the inner Muscles of the NeCk, and another through the Hole of the uppermost Vertebra into the Mem - brane that invests the Spinal Marrow, ascending farther, enters the Skull, at the Hole by which the sixth Pair of Nerves ( commonly so called ) comes out, and creeping along the Dura Mater ends near its Sinus ( which yet some fay it en - ters. The larger Branch, tending upwards, is carried through the bony Channel in the Wedge - like Bone, with a winding Du l to the Sea equi - na; at whose Basis, after it has sent out a Twig on each Side into the Dura Mater, it opens it self into many small Slips, which being interwoven with those of the Cervical Artery ( above - menti - oned ) make the Pete mirable, which is more ob - fervablein Bealls than in Men. Yet it is not all spent on the said Slips, but perforating the Dura Mater, it enters the Pia Mater with two notable Branches, which being divided into very small Twigs, are mingled with those of the Cervical Artery, with which they pass out of the Skull, and accompany the Spinal Marrow even to the Loins: Afterwards it fends a small Branch through the fe - cond Hole of the Wedge - like Bone with the Op - tick Nerve, out of the Skull to the Eye; and yet Hill supplying more Twigs to the Substance of the Brain and Pia Mater, and being united with some other Twigs of Cervical Artery it makes the Plexus Choroids. The descending Trunk of the Aorta, which is larger than the ascending, goes down by the Gul - let to which it cleaveth. And hence is a Man that is hot, so much cooled with a draught of cool Drink; for the Gullet being cooled thereby, the Blood in the Aorta contiguous to it, must needs be cooled likewise. Before it arrive at the diaphragm it fends out of its hinder side the inferiour Intercoltals, which run along the Interstices of Eight or Nine of the lower Ribs, namely, those which the SuperiouY Interco & als did not supply. They likewise fend Sprigs by the Holes of the Vertebra, made for the Nerves, to the Marrow of the Back, and to the Muscles which reft upon the Vertebra, and alio to those of the Thorax. Sometimes above this, and sometimes below it, there arileth also out of the hinder part of th aorta andArtery called Bronchia - Its, first found out and so named by Frederick Ppych, which accompanies all the Bronchia of the Wind - pipe. When it comes to the Midriff, there springs out of it the Phrenica, one on each side; these run - ning all through the Diaphragm, pass up into the Mediaiiinum, and sometimes into the Pericardiuma Then having penetrated the Midriff it descends in one Trunk to the fifth Vertebra of the Loins in which Passage it first fendeth forth the Ceeliaca which ariseth single, and is so Called, because it fendeth Twigs to the Stomach. This springeth from the; fore - part of the Trunk at the first Verte - bra of the Loins, and descending under the hollow of the Liver, upon the Trunk of the Vena Porta, it is divided into two Branches, the Bight and Left, The Bight which is the smaller, ascending, pro - duces jp its upper part the Gqftriea dextra, thac comes e. ART ART comes to the Pylorus, whence Spigelitts calls it Py - lorica: And besides, the Cjftic gemelli, which are very small, and are dispersed through the Gall Bladder. And out of its lower side there spring; . Epiplois dextra, which runs through the right side of the inner or hinder Leaf of the Caul and and the Colon that it is annexed to. . Intefiinalis, bellow ’ d on the Duodenum and, beginning of Jejunum. . Gafiro - epiploic dextra, on the right side ( to the middle ) of the bottom of j e Stomach, and al - so on the Caul that it is knit to its bottom. . Hepatic, which are two small ones: These are spent on the inveigling Membrane of the Liver ( for its Parenchyma is nourished by the Porta ) the Capsula Communis, the Gall - Bladder and Porus Bi - lariat. The Remainder of this Right Branch enters the Mesentery with many T wigs. The Left Branch of the Cceliaca, which is call ’ d Splenicus ( sometimes springing immediately from the Aorta ) is larger than the Right; and as it goes towards the Spleen, it fendeth forth of its upper i side Gajlrica major, which after it hath bellow ’ d a Slip upon the upper and middle part of the Sto - mach, is divided into two others; the first where - of is called Coronaria Stomachica, which encom - passes the upper Orifice of the Stomach like a Gar - land, and fends many Twigs to die Body of the Ventricle it self; the other Gajlrica finiltra which ( according to Diemerbroeck ) is carried towards the Right Hand into the upper part of the Stomach, and to the Pylorus. Out of its lower side spring, sill Epiplois postic, which runs to the hinder Leaf of the Omentum, and the Colon annex d to it; secondly, Epiplois finish - a, which is; bellow ’ d on the lower and left side of the Omentum. Just as the Splenick Branch is entring into the Spleen, there arises out of its upper part Vas breve arteriofum, which goeth streight to the Left part of the bottom of the Smmach; and the Gafiro - epi - plois finifira, which being sustain ’ d by the upper or fore - leaf of the Omentum, fends some Twigs there to, and also to the Left part of the bottom of the Stomach, and to both its fore and hinder sides, then it enters into the Spleen.. All these Arteries spring from the Cceliaca, and accompany the Veins of the Porta of the like deno - omination. The next that arileth out of the Trunk of the Aorta is the upper Mefentericf, which springs from the fore - part of it as the Cceliacf did. It accoy - sanies the Vena Mefariaca of the P orta, and runs through all the upper part of the Mesentery, and bellows many Branches on the Guts, Jejunum, I - leum, and that part of Colon that lieth in the right Hypo'chonder. Immediately below this, about the second Ver - terra oixhz Loins, there go out of each side of the descending Trunk of the Aorta an Emulgent Ar - tery, each of which being after its rife divided into two, and sometimes into three Branches, enters the Kidney on its own side. The Right springs out of it a little lower than the Left. both are fub - divided into innumerable Twigs in the Parenchima of the Kidneys, ( all of which are invested with the Veins in one common Capsul a borrow ’ d from the Pelvis ) and their Capillaries end in the Glands, wherein the Serum that these Arteries bring with j the Blood is separated there - from, and carried from them by the Urinary Siihons into the Pelvis. Next to these arise the Spermatic ? ( called Ar - tori pr par antes ). These. go out of the fore - parc of the Trunk very near together ( very seldom ei - ther of them out of the Emul gents, as the Left Spermatick Vein does ) and the Right passes over the Trunk of the Vena Cava About two Fingers breadth from their rife they are each joyn ’ d with the Vena praparans of their own side, and descend with them, in Men, through the Process of thePe - ritomeum to the Stones, being divided into two Branches a little before they arrive at them, one of which runs towards the Epididymis, and the o - ther to the TeRes. In Women, when they come near the Tefies ( or Ovaria ) they are divided also into two Branches, one whereof goes ro the Tefiesy and the other to the bottom of the Womb. Next below the Spermatick springs the lower Mefente - rick, out of the Trunk a little before it is divided into the Rami Iliad, This entreth the lower Re - gion of the Mesentery, and distributes many Bran - ches to the Left part of the Colon, and to the streight Gut; andlaftly, descending to th Q Antis v makes the internal Hemorrhoidal Artery. Very near to this, put of the Trunk still arise the Lumbar es, reckon ’ d four in number: Thele go out of the back - side of the Aorta, and are di - ftributed, not only to the neighbouring Muscles of the Loins, and to the P triton eum, but enters in at Holes of the Vertebra of the Loins, and run along the Membrane that involves the Spinal Marrow, and penetrates into the Marrow it less. Besides these feme reckon other two, on each side one, call ’ d Mufcul e Superiores ( which run to the Muscles of the Abdomen ) unless these be t wo of the four call ’ d Lumbares. When the Trunk is descended as low as die ' fifth or last Vertebra of the Loins, and the top of Os Sacrum, it begins to climb upon the Vena Cava, under, or behind which it passed thus far: But as it begins t get upon it, it is divided into two e - qual Branches called Rami Iliad, and at its very division there springs out of it Arteria Sacra, whose small Twigs entring in at the Holes of the Os Sa - crum penetrate into the Marrow contained, in it. The Trun os the descending Aorta being di - vided into the Rami Iliad, these are fub - divided presently into the interiour and exteriour Branches. From the interiour, which is left, proceed three others. Fir ft, The inferiour Mufcul a ( called Otherwise Glutcea ) which is bestow ’ d on the Muscles named Glutcei that make the Buttocks, and also on the lower end of the Iliack Muscle and the Pfeas. Secondly, The Hypogastrick, which is large, and at the lower end of the Os Sacrum runs to the Bladder and. its Neck, and the Muscles that co - ver the Off a Pubis. In Men it goes also along the two Nervous Bodies of the Penis as far as the Gians; and in fVomen it is distributed in numerous. Branches into the bottom of the Womb and its Neck, out oi which, for the greatest part, iolite the Menses in their Monthly Purgation. It goes also to the Podex, where it makes the external Hemorrhoidal Artery. Thirdly, The Umbilical Artery, which ascending by the sides of the Bladder, and being inferred into the Peritoneum, proceeds betwixt the two Mem - branes thereof to the Navel, out of which it passes in a Foetus in the Womb, and runs into the Placen - ta Vterina: But after the Infant is born when there is no more use of it, it elofes. upland turns into into the nature of a Ligament, in some measure sustaining the sides of the Bladder, and hindring it from priding on its Neck. From the Exteriour Branch of the Ramus Hia - tus two Arteries arise. First, The Epigaflrick., which turning upwards On the outside of the Peritoneum runs betwixt it and the A iujculi Rebli of - the Abdomen as high as the Navel, where the Mammary Artery meets it, and according to Tradition ( though false ) inofcu - lates there with it. Secondly, Pudenda, which fends forth a notable Artery on each side into the Nervous Body of the Penis in Men, and into the Clitoris in Women. Hence it is carried inwards by the joynting of the OJJa Pubis to the Pudenda and Groins, and their Glands, and is spent on the Skin of those Parts, and of the Yard, in Men. When all these pairs of Arteries have arifen out of the Rami Iliaci, they they run down out of the Abdomen to the Thighs, where they begin to be called Crurales. arteriotomy.c: ARTERIOTOMY, is the artificial opening of an Artery for the letting of Blood in an inveterate Head - ach, Madness, Falling - sickness, Pain and Inflammation in the Eyes and Ears, and the Se & i - on is made in the Fore - head, Temples or behind the Ears: The manner of it is thus j after the Li - nature is made in the Arms or Neck, the Artery is cut just as a Vein is, and when the Blood is emit - ted, you apply a very Astringent Piaifter with a Leaden Plate to the Orifice, and then swathe it well. Blanchard. ' arthritis, " Morbus Articularis, the Gout, is a Pain in the Joints of the Limbs, sometimes ac - companies with a miserably Contra & ion of the Nerves, Tendons, Ligaments, and thin Membranes about the Bones, with Swelling and Redness, and now and then with hard chalk Concretions. They account it four - fold: Chyragra the Hand Gout; Ischias, the Gout in or about the Bone connected to the Os Ilium, which therefore feme call the Hip - Gout: Gonagra, in the Knees and Podagra, in the Feet.

arthriticorarthritical.c: ARTHRITIC, or Arthritical, Gouty, Dis - ease in the Joints, ( c.

arthrodia.c: ARTHRODIA, is the Articulation of one Bone into the ( hallow Sinus of another, as the Radius receives the Humerus.

artickpole.c: ARTICK POLE, is the North Pole of the World.

articleinarithmetick.c: ARTICLE, in Arithmetick, is Ten, with all ci - ther whole Numbers that may be justly divided into ten Parts, as zo,,, ( c. they are some - times called Decads, and sometimes Round Num - bers.

articleingrammar.c: ARTICLE, in Grammar, is a small Word or Particle used to Decline or Vary the Cates, and to distinguish the Genders of Nouns and Pronouns, as Hie, Hec, Hoc in the Latin Tongue.

articulation.c: ARTICULATION, is that part of Grammar which treateth, first of Sounds and Letters ( which are called the Elements of Speech ) and then of the manner of their Combination for the compo - sing of Syllables and Words j so that he which A SC pronounces his Words clearly and diftindlly, is ( aid to pronounce them articulately. And fucli Sounds as can be expressed by Letters, and which form Words, are called Articulate Sounds

articulationinanatomy.c: ARTICULATION, in Anatomy, is a Conjun - ction of the Limbs of an Animal Body, for the due performance of Motion: Some make this two - fold, vi. Diarthrosis, which is a more loose, and Synarthrosis, which is a more close Conjunction. The Term is also used by the Botanists for the Joints or Knots that are in some S Hi rue, as those of the Ornithopolium, and in the Roots of the Polygonatum, and the Distance or Space betweeil Knot and Knot, or Joint and Joint they call the Internodium. artillery.c: ARTILLERY, is all forts of great Fire - Arms with their Appurtenances j as Cannons of all forts, Mortars, Muskets, Carbines, ( c. ARYTAiNOIDES, or Gutturales, are two Car - tilages which with others make up the top of the Larynx; and these are so called, because when their Processes are joined together, they represent the Month of an Ewer ( Gutturium ) or the in - dented Lip of a Cup or Vessel.

arymnoideus.c: ARYMNOIDEUS, is the smallest Muscle belonging to the Larynx; it ’ s in the Opinion of some, double; but has always ( says Mr. Cove per ) appeared to us ( ingle. It arises from the external part of one of the Arytenoidal Cartilages, and run - ning transversely, is inserted to the other. This pulls the Arytenoidal Cartilages nearer each other, and ( huts the Rimula adequately, by forcing down the Epiglotis, which quite closes the Glottis so that no Air can enter.

asaphy.c: ASAPHY, is a lowness of the Voice, proceed - ing from an ill Constitution, of Contemporatiort of the Organs of Speech.

asbestinepaperorcloth.c: ASBESTINE Paper or Cloth. is such as will burn in the Fire, be purified by it, and yet not consume. Tis made of the Asbejlo or Lapis Amianthus y and is by some called Linum Vivum. ASCARISjj or Afcarides, are little Worms which seed in the intestinum Reblwri, and tickle and trouble it.

asparagusinbotanicks.c: ASPARAGUS, in Botanicks, signifies the first Germen, Sprout or Shoot of a Plant; which is either edible by it self, or boiled in Broth: It comes out before the Leaves are unfolded. And hence ( /. e. a ffvreipa ) ) the famous Plant of this Name receives its Denomination.

asperaarteria.c: ASPERA Arteria, or Trachea, is an oblong Pipe consisting of various Cartilages and Membranes, which begins at the Throat, or lower part of the Jaws, lies upon the Gullet, descends into the Lungs, and is dispersed by manifold Ramifications or Braches through their whole Substance: The Upper Partis called rc and the lower Bronchus, jo which Malpighius adds a third, or lowest, called by him Vesicular: It is subservient to Speech and Respiration. That part of the Aspera Arteria which is called she Bronchus, contains all of it, but the Larynx; being the Body of the Pipe as well before as after its Insertion into the Lungs, all the Cartilages of this Bronchus are like the lowest of the Larynx, to which the uppermost of the Bronchus adheres. j These Cartilages are seated one below another at equal Distances, and keep in their Places by both the Membranes of the Trachea, which fill up their Interstices, and tye then one to another like Liga - ments. Yet these Ring ' have not their Circle en - tire, but on the backside ) f the Bronchus next the Gullet, that they might give way to the Meat in swallowing, they pass into a Membrane, so that they are in Figure like the Letter C. But this In - rerftice in their Circle, which most Anatomists af firm to be Membranous, Cafp. Bartholin ( after his Father ) says, is rather a Carnous Fibres that run from one Side or End of the Cartilage across to the other, which ) in Expiration ( especially violent ) contracting themselves, draw the Ends of the Cartilage towards one another on each Side, and thereby straiten the Pipe of the Trachea. And though the Cartilages, io far as they are contiguous to the Gullet ( being about twenty in number ) are thus semilunar as it were, yet those of the Branches of the Bronchus within the Lungs, have no Jnterftice in their Circumference, being all Cartilaginous, though not all of a Circular Fi - gure, but some Four - square, other Triangular, &c l as DiemerbroecJ ' observes, the inner Membrane is plentifully beset with miliary Glands, out of which a good part of that mucous Matter that bedaubs its Inside issues, for the lubricating of it. The ou - ter Membrane helps to conned ! the Cartilages the more firmly one to another, and the whole Tra - chea to the neighbouring Parts, that it may more safely and firmly descend into the Thorax. This is much thinner than the other j for the Inner ( ac - cording to Dr. Wallis ) has two Rows of Muscular Fibres, the Outer ( freight, the Inner oblique, the First by their Contraction shorten the Trachea, the Latter straiten it j so that he thinks they assist Expi - ration, especially when it is violent, as Coughing, ' Hawking, or the like. Yet he says, this inner Membrane has two others growing upon it, as it were, one Glandulous, and another Vascular. Through this latter do the Blood - Vessels and Nerves every where run and the Glands placed in the former, receive and keep all the superfluous Moi - fture or Lymph a deposited by the Arteries, which the Veins do not imbibe, till they can remand it by the Lymphedudls ( which spring from them ) or if it be over plentiful, so that the the Lymphedudls cannot receive it at all, then it issues both out of these Glands, and out of the Arteries into the Ca - city of the Wind - pipe, and causes a Catarrh. But the Inside of this Membrane is naturally moist, be - ing besmear ’ d with a fattifhand muccous Humour, to hinder its drying, and to make the Voice smooth - er, so that when this Humour is fretted off in Catarrhs, or the Inside of this Membrane becomes rough from any Cause, the Voice becomes hoarse j and when it is dried by too much Heat, as in Sea - vers, it becomes squeaking. The Aspera Arteria has Veins from the external Jugulars. Arteries from the Garotides, and from the Arteria Bronchialis ( first found out by Free rickJLuyfch ) which springs from the backside of the defending Trunk of the Aorta, a little above the lower Intercostals. Nerves it receives from the recurring Branches of the par Vagum, which run mostly along its inner Membrane, whence it be - comes so exquisitely sensible. When it is descended as low as the fourth Ver terra of the Thorax, it is divided into two Trunks, whereof one goes into the right Lobe of the Lungs, she ASP ASS the other into the left, and each is presently again divided into two, and those into others, till at last they end in very small Branches, which are disperse - ed among the like Branches of the Pulmonary Ar - tery and Vein, and en i in and are continued With the little Bladders that make up the greatest part of the Bulk of the Lungs. ASPERIFOLliE ( Plant a ) is one of the Divi - onsor kinds of Plants; See Plants, N. n. ) In this kind of Plants, the Leaves stand alter - nately, or without any certain order on the Stalks: The Flowers are monopet alow, but having the Mar - gin cut into Divisions, sometimes deep, some - times Ihallow; and the upper Spike or top of the Plant is often curved back something like a Scorpi - on ’ s Tail They are called Afperifolia because they are usually rough leaved, but they are not al - ways so. After each Flower of this kind of Plants, there usually succeed four Seeds: There being on - ly the Cerinthe reckoned by Mr. May to belong to this Genus, which hath lels than four Seeds at the Root of each Flower but that hath but two. The Herb Afperifolie are, the Pulmonaria Ma - ‘ culofa, Cynoglojfa, Bor ago, Bugloffa, Anchufa, Echi - um, Linum Vmbilicatum, Heliotr opium majus, A - marine major, Confolida major, Lithojpermum, Echi - um Scorpoides and Cerinthe.

asperity.c: ASPERITY, is the inequality or roughness of the the Surface of any Body, whereby some parts of it do so stick out above the reft, as to hinder one ’ s Hand, f c. from palling over it easily and freely.

asphyxia.c: ASPHYXIA, ora Cessation of the Pulfeof the whole Body, is the highest degree of Swooning and next to Death.

aspiration.c: ASPIRATION, or the pronouncing of any Syl - table or Word strongly, with a good deal of Breath and some Vehemency; as we do those Words which have the Letter H before them, as have -, hear, heat, & C. whereas they are founded much lester and easier without the H; as ear, eat, See.

aspyxia.c: ASPYXIA, a sensible decayed Pulse, the fame with Afphyxid.

assartaterminlaw.c: ASSART, a Term in Law, signifying an Of - fence committed in the Forest, by plucking up the Woods by the Roots: Also to make Glades in a Wood, to grub up or clear a Ground of Bullies and Shrubs, ( e, or to lop off the Boughs of a Tree.

assation.c: ASSATION, is a Term in Pharmacy, used for a peculiar kind of DecoSlion or Boiling of Plants, C c. in their own Juice.

assault.c: ASSAULT ( in Law ) signifies a Violent kind of Injury offered to a Man ’ s Person, of a more large extent than Battery; for it may be committed on - ly by offering to give a Blow.

ASSAULT ( in the Art of War ) is taken also for a general Attack made upon the Fortress to get it by main Force, without defending themselves in the Attack by any Works: The Words are, to give an Ajfault to such a Place; to be commanded to the Ajfault; to Land an Ajfault, to second an Af - fault; to repulse an Ajfault; to carry by AJfault, See. While an Assault lasts, and both Parties are mixt, there is no fear of Cannon on either Side, for they are afraid of destroying their own Men thereby.

assets.c: ASSETS ( in Law ) signifie Goods enough to. discharge that Burden which lies upon the Execu - tor or Heir, in satisfying the Teftators or Ancestors Debts or Legacies.

assewiare.c: ASSEWIARE, signifies to draw or drain out Water from a Marshy Ground,

assign.c: ASSIGN, ( a Law Term ) is he that is appointed or deputed by another to do any Ad, or perform, any Business, or enjoy any Commodity: And it is either in Deed Or in Law.

assignindeed.c: ASSIGN in Deed, is he that is appointed by the Person himself.

assigninlaw.c: ASSIGN in Law, is he whom the Law. fd makes, without any appointment of the Person.

assimilalion.c: ASSIMILA LION, is a Term in Anatomy, by which they express the Change that is made either of Chyle into Blood, or of the Nutritious Juice into the Substance of an Animal Body. Thus the Modern Anatomists fay. Sanguification is not per - formed by the Liver only, as the Ancients suppo - fed, but by a gradual changing of the Cyle into Blood by frequent Circulations, and the manner of this Change they call AJfimilation.

assisacadere.c: ASSISA Cadere, in Law, signifies to be Non - suited.,.

assisacontinuanda.c: ASSISA Continuanda, is a Writ directed to the Justices alligned, to take an Assize for the continue ance of a Cause, where certain Records ailed g - ed cannot in time be procured by the Party that would use it.

assisa.c: ASSISA ProroMnda, is a Writ directed to the Justices of Assize for the stay of Proceedings, by reason of the King ’ s Business, wherein the Party is employed.

ASSISA magna, was a more solemn Trial by a Jury of or more Knights, to give their Verdict in a Cause prosecuted - per Breve de Belly; i. e. where the Dispute lies not about the bare Poflefli - on, but of the Bight and Property j in this Diftin - guifhed from the Ajftfa para or Minor, where the Question is only of Poffeftlon, in which he Jury were ordinary Legal or Free - men Retu rn'd by the Sheriff.

assise.c: ASSISE de utrum, lieth for a Parson against a Lay - man, or a Lay - Man against a Parson, for Land or Tenement doubtful whether it be Lay - fee, or Free - Alms.

assizeinlaw.c: ASSIZE, in Law, properly signifies a Writ that lies where any Man is put out of his Lands, Tenements, or of any Profit to be taken in a cer - tain Place, and so disseised of his Free - hold. In an Assize it is needful always that there be one Diffeifor, and one Tenant, or otherwise the Writ Shall abate. There is also another Ajfige, called Affile effrejh Force, and lies where a Man is disseised of Tene - ments which are devisable; as in London of other Boroughs that are Franchises: For there the Te - nant Shall come into the Court of the Town of Borough, and enter his Plaint, and accordingly Shall have a Writdireded to the Mayor of Bay - lifts, &c. and thereupon Shall pass a Jury in man - ner of Ague of Novell Disseisin; and in case the Officer delay Execution, the Plaintiff Shall have another Writ of Execution, then a scut alias, and after that a Pluries, See. And from things of this Nature being done by the Judges in their Circuits - when at any Place they lie to do Justice by Com - million, that Court or Meeting is called the Af - fit es. But besides this, the Judges of the Affixes have leveral other Commissions; as, i. A Commission of Oyer and Terminer, dire & ed to them, and m many others of the belt Account in their Circuits but here the Judges are of the Quorum, so as with - out them there can be no proceeding: By this Com - mission they enquire into and punish Murders Treasons, Felonies, &c. z They have a Com " ’ million of Goal Delivery; this is directed only to themselves, and the Clerk of the Assize Associate - and by this Commission they deal with all Prifo - ners in Goal, for whatever Offences there com - mitted,. They have also a Commission of Nisi lid ) I Prim, dire & ed to the Judges themselves and the Clerk of the Assize, by which they are commission - nated to take NiftPrius, &c.. They have also a Commission of the Peace, in which all the Justices of the Peace of the several Circuits are obliged to assist them j for Default of which they are sine - ble at theDifcretion of the Judges.

Assize of the Forest, is a Statute or Condition, touching Orders to be observed in the King ’ s Forest.

assizeofbreadandbeer.c: ASSIZE of Bread and Beer, is the Power a Ma - giftrate has of affixing or adjusting their Weights inn fiirPQ

association.c: ASSOCIATION, is a Patent sent by the King, either of his own Motion, or at the Suit of the Party Plaintiff to the Justices of Assize, to have other Persons associated to them to take the Assize: And upon this Patent of the Association, the King will fend his Writ to the Justices of Assize, by it com - minding them to admit them that are so sent.

assodesfebris.c: ASSODES Febris, is a kind of burning Fever, in which the lick Person incessantly rumbles and losses, being exceeding restless, and subject to Sickness at the Stomach, and Vomiting, by reason that the Distemper usually arises from the Vexati - on ol the Stomach, by sharp and choleric Hu - hours, biting the Orifice or Coat thereof. Blanch.

assoyle.c: ASSOYLE, ( a Law Term, ) signifies to deliver or discharge a Man of an Excommunication.

assumpsit.c: ASSUMPSIT fin Law ) or Nude Contrail, is a voluntary Promise made by Word, by which a Man assumes and takes upon him to perform, or pay a - ny thing to another: Or a Promise may arise in Law, as upon thefaleof Goods, c.

astragalinarchitecture.c: ASTRAGAL, in Architecture, is by the French called the Talon, by the Italians Tondino, and is a kind of half Tore, sometimes wrought ( in the Rich - er Orders ) like a kind of overcast Hem or Edge ' to the larger Tore; which frequently is placed be - tween, as in the Ionick. Base, with two Scotia ’ s or Trochiles; and sometimes, but rarely, just about the Plinth of the Base. Sometimes it is taken for the Collar or CinCture next the Hypotrachelium and Diminution of a Pillar lifted on both Edges; and it runs alio round under the Echinus of the lonick. We find it also. sometimes dividing the Fsfcia of the Corinthian Architrave, where it is wrought in Chaplets, and Beads or Berries j and sometimes tis used both above and below the Lifts, and joining immediately to the Square or Die of a Pedestal, where the Stylobata is introduce - ed. asiolabe.c: ASIOLABE, is a Mathematical Instrument serving to take the Height of the Sun or Stars. It consists of an entire Circle, whofeLimb for what Part of it is necessary ) is divided into Degrees and Decimal Parts of a Degree, with a moveable Rul - er or Label which turns upon the Centre, and car - ries two Sights. At the Zenith is a Ring to hang it by in time of Observation, and then you need only turn it so to the Sun, that the Rays may pals freely through both the Sights, and the Edge of the Label cuts the Altitude in the Limb. This A - astrolabe, though now not much in use at Sea, yet if well made, graduated and poised, and of a great Thickness and Weight, that it may hang the fteadier, it may be a very serviceable Instrument, / especially between the Tropicks, where the Sun comes near the Zenith; and in calm Weather. There are also some Projections of the Sphere which are called by this Name, as that of Gemma Fri ius and Stoffler. The Common Sea Aftrolabei

astrology.c: ASTROLOGY, is an Art which pretends to foretell future things from the Motion of the Hea - venly Bodies, and their AfpeCfs to one another; and also from some Imaginary Qualities, which the fooliffi Admirers of this Cheat will have to be in the Stars, as the Causes of great Sublunary Ef - sects; though they have no tolerable Grounds to prove that there are any such things. And there - fore as I wilh that such a ridiculous Piece of So - very as this may be quite forgotten, so I have eve - ry where omitted explaining any of its Terms, unless they fall in with Astronomy.

astronomicalcalendar.c: ASTRONOMICAL Calendar, is an Instrument engraved on Copper Plates, printed on Paper, and pasted on Board, with a Brass Slider, which car - ries a Hair, and slews, by InfpeCfion, the Suns Meridian, Altitude, Eight Ascension, Amplitude, Declination, Time of its Ejftng and Setting, &c. to greater nicety than the largest Globes now made.

astronomicalplace.c: ASTRONOMICAL Place of a Star or Planet, is its Longitude or Place in the Ecliptick, reckon - ed AS Y td from the beginning of Aries, in Confequentia, or according to the natural order of the Signs.

astronomicalquadrant.c: ASTRONOMICAL Quadrant, is an Instru - anent curiously framed, and the Degrees exactly and minutely divided by the help of a Screw on the Edge of the Limb, fitted with Telescopes, and either apply ’ d to a Wall in the Meridian; or on a strong Axis or Pedestal, with two Semicircles placed at Right Angles on two endless Screws, which rea - dily direct or guide the Instrument to take Obfer - / nations of the Sun, Moon or Stars. L ASTRONOMY, is a Mathematical Science, teaching the Knowledge of the Stars or Heavenly Bodies, and their Magnitudes, Distances, Eclipses; Order, and Motions: By some ’ tis taken in so large a Sense, as to contain in it also the Do - trine of the Mundane System, the Laws of the Planetary Motions, &c. which others reckon as a part of Physicks or Natural Philosophy.

The following general Observations about A - Jymptotes and Afymptotick. Curves, I had communi - cated from Mr. Humphrey Ditton, now Master of the New Mathematical School in Chrijl's Hospital, a Perlbn peculiarly skilful in these Matters, and are as follows. Sortie General Observations about Asymptotes, and Afymprotical Curves. I. Though it be certain that all luch Curves as have Asymptotes be of the Number of those which ( running on in Infinitum ) do not include a Space; yet is not true, on the other hand, that where ever we have a Curve of that Nature and Property, we find an Asymptote also. For this in - finite Continuation of the Curve; is visible in all those of the Parabolick Family, and yet none of all these can have an Asymptote -, that is, not any Right Line placed in any Position to the Curve, which can infinitely approach to it, and yet not cut it, as is not hard to be demonstrated. II. Of those Curves that have an Asymptote, some there are that have two, others that have on - ly one. Inftanees of the former kind are all the forts of Hyperbolick Curves, which from the Prin - cipe of their Genesis ( as being formed from Re - ciprocal Series ) are easily proved to have two A symptotes. And of the latter fort we have the Conchoid, the Cijfotd, and the Logarithmic ! Curve, I the: B AS Y the Nature of. which considered, as clearly hews that they have one and no more. III. As a Right Line and a Curve may be A - asymptotical to one another, soals may Curves and Curves: And here are two or three Varieties to be considered. i. Any of these Curves that have from their own Nature and Construction an Asymptote, are capable of being Asymptotical to one another. Thus in Conick Sections ' tis demonstrated, that Hyperbola ’ s that have the fame common Asymptote, are alio themselves Afymp totes to each other; and this hall afterwards be ( hewn universally of all such Curves. . Not only those Curves which are endowed with an Asymptote, but even such as in their own Nature admit of no such thing, may also have this Affe & ion. The Parabola ( for instance ) we know has no Rectilineal Asymptote belonging to it j and yet two Parabola ’ s, with their Axes placed in the fame Right Line, will be Asymptotical to each other j as De la Hire has demonstrated, Sc ft. Co - nic. Lib.. . But no Curve that has any Asymptote be - longing to it, can ever be Asymptotical to another whose Nature refuses a Reftilincal Asymptote; for if it were supposed to be so, then this latter Curve would have the Asymptote of the former Curve for its own Asymptote too, which is contrary to the Hypothesis of irs having none at all. Thus, for Instance, a Parabola and an Hyperbola can never be Asymptotical to one another; for were it so, the Asymptote of the Hyperbola would be also an Asymptote to the Parabola; which is impossible, since that Curve can have no Asymptote. IV. The Pressure of the Atmosphere, Mr. Boyle un - dertakes to demonstrate from many Experiments, as, . That two polished Marbles of about three Inches Diameter, and which would in the open Airfuftaina Weight of lb. before they would fall asunder, would, in the exhausted Receiver, fall asunder with a Pound, and sometimes with half a Pound Weight. Nay, though when the Re Receiver was evacuated, the upper Marble being let down to touch the other, it would by no means adhere to it; yec when this was tryed after the Re - admidion of the Air into the Receiver, the Marbles then, on their being brought to touch each other, would asftrongiy adhere as at the first. Nay, in his Book against Linus he suggests, that ’ tis pro - table it may be some Hundreds, and even Thoufdnds of Miles high, in case the Atmosphere be not a bounded Portion of the Air, but reach is high as it. But the Expansion of the Air encreasing in file lame Proportion as the incumbent Weight of the Atmosphere decreases, that is, as the Mercury in the Barometer finks, the upper Parts of the Air are much more rarified than the lower, and each Space answering to an Inch of Quicksilver, grows greater and greater; so that the Atmosphere, must be extended to a much greater Height. ATMOSPHERE of confident Bodies: The Ho - nourable Mr. Boyle hath written a small Essay ora this Subject, in which he proves, that very many, and therefore probably all Solid, firm and confflent Bodies ( i. e. such as are not Fluid ) have, at some certain times ( at least ) effluvia of Particles of Matter which exhale from them: For he found, that many such Bodies would in a little time be very sensibly diminished in Weight: That some Electrical Bodies, as Amber and Glass, would ex - ert that Property uniformly all round them when they were heated; which they usually exhibit up - on Rubbing or Chafing; vi. That of attrading small Bodies to them: That Glass, Stones and hard Metals, would, on being rub ’ d one against another, strongly emit not only sensible, but even offensive Odours, &c,

ATMOSPHERE, from what hath been shewn in Fd. I. under this Word, it appears to be plainly impossible to Account for To great a Rarefaction and Condensation as is Discovered to be in the At - molpherical Air, without the Suppofidon of the Particles of Matter, being endued with a Repelling oi. a or Levitating Force, whereby they mutually avoid one another, till they come within the Distance, where the Attractive Force begins. See AttraBion For as the Learned Mr. Halley observes, at the Close ot his Proposition about the Heights of the Mer - curia Cylinder, at any Elevation above the Ear - thy Surface. See Phil. Trans. N.. It seems a very hard Question, that the Texture or Composition of Parts can be capable of so great an Expansion and Contraction as is found to be in the Air, and can scarce be Ac counted for, from comparing it to Wooll, or such like Spungy Bodies.

atome.c: ATOME, is such a very small Particle of Mat - ter, that it cannot Physically be cut or divided into lesser Parts: Epicurus and his Set of Philosophers, first called the component Principles of all Bodies,, which they supposed to be infinitely small and hard, by this Name of Atoms. The ! t Atoms may be supposed to have these inseparable Properties; . That they are all of the fame Nature, Sub - stance or Matter; for all Matter abftraded from ! Form is the fame.. That they have all some Magnitude or Quantity; for they are not Indi - visible Points, but Fhyfical Bodies of some ( " though small ) determinate Bulk.. They have also all of them some determinate Figure or Shape. And,. They must have also, each of them, some real Gravity or Weight. To these Sextus Empiricus adds eHiltTuvU or Rent enc; but this rather may be supposed to be the Consequence of their being Solid and InfeBile, which they are, as they are Atoms. The Original Qualities of Atoms can only be their Si e and their Figure, and these taken toge - ther make their Form.

arabilk.c: ARA Bilk, is supposed to be a kind of a Sul - phureous Terrene and Adust Salt, which being bred in the Body ( some will needs have it in the Spleen ) is circulated about in the Blood, and by that means makes an undue Fermentation in it, and is the Occasion of Melancholly and other such like Distempers. ‘ ATREUS, ATReUS, is One whose Fundament or Privy Parts are not perforated.
