attachamentbonorum.c: ATT ACH AMENT Bonorum, a Distress ta - ken upon the Goods or Chattels of any one such for Personal Estate or Debt by the Legal Attachia - tors or Bay lids, as a Security to answer the Adion.

att.c: ATT A CHI AMENT A de S pins & Bofio, is the Privilege granted to the Officers of a Forest to take to their own use Thorns, Brush and Windfall, within such Precinds or Liberties committed to their Charge.

attachment.c: ATTACHMENT, ( in Law ) is a Taking or Apprehending by Command or Writ: It differs from at Arrest in this, that an Arrest lies only up - on the Body of a Man, whereas an Attachment is sometimes on the Goods only, and sometimes on Body and Goods.

attachmentofprivilege.c: ATTACHMENT of Privilege, either gives Power to apprehend a Man in a Place privileged, or by Vertue of an Office or Privilege, to call ano - ther into that Court whereunto himself belong - ed !. v

attachmentforeign.c: ATTACHMENT Foreign, is a Process which is used to attach the Goods of Foreigners found within the Liberty or City, for a Debt due to the Party himself. A TTACHMCNT of the Forefl, is a Court held there every Days throughout the Year.

attack.c: ATTACK of a Siege, ( in the Art of War ) is the Effort made by theBefiegers with Trenches, Mines, Galleries and Breaches, in order to make them - themselves Matters of a Fortress in Storming one of its Sides..

attackfalse.c: ATTACK False, is that which is not vigorously prosecuted, fervlngonly to make a Diverlion among the Besieged, and to oblige them to divide their Forces, that the true Attack may be carried on with greater Success. To ATTACK in Flank., is to attack both Sides of the Bastion. To gain a Place by bright Attack., is to carry it by formal Attack and regular Works, without a general Storm. ATTAlNDURE, is when a Man hath commit - ted Felony or Treason, and Judgment is passed up - on him. The Children of a Person attainted of Treason cannot be Heirs to him, or any other An - cessor; and if he were Noble and Gentile before, thereby his Posterity are degraded and made Base; and this Corruption of Blood cannot be solved but by an Ad of Parliament, or unless the Judgment be reversed by Writ of Error.

attaint.c: ATTAINT, ( in Law ) is a Writ that lies where a false Verdid is given by twelve Men, which, if found to be a false Verdid, the twelve Men are Attaint, and the Verdid shall be, that their Mea - dows shall be ered, their Houses broken down, their Woods turned up, and their Lands and Tene - ments forfeited to the King But if it pass against him that brought that Attaint, he shall be impri - foned, and grievously ransomed at the King s Will.

attention.c: ATTENTION, is to register in the Memory those Trains of Ideas which continually offer themselves to the Mind, and are taken notice of.

attenuatingmedicines.c: ATTENUATING Medicines, those things which opening the Pores with their Acute Parti - cles, cut the thick and viscous Humours in the Bo - dy into such small Particles as that they may east - ly be circulated through the Vessels, and so there is made by degrees an

attenuation.c: ATTENUATION, or lessening of the Power or Quantity of the Morbifick Matter. ATTlCK, a kind of Order in Architecture af - ter the Manner of the City of Athens. Vitruvius makes it the Name of a Basis, which the Modem Architeds have since given to the Dorick Pillar In our Buildings, the Attick. is a little Order plac - ed upon another much greater, having, instead of Pillars, nothing but Pi Infers of a particular Form or Fashion,

attiretheheralds.c: ATTIRE, the Heralds call the Horns of a Stag or Buck his Attire.

attireinbotany.c: ATTIRE, in Botany, signifies, according to Dr. Grew, the third part belonging to theFlowerof a Plant; of which the two former are the Empale - ment and the Foliation. This Attire he finds to be of two kinds, Scmini - form and Florid; the Semini - form Attire c consists of two Parts, Chieves ( or th e Sta - mina. as some call them ) and Semets or Apices, one upon each Attire. The Florid Attire isufually called Thrums, as in the Flowers of Marigold, Tan - sey, &c. These Thrums the Dr. calls Suits, which consist of two, but most times of three Pieces; the outer Part of the Suit is the Floret, whose Bo - dy is divided at the Top like a Cow / lip Flower into Parts or distend Leaves.

attollensauriculam.c: ATTOLLENS Auriculam, is a Muffle which confiftsof divers fleffiy Fibres, and is annexed to that Part of the Pericranium rhat covers the Tem - coral Muffle, whence it descends directly to its Implantation at the Superiour Part of the second Wrinkle of the Cartilage of the Ear. Its Name fhewsits Use.

attolensoculos.c: ATTOLENS Oculos, or Superbus, one of the fix Pairs of Muffles that belong to the Eye, serving to lift them upwards.

attolensnares.c: ATTOLENS Nares, a Muffle of the Nose, whose Name ffiews its Use.

attollentes.c: ATTOLLENTES, are a Pair of Muffles which adding both together, draw all the upper Lip di - redly upward and outward; but if only one, then one Side of the Lip is drawn obliquely.

attonitusstupor.c: ATTONITUS, Stupor, feu Morbus Attonitus ? See Apoplexy.

attornato.c: ATTORNATO faciendo vet recipiendo, is Writ which a Man owing Suit to a County, Hun - dred, Wapentake, or other Court, and desiring to make an Attorney to appear for him, whom he doubteth whether the Sheriff or Bayliff will admit or not, purchafeth to command him to receive and admit him.

attornment.c: ATTORNMENT, fin Law ) is when one is Tenant for term of Life, and he in Reversion or Remainder grants his Right or Estate to another, then it behoves the Tenant for Life to agree thereto; aad this Agreement is called an Attourn ment.

attractingordrawingmedicinesorthings.h: ATTRACTING or Drawing Medicines or Things
attractingordrawingmedicinesorthings.c: ATTRACTING, or Drawing Medicines or Things, are those which opening the Pores with their little Particles, and dilating the Humours, and expelling them, where their Resistance is smaller, not only ffiews the Parts, and makes them Red, Red, but by driving more Vapours and Humours out of the Skin and Fieffi, than can make their way through s the thick inner Skin, gather them under it, and'fwell it into little Bladders,

attraction.c: ATTRACTION, is the drawing of one thing to another. Whether among the Operations of Natural Bodies one upon another, there be any such thing as Attra & ion, properly so speaking, is a Question that hath been much debated athongft Philosophers: And perhaps most of those Effects - which the Ancients, not knowing so well the Causes of, did use to attribute to AttraPHon, may now be very well solved by Pulsion. See James Bernouli, de Gravitate Ait her is, Amsterdam, in. However the Word is retained by good ' Naturalists, and in particular, by the Excellent Sr. Isaac Newton in his Principia; but without there determining any thing of the Quale of it, for he doth not confider things so much Physical - ly, as Mathematically. This therefore being pre - mifedj he lays it down as an Axiom; That since Aftion and Rp - action arc always equal and directly contrary to each other; therefore if any thing At - ' tradt another, it is it self also as much attradled by that other thing; taking Attraction in the largest and most general Sense, for the Conatus of one Body towards another however it be caused. And in Cor.. Prop. he ( hews, . That if two Bodies mutually do attraSl each other ( by which he means the fame as gravitate towards one another ) by Forces proportionable to their Distances, they will describe both about the common Centre of Gravity, and about one ano - ther Concentrical Ellipses; and vice versa, if any Body do describe such Figures, their Gravitating or Attra & ing Forces are proportional to their Di - stances. Z. That if they Attradfc each other with Forces proportional to the Squares of their Distances, they will describe both about the common Centre of Gravity, and also about one another, Conicl Se & ions, having their Umbilici in the Centre a - bout which the Figures are described; and vice versa, &c. . He demonstrates also, That any Particle of Matter within the Superficies of any Sphere or Globe, is attradled or gravitates by a Force proportional to its distance from the Centre; but without the Surface of the Sphere, by a Force proportional to the Square of its Distance from the Centre, Prop - -. Hence it will follow, he faith; . That at equal Distances from the Centre of Homogeneal Spheres, The Attraction will be as the Sphere. z. And at any Distance whatever, the Attracti - on is as the Sphere divided by the Square of the Distance. ; Which last holds also in the Attractions of Spheres towards one another; i. e. the Attracti - ons are as the attracting Globes divided by the Squares of the Distances, though the Globes mu - tually attract each other. The Quantity of the Force of Attraction in all Bodies at equal Distances, is exactly proportion - table to the Quantity of Matter in the Attracting Body, as being in reality nothing but the Result or Sum of the united Forces of all those single Particles of which it is composed. See Vol, II.

ATTRACTION, Sir Isaac Newton at the end of the Latin Edition of his Excellent Book of Op - ticks, Qu. a a. fire ws that of thole Bodies which are of the fame Nature, Kind, and Virtue, by how much less any Body is than another, the greater is its At - tracking Force, in proportion to its Magnitude. Thus ’ tis found that the Magnetic Attraction is stronger in a Small Load - stone, in proportion to its Weight, than in a Larger: For the Particles of small Magnets, being nearer one to another, and can more easily Combine or Join their Forces into one. Wherefore the Rays of Light, being the least of all Bodies that we know, must needs have the greatest and strongest Attracting Force and how ve - ry strongly those Particles do Attract, may be Col - elected by the following Calculation. The Attra - ction of a Ray of Light, with regard to the Quan - tity of its Matter, is to the Gravity which any projected Body hath, in proportion to the Quanti - ty of matter in that Body:: in a Ratio Com - pounded of the Velocity oi a Ray of Light, to the Velocity of that projected Body, and of the Flex - D are t AT T ure or Curvature of the Line which the Ray de - fcribes in the place of its RefraCtion, to the Cur - nature or Flexure of the Line which the laid pro - jected Body describes. That is, supposing the In - clination of the Ray, to the Refradting Surface be the fame with that of the Horizon. And from this Proposition he Calculates that the At trad: ion of the Rays of Light is above a Thousand Millions of Millions of Times greater than the Force of Gravity on the Earths Surface, according to the Quantity of matter in each, and supposing Light to come from the Sun thither in about seven or eight Minutes. And in the very point of ContaCf of the Rays, their Attracting Force may be yet much greater. Now luch a prodigious Force of AttraBion in the Rays of Light cannot but have wonderful Ef - sects in those particles of Matter, with which they are joyned in the Composition of Bodies; and must cause that those particles AttraCt one ano - ther, and that they are moved variously among themselves. ’ Tis very probable therefore that the Small Par - titles of Bodies have certain Virtues, Powers or For - ces, by which at a small distance they may aCt not only on the Pays of Light to PefraB, PejleB or In - sect them, but alio mutually on one another, in order to Produce nioft of the Phenomena of Nature. ’ Tis very well known that some Bodies do thus aCt on one another by the AttraBions of Gravity, Mag - netifm and EleBricity: And these Examples shew what the Peafon and Order of Nature is and make it very probable that there may be yet some other AttraBions, for Nature is very uniform and agree - able to it self. Now the AttraBions of Gravity, Magnet ism and EleBricity extend themselves to considerable Di - fiances, and therefore are commonly observed and taken notice of by every one. But ’ tis very pofli - ble that there may be many others also, which are contain ’ d in such narrow Limits, and performed within such a little Distance as yet to have escaped all our Observations. For when Salt of Tartar runs per deliquium or diffolves into an Oil as the Chymifts call it, ’ tis ve - ry probable that it is occasion ’ d by some AttraBion which is mutual between the Particles of the Salt, and those of Water, which rove up and down in the Air in the Form of Vapour, and the reason why common Salt, Nitre and Vitriol, don ’ t run thus per deliquium, is because they are without any such Attractions; and when Salt of Tartar hath drawn as much Water out of the Air as its Quan - tity will bear, it draws no more, because when it ’ s Saturated the Attraction is at end. It must be also from its Attractive Force, that the Water thus im - bibed by the Salt, cannot he separated from it in dist il - lation, hut hy a very violent Heat; whereas Water will usually distill off with a very easie Heat, from other Things. ’ Tis much the fame thing with Oil of Vitriol, which till it is Saturated with it, At - tracts the Moisture of the Air in very considerable Quantity, and afterwards parts with it with great difficulty. And when Oyi of Vitriol and Water being mingled together in the fame Vessel, grow so hot, as it is known they will do, it appears plainly by that Heat that a very great Motion is excited in the Particles of the two Liquors; and from that Motion it appears that their Particles in mingling Co - alefce with a great Force and Impetufioty and consequently AttraCt or Gravitate towards one ano - Her with an accelerated Motion, Thus also when A T T Aquafortis, Spirit of Vitriol or Nitre, or any other Corro CiveMenfiruum diffolves Filings of Iron or any other Metal with Heat and Ebullition; ’ tis plain that the Acid Particles of the Menflruum attract and rush upon those of the Metal with a very great Force enter into their Pores with violence, and dis - joyn or separate the small Corpuscles of which the Metal is composed one from another tho ’ the Par - titles of the Acid Menstruum are drawn off ' at first when they are made a moderate Heat, yet af - ter their Union they with the parts of the Metal, cannot be drawn off as yet by Distillation, but by a most intense and violent Heat, When Spirit of Vitriol poured upon common Salt or Nitre, makes an Ebullition and Coalelces with the Salt; and when after this if the Compost be Distilled, a Spirit of Salt or Nitre will be drawn off much easier than without such a Mixture j it shews plainly that the Fixt Alkali of the Salt At - trans the Acid Spirit fof the Vitriol much more strongly than it doth its own Spirit, and because it cannot retain then both it Parts with its own Spirit freely. When Oil of Vitriol is distill ’ d from an equal Weight of Nitre, and from both is drawn off ' a Compound Spirit of Nitre, and that Spirit is poured upon half its Weight of Oil of Cloves, of C ar,: w ay - feed, or any Ponderous Oil diftili ’ d from vegetable or animal Bodies, or upon Oil of Tur - pontine, mix ’ d with a little Ballam of Sulphur to thicken it j when in any of thele Mixtures an a & u - ai Flame will be produc ’ d, ’ tis apparent that the Particles of the Spirit and Oil must rush towards one another with a strong accelerated Motion, and struggle and fight with a most violent Force and Impetus. Tis the fame Thing when that compoud Spirit is poured upon well rectified Spirit of Wine, for a Flame will immediately arise on their Mix - ture, The Pulvis fulminans, as they call it, which is compos ’ d of Sulphur, Nitre and Salt of Tartar, goes off with a more quick and violent Explosion than even Gun - powder it self. The acid Spirits of the Sulphur and the Nitre ruffling together with such Violence, that all the Parts of the Powder are Ta - riffed, as it were, at once and altogether. Thus also common Crude and impure Brimflone it self, if it be powder ’ d and mingled with an equal Weight of Filings of Iron or Steel, and with a lit - tle Water be made up into thick Past, like Dough the Sulphur will aCi so upon the Iron, that in five or fix Hours Time, the Mass will grow so hot as not to bear handling, and at last will plainly burn and emit a Flame. Now from all these Experiments, and from the Consideration of the great Quantity of Sulphur that there is in the Earth, and of the great Heat of the inner Parts of it, from the hot Springs, the burning Volcanos, the Fire Damps and burning Exhalations that are found in the Bowels of the Earth; from the Considerations of Earth - quakes, Whirl - winds and the wonderful Convulsions that the Sea is some times put into we may understand, That the Particles of Bodies, - before at reft ( and ’ tis the fame Thing also in all Fermentations, &c. ) may be and are put into most violent Motions, by some Principle of very great Force und ACHvity, which yet doth not discover it self till the Parts approach and come very near one another; but that they do then attrap one another with great Force and Rapidity, and thereby pro - due their wonderful Effects. Again, when Oil of Tartar Per deliquium is poured upon the Solution of any Metal, their is a Precipitation of - the Metalline Particles produc ’ d,. which. which all fall down to the Bottom of the Vessel from whence it appears, That the Particles of the Liquor are more strongly attracted by thole of the Oil of Tartar than by those of the Metal; and by that Attraction are precipitated down from the Liquor: So alio when a Soluti - on of Iron in Aqua Fords will dissolve Cadmia, and precipitate its Iron; or when a Solution of Copper will dissolve Iron, and let go the Copper, ( fee depart ) Sec. This seems to prove plainly, that the Acid Particles are more strongly ater ailed by those of the Metal that. they dissolve, than by those of that Which is let go. When we find that those Men - ftruums which will dissolve one kind of Metal or mix d Body, and wont touch another, it muff be attributed ro the Attraction that there is between the Particles in some Cafes, and there being no such in the other. And in the General it is owing to this Principle, that Heat, according to Aristotle ' s Definition of it doth congregate or gather together homogeneous Things, and separate those which are of a different Nature: After this He hews how On this Principle, and by the Help of Chymical Analyfes, to come to the Knowledge of what kind of Parts natural Bodies are composed. The Reason why Drops of Water, or other li - quid Body usually put on a spherical Form, he faith, is also from the mutual Attraction of their Parts; after the fame Manner as the Earth and Seas make one round Body by the mutual Attra - ction or Gravitation of their Parts. And because when Metals are dissolve ’ d in Acids, they attrap but a small Portion of the Menstruum to them, therefore he concludes, that their Force of Attraction extends but a very little Way. And as in Algebra, when affirmative Quantities vanish and terminate, their negative begin: So in Me - chanic's, where Attraction ceases to exert it self, a kind of repelling Force should succeed; and that there is in Nature such a Force, seems to follow from the Reflection and Inflection of the Rays of Light; for in both these Cafes, the Rays are repel - led from Bodies without the immediate Contact of the reflecting or infleCting Body. And the lame Thing seems concludable from the Emission of Light; for a Ray of it, as soon as it is fliaken out of the lucent Body by the vibrating Motion of its Parts, and is got without the Sphere of its Attraction is propelled with a very great Degree of Velocity; and the lame Force which in Refle - xion serves to resell the Ray, now serves to emit it. The Production of Air and Vapours doth alio shew, that there is a repelling Force; for those Par - titles which are forced out of the Bodies by Heat or Fermentation, as soon as ever they are out of the Sphere of the Attraction of these Bodies, do immediately recede from it, and from another with a great Force, and do avoid coming together again; so that sometimes they take up above a Million of Times the Space which they did before, when they were in theForm of a Dense Body, which is so very great a Contraction and liapanflon as is hardly conceivable, if the Particles of the Air be only elastical, rimose and coiled up one within an - ther, like the Tendrels ol Vines, or Springs of Marches, as some have imagine ’ d: Nor indeed, Will any other Hypothesis Account for this wonder - ful Phenomenon, but this of their being end ’ d With a repelling Force, by which they mutually avoid one another, as well as the Bodies from Whence they at first came. - a x

attribute.c: ATTRIBUTE, is whatever Property belongs properly to any Substance or Being, and is af - firmed of it, or duly attributed to it, or predicated of it, as the Logicians speak.

attritioninphysick.c: ATTRITION, in Physick, is the Rubbing of one thing against another as when Amber and c - ther Eledtrick Bodies are rnbb ’ d, to make them at - tract or emit their Elect rick Force.

attritionintheology.c: ATTRITION, in Theology, is a Sorrow for offending God, arising from.. the Apprehension of being obnoxious to Punishment and Mifcry on the Account of such Offence,

attorneyorattorney.c: ATTORNEY, or Attorney, in a Legal Accep - tation, signifies one appointed by another Man to do any thing in his stead; and is as much as Procu - razor or Syndicus in the Civil Law; or Attorneys are such Persons, as are by the Consent, Command - ment or Request of another, to take heed, fee to; and take upon them, the Charge of another Man ’ s Business in his absence.

avantfojfe.c: AVANT Fojfe, or Ditch of the Counterscarp, in Fortification, is a Moat or Ditch full of Water run - ning round the Counterscarp on the outside next the Campaign at the Foot of the Glacis. It is not eli - gisle to have such a Water - Ditch where it can be drained dry; because it is a Trench ready made for the Besiegers to defend themselves against the Sallies of the Besieged. Besides, it hinders put - ting Succours into the Place, or at Ieaft makes it more difficult so ro do.

avastaword.c: AVAST, a Word used very commonly aboard a Ship, signifying to stop, hold or stay.

audiencecourt.c: AUDIENCE Court, is a Court belonging to the Archbiffiop of Canterbury, of equal Authority with the Arches Court, though inferiour both in Digni - ty and Antiquity.

audiendo.c: AUDIENDO & Terminando, is a Writ, but more properly a Commission, directed to certain Persons, when any Riotous Assembly, Infurre & i - on, or heinous Mifdemeanour, or Trespass is com - mitted against any Place.

auditaquerela.c: AUDITA Querela, is a Writ that lies where one is bound in a Statute or Recognisance, or where Judgment is given against him for a Debt, and his Body in Execution thereupon; for if he have a Release, or any other sufficient Discharge, but has no Day in Court to plead it, then he ffiail have this Writ against him which hath recovered, or against his Executors.

auditorynerve.c: AUDITORY Nerve is the seventh Pair of Nerves that comes from the Medulla Oblongata, arising from the hinder part of the Procejfus Annularis; it enters the Hole in the inner Process of the Os Pe - tr ofum. It is divided into two Branches; that which is soft is called Portio Mollis, and it is distributed into the Labyrinth, Cochlea, and the Membranes which cover theGavities of the Ear. That which is hard, is called Porti Dura; it goes out of the Ear by the Hole which is between the Procejfus Maftoidts arid Styloidesj it is divided into twdi Branches, of which one goes to the Mttfeles of the Tongue, dr Os Hyoides, and it gives a small Branch to the eighth Pair; the other is distributed in the External Ear, Nole, Lips and Cheeks.

auditor.c: AUDITOR, according to ous Law; is an Os cer of the King or some other great Person, which yearly, by examining the Accounts of all under Officers accountable, makes up a general Book with the Difference between their Receipts and Charge, and their Allowances; commonly called Allocations; as namely; the Auditor's of the Exche A V E que take the Accounts of those Receivers, who colled: the Revenues of the Augmentation, as al - io of the Sheriffs, Efcheators, Collectors and Cu - ftomers, and fet them down and versed them.

AUDITOR of the Receipts, is an Officer of the Exchequer that files the Teller ’ s Bills, and makes an Entry of them, and gives the Lord Treasurer a Certificate of the Money received the Week be - fore. He maketh Debentures to every Teller, be - fore they pay any Money, and taketh their Ac - counts: He keepeth the Black Book, of Receipts, and the Treasurer s Key of the Treasury, and teeth everyTeller ’ money lock ’ d up in theNewTreafury.

auditors.c: AUDITORS of the Prejl or Imprcft, are Offi - cers in the Exchequer, who take and make up the great Accounts of Ireland, Berwick, the Mint, and of any Money imprest to any Man for the King ’ s Service.

avelanetheform.c: AVELANE, the Form of a Cross which the He - ralds give us, which resembles Filberds in their Husks or Cafes, joined together at the great End - from whence it seems to take its Name, for a Filberd is Nux Avellana.

aventure.c: AVENTURE, ( but more properly ) Adventure, is a Term in Law signifying a Mischance, causing the Death of a Man without Felony, as when he is suddenly drowned or burnt, falling into the Wa - ter or Fire, or killed by any Disease or Mischance.

avenue.c: AVENUE, ( in Fortification ) is an opening or inlet into any Fort, Bastion, or such like P'ace.

average.c: AVERAGE, ( in Law ) is that Service which the Tenant owes to his Lord, to be done by theBeafts of the Tenant. It all dignifies a certain Contribution which Merchants and others pay proportionably towards their Losses that have their Goods call away in a Tempest, for the saving of the Ship or Goods, or the Lives of them that are therein.

averiis.c: AVERIIS c apt is in Withernamps a Writ for the taking ofCattelto his use, thathath hisCattel unlaw - fully takenby another, and driven out of theCounty where theyare taken, that they cannot bereplevy ’ d.

averment.c: AVERMENT, ( in Law ) is where a Man pleads a Plea in Abacement. of the Writ, or Barr of Acti - on, which he says he is ready to prove, as the Court will award. This offer to prove the Plea Is called an Averment.

averpeny.c: AVERPENY, is to be quit of divers Sums of Money for the King ’ s Arrearages.

averruncationinagriculture.c: AVERRUNCATION, in Agriculture, figni - fies the lopping off superfluous Branches.

augeanastronomicalterm.c: AUGE, an Astronomical Term, the fame as A - f ogceum, is that Point of the Orbit ) wherein a Pla - net being, is furthest distant from the Central Bo - dy about which it revolves, and is then flowed: in Motion, insomuch that from this Point the distance of a Planet is reckoned, to find thereby the Ine - quality of its Motion.

augmentation.c: AUGMENTATION, was the Name of a Court ereCted by King Henry the Eighth, for the encrease of the Revenues of the Crown, by the Suppreffi - on of the Abbies and Religious Houses: This Court was dissolved in Q. Marys Reign; but the Office of Augmentation remains to this Day, wherein there are many Records of great ule and I importance.

aumone.c: AUMONE, ( Tenure in Aumone ) is a Tenure per liberam E ’ eemofynam, as where Lands are gi - ven to some Church, or Religious House, upon Con - dition that some Service or Prayers shall be offered at certain times for the good of the Donor's Soul.

avowee.c: AVOWEE, is he to whom the Right of Ad - vowfon of any Church appertaineth, so that he may present in his own Name; and is called Avowee; for a difference from those that sometimes present in another ’ s Name, as a Guardian that prefenteth in the Name of his Ward: And also to be distil - guifhed from those which have the Lands where - unto znAdvowfon appertaineth, but only for term of theirLives, of Years, or by Intrusion, or byDiffeifin.

avowry.c: AVOWRY ( a Law Term ) is, when one takes a Distress for Rent or other thing, and the other files Replevin; now he that took the Distress juftifying the ACt, is laid to Avow it.

auriculaecordis.c: AURICULAE Cordis, are two Appendages to the Heart, seated at its Balls over the Ventricles they are so called from some Resemblance that they bear to the Ears of a Man ’ s Head. They a - rife from a long Basis, and end in an obtuse Point, thereby forming an obtuse Triangle. They are of the lame Fabrick and ule with the Ventricles over which they stand, being Muscles as they are, made up of the lame order of Fibres, which are carried into opposite Tendons; whereof that at the Basis of the Heart is common to it and the Auriculaf, and the other runs along their upper part. The Right Auricle is larger and softer than the Left. he Superficies of both is smooth when they are full, but wrinkled when empty, and more so in the Left than in the Right One. On being cut o - pen they exhibit many fleshy Columns running from the Upper Tendon to the Lower, and be tween them there are pretty deep Furrows or long Cavities, but sewer in the Right Auricle than in the Left. They are dilated and contracted in like manner as the Heart is, but at different times for the Systole of the Ventricles is at the fame time with the Diajlole of the Auricles and vice versa j so that, the Auricles are receiving their Blood from the Veins, while the Ventricles are expelling theirs into the Arteries: But when the Ventricles are relaxed and empty in their Diajlole, then the Auri - cles force the Blood into them by their Syjlolei Theyare nourifhedby Branches ofArteriesfpringing from the Coronaria, which Dr. Ruyfch ( who seems first to have taken notice of this calls therefore Arterice Auriculares, and no doubt but they have Branches also of Veins to attend them. Their Use is to receive the Venal Blood which comes immediately out of the Vena Cava and Pulmonark, and to measure it as it were ( faith Gibson ) into the Ventricles; and to expel it thither with the great - er Force, the Internal Fibres or Columns of their Cavity arising from their Root where they are joined to the Balls of the Heart, reach direCtly out - wards towards the Vena Cava zndPulmonam; and in the Diajlole of the Auricula, grasp the Blood contained in their Cavities like so many Fingers, and fqueezeit into the Ventricles, now relaxed in their Di all ole.

aurigaaconstellation.c: AURIGA, a Constellation consisting of Stars in the Northern Hemisphere.

aurumfulminant.c: AURUM Fulminant, or Saffron of Gold, is thus made; put a Drachm of thin Plates of Gold into a Matrass, and then pour on it by little and little ( or else there will be so great an Eflerve - science, that the Matter will boil over the Glass ) or Drachms of Aqua Regal is. Set the Matrass in warm Sand, and when the Ebullitions are over, the Menstruum will have dissolved as much of the Gold Gold as it can contain. Pour off the Solution, by Inclination, into another Glass, and then pour into the Mixture gradually, some of the Volatile Spi - rit of Sal Armoniacl i, or Oil of Tartar per deli - auium, and the Gold will precipitate to the Bot - tom of the Glass: Let it stand a while till all is sal - len down, then pour off the Liquor, and wash the Powder carefully with warm Water till it grows insipid: Then dry it in a Paper by a gentle Fire, taking care it do not fire, which ’ tis apt to do with a terrible Noise. If you dissolve a Drachm of Gold, there will be Scruples of Aurum Fulminant well dried. It takes its Name from its fulminating or making a great Noise like Thunder, when ’ tis heat - ed over the Fire in a Spoon, for it will go off like a Gun, but without doing any Mischief, its Force being chiefly downward. The Effect seems to come from some Parts of the Aqua Regal ss, which re - main still sticking in the Gold, and these being of a very Spirituous and Volatile Nature, do break out with great Violence when the Powder comes to rake Fire. Those who would know a way to make as great, but yet a much less expensive Noise, may see the Word Pulvis Fulminant. If half its W eight of Sulphur powdered, be mingled with Aurum Ful - minant, its fulminating Quality will be destroyed. Though on several Trials designedly made to make Gun - powder take Fire in Mr. Boyle ’ s exhaust - ed Receiver, it could not be effected; yet he found that Aurum Fulminant would take Fire there, and go off, both by means of a Burning - Glass, and of a Piece of hot Iron.

aurummofaicum.c: AURUM Mofaicum, is made by mixing and subliming Mercury, Tin, Sulphur and Sal Armoni - ack all together.

aurumpotabile.c: AURUM Potabile: The Alchymists pretend to be able to separate the Salt and Sulphur of Gold, and then dissolving it in a Liquor, it may be drank, and therefore is called Aurum Potabile: But this is a meer Imposture, the Aurum Potabile being no - thing usually but some rich Cordial Liquor with Pieces of Leaf - Gold in ir

austeretast.c: AUSTERE Tast, is such an one as moderately constringes the Mouth and Tongue with some Afpe - city, as is the Tast of unripe Fruits.

australsigns.c: AUSTRAL Signs, are the fix last Signs of the cdiac !; so called, because they are on the South Side of the Equinoctial.

authenticksthewordauthentic.c: AUTHENTICKS, The Word Authentic fig - nifies of good Authority; and therefore the d Volume or Tome of the Civil Law, is Called The Authenticity, from the Greek Word nvS - svletr, be - cause it hath its Authority from it self, and proceed - ing from the Emperour s own Mouth; or else that they are Originals to other Writings which are transcribed out of them. They are a Volume of new Constitutions, fet out by Just ini an the Em - perour, after the Code, and brought into the Body of the Law, under one Book. There is not in these that good Order and Me - tho observed, as there is in the Code, or in the Di - gest; but as any doubtful Point came to be confi - dered, you have here the Princes Determination of it; and that fet down as the Cafes occasionally occurred. The whole Volume is divided into Nine Colla - tions, C institutions or Sections ( I mean in the La - tin Version, for in the Greek there is not this Di - vision into Collations ) and these are subdivided into Novels, each of which is distributed into several Chapters. They are called Novels, because they were New Laws in comparison of the Code and Digcfl - just as the Constitutions of the Empe - hours which were newly published after the Baftli - ca were called the Novels of Leo, Nicepkorw, Mi - chanel, See.

autography.c: AUTOGRAPHY, is the peculiar Hand Writ - ting of any particular Person; or the Original of of any Treatise or Discourse, in relpedfc of a Co - py.

automata.c: AUTOMATA, are Mechanical or Mathema - tical Instruments or Engines, that going by a Spring, Weight, &c. seem to move of themselves, as a Watch, a Clock, - &c.

autopsy.c: AUTOPSY, is Ocular Inlpe & ion, or seeing a thing vi ith our own Eyes.

auxiliaryverbs.c: AUXILIARY Verbs, in Grammar, are such as help to form or conjugate others; as to have and to be in the Englijh Tongue, Eftre and Avoir in the French, Italian, Spanish, cc.

auxiliumcuria.c: AUXILIUM Curia, a Precept or Order o Court, for the citing or convening of one Party at the Suit of another.

auxiliumpetere.c: AUXILIUM Petere, in Law, signifies to pray Suit in a Cause; that is, when an inferiour Te - nant is impleaded, and not capable to defend the Right in his own Name; he prayeth Aid of the Superiour Lord to assist and justify his Plea.

auxiliumbeats.c: AUXILIUM Beats, King ’ s Aid, or Money le - vy ’ d for the Ring ’ s Use, and publick Service.

auxiliumvicecomitum.c: AUXILIUM Vicecomitum, the Aid or Cufto - mary Dues paid to the Sheriff, for the better sup port of his Office.

award.c: AWARD, ( a Term in Law ) properly signifying the Judgment of one that is neither assigned by Law, or appointed by the Judges for the ending a Matter in Controversie, but is chosen by the Par - ties themselves that are at variance.

awninbotany.c: AWN, in Botany, Arista, is the Beard growing out of the Husk of Corn or Graft.

awning.c: AWNING, aboard a Ship, is when a Sail, g Tarpaulin, or the like, is hung over any part of the Ship above the Decks, to keep off the Sun, the Rain, or the Wind. In a Long - Boat, they make an Awning by bringing the Sail over the Yard and Stay, and looming it out with the Boat - Hook. AX or Axe, the fame with Axis, which lee;

axillarveins.c: AXILLAR Veins, ate the two Branches of the ascending Trunk of the Vena Cava, called Bami Suiclavii, which running obliquely under the Claviculce, as soon as they are past them, and go up to the Armpits, are called Axidares: And each of these parts it self into two Veins, the Cc - phalica and Baftlica.

axillaryartery.c: AXILLARY Artery, is that part of the Subcla - vian Branches of the ascending Trunk of the Aor - ta, that is got out of thcThorax and comes into the Arm - pits.

axiom.c: AXIOM, is such a common, plain, self evident and received Notion, that it cannot be made more plain and evident by Demonstration because ' tis its self much better known than any thing that can be brought to prove it; as, That nothing can act where it is not: That a thing cannot be and not be at the fame time: That the Whole is greater than a Part: That where there is no Law. there isnoTrtmf - greftion, &c.

axis.c: AXIS, is the third Vertebra from the SkulL
AXIS of a Cylinder, is that Quiescent Right Line ' Line, about which the Parallelogram is turned, which by its Revolution forms the Cylinder.
AXIS of a Comely Section, is a Line palling through the Middle of the Figure, and perpend - cular to the Ordinates.
AXIS of a Figure, is a Streight Line, conceived to proceed from the Vertex to the Base.
AXIS of a Circle or Sphere, is a Streight Line palling through the Center from one Side to ano - ther; and is the fame with the Diameter.
AXIS of the World, is an imaginary Line con - ceiled to pass through the Center of the Earth from one Pole to another.
AXIS of the Zpdiacl, is also conceived to pass through the Earth, and. to be terminated in the Poles of the Zpdiack.

AXIS of any Glass ( in Opticks ) is a Right Line drawn perpendicularly through the Centre of the Glass; or if it be a Convex Glass, through the thickest Part; if a Concave, through the thinnest Part ( which in each is called the Pole of the Glass ) direCtly on to the Centre of the Sphere, the Glass Figure is a Segment of.

axisofflotationorcircumvolution.c: AXIS of Flotation or Circumvolution, is an i - imaginary Line, about which any plain Figure is conceived to be turned to make a Solid: Thus a Sphere is conceived to be made by the Rotation of a Semi - circle about its Diameter; and a night Cone by that of a Right angled Triangle about its Perpendicular.

axissecundm.c: AXIS Secundm, in the Hyperbole and Ellipjis, is the Conjugate Diameter, which fee. This is some - times called the Axis Rectus.

axisinopticas.c: AXIS, in Opticas, is the Ray which of all that are sent to the Eye falls perpendicularly on it, and which, by consequence, passeth through the Center of the Eye.

axiscommonormean.c: AXIS Common or Mean, is a Right Line drawn from the Point of Concourse of the two Optick Nerves through the Middle of the Right Line which Joins the Extremity of the fame Opticl Nerves.

axisofincidence.c: AXIS of Incidence, in Dioptricks, is a Right Line drawn through the Point of Incidence, and perpendicular to the Refracting Surface.

axisofrefraction.c: AXIS of Refraction, is that which is made by the Ray of Incidence, direCtly prolonged on the Inside of the second Medium by the Ray of Re - fraction.

axisinperitrochio.c: AXIS in Peritrochio, is a Machine for the rai - ling of Weights, consisting of a Cylindrical Beam ( which is the Axis ) lying Horizontally, and sup - ported at each End by a Piece of Timber; and somewhere about it, it hath a kind of Tympanum or Wheel, which is called the Peritrochium, in whose Circumference are Holes made to put in Staves ( like those of a Windlefs or Capftain ) in order to turn the Axis round the more easily, and thereby to raise the Weight required by Means of a Rope which winds round the Axis. See Vol. II.

From the Fabrick of the Engine, tis plain tha the Weight W is at every Revolution of the Axis rais ’ d so much, " as is the Girt of the Axis; and con - sequently the larger the Axis, th e. quicker rises the Weight ( with a proportionable Power ) but yet the harder And the less the Axis is, the flower fifes the Weight, bus the easier. Wfe'efofe A Z I A Z I Wherefore if the Weight be to the Power, as the Perimeter of the Peritrochium is to the Perime - ter of the Axis; then will the Velocity of the Po - wer to that of the Weight, be as the Weight to the Power; and consequently the Moment of the Power will be equal to that of the Weight; Wherefore ’ tis Plain, that the greater the Perime - ter or outermost Wall, the longer the Stick or Lever DC: Or on the other, the lesser the Dia - meter of the Axis, the easier will the fame Force move the Weight assigned.

axisindeterminate.c: AXIS Indeterminate of an Hyperbola, is a Right Line which divides into two equal Parts, and at Right Angles, an infinite number of Lines drawn parallel to one another within the Hyperbola.

axisdeterminate.c: AXIS Determinate, in that Figure, is a Right Line drawn between the Vertexes or Tops of the opposite Se & ions or Hyperbola.

axisconjugatus.c: AXIS Conjugatus, in the Hyperbola: See Conju - gate.

azimuthcompass.c: AZIMUTH Compass, is an Instrument made in a large Box, with Jambols and a broad Limb, having Deg. diagonally divided, with an Index and Thread to take the Sun ’ s Amplitude or Azimuth, in order to find the Difference between theMagneti - cal Meridian and the Suns Meridian, which shews thtVariation of the Compass.

azimuthsorverticalcircles.c: AZIMUTHS, or Vertical Circles, are great Circles interfering each other in the Zenith and Nadir, ( as Meridians or Hour - Circles do in the Pole ) and cutting the Horizon at Right Angles. On the Globes these Circles are not drawn, but are represented by the Quadrant of Altitude when it is screwed in the Zenith. And on these Azimuths is reckoned the Sun's ! Altitude, when he is not on the Meridian.

azoth.c: AZOTH, among the Chymists, signifies some - times an Universal Medicine, sometimes the Mer - cury of a Metal.

azuretheherald.c: AZURE, the Herald ’ s Term for a Blue Co - lour in the Coats of all Persons under the Degree of a Baron j but in the Escutcheons of the Noblemen ’ tis called Saphir; and in those of Sovereign Princes ’ tis called Jupiter. In Engraving ' tis represented by Strokes or Hatches drawn only Horizontal - ly, thus, as in the annexed Figure.

azugus.c: AZUGUS or AZYGOS, is a notable Brandi of the Vena Cava, called Vena fine pari, because it is single, having no Fellow It descends through the right side of the Cavity of the Thorax, and when ’ tis come as far as the Eighth or Ninth Vertex Ira, it begins just to keep the Middle, and fends forth on each Side Intercostal Branches to the Inter - ftices of the Eight lowest Ribs, and there is divid - ed into two Branches, of which the Larger de - ascends to the Left, betwixt the Processes of the Diaphragm, and is inserted sometimes into the Cava above or below the Emulgent, but oftner into the Emulgent it self. The other, which goes down on the Right - hand, enters the Cava, commonly a lit - tle above the Emulgent, but very seldom is join - ed to the Emulgent it self.

abc.c: ABC is the Prism, upon one of whole Sides is put a Past - board or thick Paper A B, or the like, with a little round Hole at E, which being ex - posed to the Sun ’ s Rays D E, they are refracted and carried ( in Colours ) toward H I. HI is a Lens ( or a common Magnifying Glass ) broad enough to receive all the coloured Rays; where they being made to converge by the Glass, they will be united in O, the Focus of the Glass, Hold a Piece of Paper L in the Focus, where all the Colours are united, and the little Spot a. t O will be versed Light or Whitenels: But if the Pa - per K L be held farther or nearer off ( as at M or N ) the Colours will appear. If any Colours be intercepted, as at P, the Light near O will not be clear White, but inclining to the remaining Co - lours. If the Blue be wanting, the White will be somewhat Reddish or Flesh - colour, and if the Red be wanting, the White will encline to be something Bluish: And if only one Colour be let come to the Lens, that Colour, without Alteration, will be trans - / err ’ d to the Paper K. L, This Mr " This Experiment hews, ( i. ) That all the Co - lours being united make Eight or Whiteness. ( z. ) That if any Original Colour be wanting, the White will not be pure. (. ) That a Simple Co - lour is not alterable by farther Refractions, which also will appear if another Pnfm be put Lt O Experiment IV Let ABGH be a Piece of fine Silk of a lively Scarlet Colour, whose Edges AB and GH are streight, parallel and smooth; let DES be a - J c cl.. D H Ks ias OB IS I II Bfllhas A nother Piece of Violet Blue Silk, like and equal to the other. Let them be placed, as in the Figure, on some black Cloth or Door, with their Edges in a straight Line: View them through a Prism at about two or three Yards distance: The Ax of the Prism being parallel to the Position of the Silks: So will the blue Piece CF appear lower than the other as in des. TheReafonof which Appearance is, that Blue is more Refran - gisle than Red. This will more fully appear, if instead of the Blue Silk C F, there be let fall in the Place of C F, the blue Rays from another Prism ( the other Colours being intercepted by a Paper with a square Hole for the Blue to pass through. ) If the Silk A H and the blue Square C F be view ’ d through a Prism ( as before ) the Blue will appear far below, as at IQ L, this being a more perfect Blue than any Silk can be of. Experiment V. Let MN be the black Cover of a Book, Pa - i per coloured Black, or the like.; upon which lay in a straight Line or little Squares of White Paper, about the Bigness and at the Distance as in the Figure, first Column: View these through a Prism, so as that the Row of little Squares have its one End towards you, or be in a Plain perpendicular to the Ax of the Prism, and about two Foot distance from the Glass; so will you fee a Stream, of Colours proceeding from every Square towards the next nearer you, the Colours arising out of each white Square. Move these Squares near to one another, or put others between them, as in the Second Column ( still keeping them in a straight Line ) and you will fee as they come near, that the Colours mixing one with another will al - ter, approaching nearer to White till the Squares touch, and then all the Colours being - perfectly mix ’ d they produce Whiteness, and appear as in the third Column, a white Line, only tang ’ d with Red at the Top and Blue at the Bottom, there be - ing no other Colours coming from above to mix with the uppermost Red, nor any Colours below the Blue at Bottom for it to mix with. If you turn the Paper M N aside a little from its Per - pendicularity to the Glass, the third. Column, which before appeared White, will all appear in Colours arising out of the White, and beaming towards you, being always in a Plain perpendicular to the Axis of the Prism. From this Experiment and the foregoing Do - citrine we have the Reason why a Sheet of white Paper, or the like, appears coloured only at the Edges, for there only the Colours want others to mix with them: In the Middle, taking any Point the several Colours from so many other Points meet there as make White. For Instance, Let r r be any little Particle in the Middle of a white Surface, whole other Colours beaming towards B, leave the Particle r r it self Red, as the Squares will do in the last Experiment. The Yellow of the Particle yy, the Green of the Par - ticle gg, the Blue of the Parti - cle bb do all meet on the Par - jB tide rr, which is Red. ( For if bb were a white Par - ticle, and all Black about it, its blue Colour would be seen upon rr; and if gg were another, its Blue would be below r r, and its Green upon it, &c. ) and so there being a Concurrence of all the Colours that make up White, it consequently appears White, be laid of any other Particle lying so far from the Edges as to have other Particles between to trans - mit their Colours. If a Square Paper be held so straight before you that the two Side Edges be in a plain Perpendicular to the Axis of the Glass, they will be White and no Colours appear but at the Top and Bot - tom, the Streaming of the Colours being in such a perpendicular Plain, as may be observed by look - ing at any white Spot through the Glass, and then turning it a little obliquely to the Horizon, or one End higher than the other. So in the Position of the Glass D E ( see the following Fig. ) the white Spot ascends its Colours towards b, and in the Position F G the Colours stream from a to c. If a black Spot, as A, up - on a Paper be view ’ d through the Prism, the Top will have Green and Blue upon it, and un - der the lower Part will appear Red and Yellow r tse ? v gl yu r L L s. b ... b y y - T V The fame is to the Reason of which is, that the Blue comes from the White above it, and appears on the A Black, there being no other Colours to mix with k: The Red appears under the Spot, because the black Spot transmit no other Colours to mix with the Red Experiment IV, Hold the Prism so to the Sun, as thatthe Co - lours may appear upon a large plain Wall, as at AS; turn the Prism swiftly about its Axis, so as that the Colours may move swiftly up and down, ‘ from B to C. C So will there appear no Colour distend, but a faint white Streak between B and C, which so ap - pears, because by the swiftness of the Motion the several Colours are confounded and mixed, and therefore appear White. Then move the Glass in ( uch manner, that the Colours, may move side - ways and swiftly from B to D, in which Cale the Colours will not disappear, but make a fort of Lift of several Colours, because they are not mix ’ d to make Whiteness, but each Colour keeps in its own Line. Experiment VII. In a dark Room, having a little Hole for the Sun ’ s Rays to come in, apply the Prism to the Hole, so as that the Colours may appear on a Wall. Hold a Quantity of Smalt, or Powder - Blue, or blue Silk in the Colours severally, and it will ap - pear clear of the Colour of the Rays that fall on it, ( vi. ) Red while the Red Light falls upon it, and Yellow when the Yellow Light falls on it but of all the Colours ’ twill most strongly rested the Blue, the Surface being most disposed to re - fled thole Rays, &c. Then view a Quantity of Vermilion, or a little Piece of Scarlet Silk in the Blue Light, and ’ twill appear Blue, and Green in the Green Light; but of all the Colours ’ twill most strongly rested the Scarlet Rays, and appear deepest of that Colour. This Experiment confirms the th Proposition, That Bodies appear of the Colour of those Rays that are most plentifully reflected from the Body; to the Eye Thus far Mr. Perils. I can now only give you sore of the Propositions of St. If. Neve tons excellent Book of Opticas, relating to the Doctrine of Light and Colours, with some - thing from him by way of Proof and Illustration in the most Eminent and Material Points. Prop. t Lights which differ in Colour, differ also in Def grees of Refrangibility. Prop. if. The Light of the Sun consists of Rays different - ly Refrangible. Prop. Hi The Sun ’ s Light consists of Rays differing iri Reflexibility j and those Rays are more flexible which are more Refrangible than o - thers. This, which seems to be a surprising Property, of Light not before discovered, he proves in his th and th Experiments of the First Book; where ' tis evident, that the Rays within a Prism, and refracted by its Base at their going out into Air, being by the Revolution of the Prism round its Axis made so oblique to the Base, as thereby to begin to be totally reflected by it: Then he shews that thele Rays became first of all totally reflected, which before at equal Incidences with the reft had suffered the greatest Refraction; and the fame thing be found to happen also when the Refledion was made by the common Base of two Prisms placed so together as to make a Parallelepiped, as in the th Experiment. Prop. IV. Probl. I. To separate from one another the Homogeneal Rays of compound Light. Prop. V. Homogeneal Light is refracted regularly with - out any Dilatation, Splitting or Shattering of the Rays; and theconfufed Vifionof Ob - jeds seen through refracted Bodies by He - rogeneal Light, arises from the different Re - frangibility of several forts of Rays, This he proves in his th, ith, th and th Experiments from whence it appears, that the cross Position of a second Prism to refra the Light of the Sun which came to it from a former Prism, placeed at the small Hole of a darkened Room, did not at all dilate the Image or coloured Speftrum as to Breadth, nor increafeitsDimenfions that way: As also, that Homogeneal Light, refra - ded by a Prism, did not exhibit an oblong colour - ed Image, as Heterogeneal Light doth, but that a round round Spot of it was by the Prism refracted exact - ly in the lame Figure and of the fame Colour it was before the new Refraction; and moreover that Flies and such like small Objects placed in Homogeneal Light, and viewed through a Prism, were not thereby at all rendred confused and in - distinct as to appearance, whereas if placed in Heterogeneal Light, and viewed after the lame manner, they seemed egregiously confused.

ariseorfreefe.c: ARISE, or Freefe, in Architecture, is that round part of the Entablature which is between the Archi - trave and Cornice This the French call the Gorgerin or Collier.

arbiterexternus.c: ARBITER Externus, is a Hole in the Os Ma xillare, below the Orbit, thro ’ which the Nerves and Vessels which come from the Teeth, pass to the Cheeks.

arbiterinternus.c: ARBITER Internus, is a Hole in the Coronal Bone, within the Orbit a little above the Os Pla - num, thro ’ which passes a Branch of the fifth pair of Nerves which goes to the Nose.

arise.c: ARISE; the Sea word for hailing up any thing by a dead Rope, or one that doth not run in a Block, but ’ tis done by Hand or by main Strength: Thus if any Cask, Chest, or other Goods hath only a Rope fastned to it, and so without a Tackle is pulled up into the Ship by Hand, they fay it is Trifed up.

ards.c: ARDS of a Ship, are those long pieces of Tim - ber which are made a little tapering at each end, and are fitted each to its proper Mast to carry the Sails, which are fastned to these Yards at their Head, and are hoised up and let down together with the Yards, by the Halliards. For the Proportions of the Yards of a Ship, they commonly allow of the Length of her Keel, or of the Length of her Mainmaft, for the Length of her Main - yards; and for the thickness of them, they allow of an Inch for every Yard in Length; the Top - yard is - f of the Main - yard, and the Fore - yard is r of the Main - yard, or as some fay I: The Spritfail - yard and Cross - jack, are of the fame Length, vi. the Missen - yard; and the Thick - ness of the Missen yard and Spritfail - yard is l Inch to a Yard in Length. All small Tards are half the great Yards from Cleat to Cleat: When a great Yard is down a Port l aft, it gives the Length of all Topsail - sheets, Lifts and Ties, Jeers and Bunt - lines; as also of the Leech - lines and Halliards, measuring from the Hounds to the Deck: And when it is Hoised, it gives the Length of Clew - lines, Braces, Clew - gar - nets, Tackles, Sheets and Bow - lines. The Terms belonging to the Yards, are, i. Top the Yards; that is, make them hang even. The Clew - lines do most properly Top the Main and Fore - yards; but when the Top - fails are flowed, then the Topsail - sheets willTop them.. Brace the Yard, i. e. Traverse aft the Yard - Arm, whose Brace is haled. So that Traverse the Yard, is the fame as to fay. Brace it aft.. Square the Yards, i. e. See that they hang right across the Ship, and one Yard - Arm not Traveffed more than the o - ther. YAREjj is the Sea Word for Nimble, Ready, Quick, or Expeditious.

abacus.c: ABACUS: Besides the former Account of the Abacus, I find that Mduclirc, in the Ionick Order, designs what the Work men call an O. G, with a Fillet over it for the Abacus: Which Fillet is half the breadth of the O. G, and he calls it the Fillet of the Abacus. In the Corinthian Order, he Describes the Abacus as a seventh part of the whole Capital, Palladio calls the Plinth about the Boul - tin ( or Echinus ) the Abacus: Which from its Form, faith he, is commonly called Dado or the Dye; and this is j of the whole height of the Capital Scamo i calls a certain Hollow or Calement, which is the Capital of the Pedestal of the Tuscan Order, by this Name Abacusi

abase.c: ABASE, in the Sea Language, is to Lower or Take in. To Abase the Flag, is to Take in the flag.

abbacy.c: ABBACY, is the Government Of a Religious House, with the Revenues and Persons Subject to an Abbat.

abbot.c: ABBOT, is. a Spiritual Lord, having the Rule of Religious Houses according to our Common LaW: Some Abbats in England were called Mitred Ab - bats; and such were exempted from the Jurisdi - ction of the Diocesan, having Episcopal Authority themselves within their Limits, and were also Lords of Parliament. Theie were sometimes call ’ d Ab - bats Sovereign and Abbats General. The other Abbats were Subject to the Diocesan in all Spirit - tual Government. There were also Lords Priors, which had exempt Jurisdiction, and were Lords of Parliament. Of these Lords Abbats and Priors, Sir Ed. Coke faith these were that Sat in Par - ligament, ij Abbats and Priors. But sometimes their Number was varied, there being but if Abbats and Priors in a Parliament held in the stich..

abreuvoirs.c: ABREUVOIRS, are the Interval or Spaces between the Stones, or the Joints where the Mor - tar lies in any Pillar, Wall, or Building.

accord.c: ACCORD, according to the Modern ( French ) Account of Muflck, is the Production, Mixture and Relation of two Sounds; of which the one is Grave and the other Acute. They make two Kinds of Accord; those which are pleasant and agreeable, and which they call C on finances and such as are harsh and unplealant, which are call ’ d Dijfonances. Which see in Vol. I.

acerides.c: ACERIDES, is a Piaifter made without Wax, such as that calld Emplajlram Norimbergenfe.

actioncivil.c: ACTION Civil, is that which tends only to the Recovery of what is due to any one by Contract, ( c. as if a Man seek by Adion to Recover a Sum of Money formerly lent.

actionpenal.c: ACTION Penal, is that which aims at some Penalty or Punishment in the Party Sued, whether Corporal or Pecuniary; as in the Action Legis Ac - quill e in the Civil Law, and in the Common Law in Case of Appeals for Murder.

actionprejudicialorpreparatory.c: ACTION Prejudicial or Preparatory, is that which grows from some doubt in the Principal; as suppose a Man Sue a younger Brother for Land descended from his Father, and ’ tis objeded that he is a Bastard: The Bastard must be first Tried that is call ’ d Allio Prejudicalts, because it must be first Judge ’ d or Determin ’ d. ACTION

actionaunceftrel.c: ACTION Aunceftrel, is in opposition to Person - nal, being that which a Man hath by some Right descending from his Ancestors: This is either Drop - turel Or Possessory z See Co. z Injlit. f..

actor.c: ACTOR, is fotnetiines used fora Prodor or Advocate in Civil Courts or Causes. Attor demi - nions was also the Term formerly for the Lord ’ s Bailey or Attorney. Attor Ecclefice was sometimes the Foreign Term for the Advocate or Pleading Patron of a Church. All or Vida was the Stew - ard or Head Bailey of a Town or Village.

addictionindiem.c: ADDICTION in Diem, in the Civil Law, is an Agreement between Buyer and Seller, that the Seller may Contrad with any other Person who will offer a better Price, before a certain Day.

addition.c: ADDITION, is the Term in our Common Law for the Title which is given to any Person besides his Christian and Sir Name, in order to distinguish him by his Degree, Estate, Mystery, Trade, Place of Abode, &c. And ’ tis particularly prov ’ d by the St at. H.. c.. that in Suit of Action where Process of Uc - lars lies, such Additions shall be given to the Name of the Defendant; and that Writs not having such Additions shall Abate, if the Defendant take Ex - ceptions thereunto.

advancefosse.c: ADVANCE Fosse, is a Ditch of Water round the Esplanade or Glacis of a Place, to prevent its being surprised by the Besiegers: But of late this Work hath beed difus ’ d, because as soon as the E - enemy could drain it, it was a Trench ready made for the Advantage of the Besiegers.

advocationdecimarum.c: ADVOCATION Decimarum, is a Writ that lies for the Claim of a fourth part or upward of the Tithes belonging to any Church.

advowee.c: ADVOWEE or AVOWEE, in Latin Advocatus, was formerly us ’ d for him that had Right of Pre - sensation to a Benefice j and the Avowee Paramount was the highest Patron or the King. By the Sta - tute of Provifors.. E.,

advowson.c: ADVOWSON of a Religious House as the Builders and Endowers of a Church were the Pa - trons of it, so those that Founded any Religious House, had the Advowson or Patronage of it. Some - times the Patron had the some Nomination of the Prelate, Abbot or Prior, either by Iriveftiture ( or delivery of a Pastoral Staff ) or by direct Present - tation to the Diocesan. And if a free Eledion was left to the Religious, yet a Conge d ’ ejlire, or Licence of Election, was first to be obtain d of the Patron and the Person Eleded was Confirm ’ d by him. If the Founder ’ s Family was Extend, the Patronage of the Convent went to the Lord of the Mannor.,

adz.c: ADZ, is an Instrument whose Blade is made thin and something bending, and hath not its Edge Parallel to its Handle, as the Ax and Hatchet hath, but placed athwart to it. It is Ground to a Basil on the inside to its outer Edge. Its general Ule is to take off thin Chips of Timber or Boards, and such Irregulariities as the Ax can ’ t come at, and where a Plane, tho ’ rank Sett, will not make riddance e - enough. ’ Tis much us ’ d in taking off the Irregu - rarities of Floors when they are pinned and framed together and sometimes on Polls framed upright, and ranged in with other Work framed to them, where the Edge of the Ax can ’ t come. estuary, is an Arm of the Sea running up a good way into the Land, like the Bridow Channel, &c,,

age.c: AGE, in the Common Law, is that particular Time which enables a Person to do that, which before he could not do for want of Age: Thus at Years a Man is said to be at the Age of Difcre - tion and at, at full Age. At Years of Age a Man may take the Oath of Allegiance at a Leet at he may consent to Marry, and in Soccage chuse his Guardian at he is of Age for the Lord to have Aid pur fuir fits ' Chivalier, and may be sworn to keep the Queens Peace at he is bound to Appearance before the Sheriffs and Co - roner for enquiry after Robberies. A Woman might heretofore at Years of Age, / her Father being the Lord, Deftrain his Tenants for Aid pur fill marie and at those Years content to Marry faith Bratton. At Years die is dowable for then, or within half a Year after ( Fleta. tin.. c. zi. Lit. Lib., c.. ) she is able promereri dotem virum fuflinere: But this Bratton limits to Years. At iz she is able to ratify and confirm a former Consent gi - ven to Macrimony at she is able to receive her Lands into her own Hands, and shall be out of Ward,, if Hie be at that Age at her Ancestors Death at Ihe shall be out of Ward, tho ’ the was under at the Death of her Ancestor at Ihe is able to A - lineate her Lands and Tenements;

agogice.c: AGOGICE, is the Art of making Images or Fi - gures in Metals, when Wax is us ’ d to effed or fur - ther tbe Design.

aide.c: AIDE, in the Law, hath several ! Significations; sometimes ’ tis the fame with Subsidy sometimes a Protestation due from Tenants to their Lords. - This Word is also us ’ d in matter of r ending for a Petition made in Court, for the calling in of the help from another that hath an Interest in the Cause in Question. Thus a Tenant for Term of Life, by Curtefy, Tenant in Tail after possibility, of Issue extend, for Term of Years, at Will, by Elegit or by Statute Merchant, being impleaded touching her Estate, may pray in Aid of him in the Reversion that is, desire the Court that he may be called in by Writ, to alledge what he thinks good for the Maintenance both of her Right and his Own but this Course hath been difus ’ d. If a Kings Tenant holding in Chief be demanded a Rent of a common Person, he may pray in Aid of the King and so may a City or Burgh, having a Fee - Farm of the Crown, when any thing is de - mended against them belonging thereunto.

alarm.c: ALARM - Po / R is the Ground appointed to each Regiment by the Quarter - Master - Seneral, for them to March to in Case of an Alarm: in a Gar - prison ’ tis the Place where every Regiment is order ’ d to draw up in, on all occasions.

albula.c: ALBULA,. This Word is used sometimes for a Spot in the Eye, and then seems to be the fame with Albugo But Si the Plural Albula, signifies such Vob / A L G very astringent Mineral Waters as have a great deal of Allum in them, and are chiefly used ex - ternally for Cleaning and Healing of Wounds and. Ulcers.
