algebraic.c: ALGEBRAIC - C rw, in Geometry, is of such a Nature, that its Abfcijf or intercepted Diame - ters bear always the fame Proportion to their Re - fpedive Ordinates. Thus if the Product of any Abfcijf a Multiplied into one and the fame Deter - minute Quantity be always equal to the Square of its Corresponding Ordinate: Then if that Deter - minute Quantity be call ’ d p, the Abscissa x and the Ordinate yi The Expression of the Nature of the Curve by way of Equation will be p x yy, where p is the Parameter or Latus ReBum of the Figure g and the Curve is the Common Apollonian Parabo - la and because the two Indeterminate or Flowing Quantities x and y, do here denote Strait Lines Therefore the Curve is call ’ d an Algebraic ! or Geo - metrick. Curve. And ’ tis plain that the Number of such Curves must be infinite j because there may - be an Infinity of Proportions or Relations between the Ordinates and the Abfiijfa, B R, But ' f A L I. But when the Nature of any Curve is exprest by an Equation, wherein one of the Indeterminate or Flowing Quantities Represents a Curve Line; Then that Curve is call ’ d a Transcendental Curve, and if the Curve which enters the Equation be Geometrical j or a CurVe, as they call it, of the first Kind or Degree; then the Trenfcendent Curve is call ’ d a Curve of the second Kind or Degree: And when the Curve which enters the Equation rere - lents a Curve of the second Kind or Degree j then the Transcendental Curve is call ’ d one of the Third Kind; and so on Infinitely. ALlXJM - lVorlis, AHum is made of a Stone, of Sea - weed and Urine. The Stone is found in most of the Hills between Scarborough and the River of Tees in the County of Tof, and also near Prejion in Lancajhire; tis of a Blewifh Colour, and will cleave like Cornijh Slatei The Mine which lies deep in the Earth and is pretty well Moiftned with Springs is the best. The Dry Mine is not good, and too much Moisture Cankers and Corrupts the Stone, making it Nitrous. In this Mine are found several Veins of Stone call ’ d Doggers, of the fame Colour but not so good. Here are found those al - io which are commonly call ’ d Snake - Stones. For the more convenient Working of the Mine which sometimes lies ao Yards under the Surface or Cap of the Earth ( which must be taken off and Barrow ’ d away ) they begin their Work on the Declivity of a Hill, where they may be also well furnifii ’ d with Water. They Dig down the Mine by Stages, to lave Carriage, ands thro ’ it down near the places where they Calcine it. The Mine before it is Cal - in ’ d, being expos’d to the Air will Moulder into pieces, and yield a Liquor whereof Copperas ray be made: But being Calcin ’ d it ’ s fit for Allum; as long as it continues in the Earth, or in Water, it remains an hard Stone. Sometimes a Liquor will issue sit of the Side of the Mine, which by the Sun ’ s Heat is turn ’ d into Natural Allum. The Mine is Calcin ’ d with Cinders of New - Cajlle Coal, Wood and Furzes. The Fire m. ade about two Foot and Thick, two Yards Broad, and io Yards Long; betwixt every Fire are hops made with wet Rubbish; io that any one or more of them may be kindled, without prejudice to the reft. After there are or io Yards Thickness of broken Mine laid on this Fewel, and or of them so covered; then they begin to kindle the Fires, and as the Fires rife towards the Top, they still lay on fresh Mine: So that to what Height you can raise the Heap, which is oftentimes about ao Yards, the Fire without any farther help of Fewel will burn to the Top stronger than at the first kindling, so long as any Sulphur remains in the Stones. In Calcining these Stones, the Wind many times does hurt, by forcing the Fire too quickly thro ' the Mine, leaving it black and half burnt, and in others, burning the Mine too much, leaving it Red. But where the Fire passes sourly and of its own accord, it leaves the Mine whole, which yields the best and greatelLCluantity of Liquor. The Mine thus Calcin ’ d is put into Pits of Wa - ter supported with Frames of Wood, and ram ’ d on all Sides with Clay: They are about o Yards Long, Broad, and Deep, and fet with a Cur - rent that turpeth the Liquor into a Receptory, from whence ’ tis Pumpt into another Pit or Mine. So that every Pit of Liquor, before it comes to Boiling, is Pumpt into four several Pits of Mine; g, nd every Pit of Mine is steeped in four several ’ Liquors before it be thrown away, and the last Pic being always of frefu Mine. his Mine thus Steeped in each of the several Liquors Hours, or thereabouts, is of Course four Days in puffing the four several Pits from whence the Liquors pals to the Boiling - house. The Water, or Virgin Liquor often gains in the first Pit, two Pound Weight; in the second it increafeth to five Pound, in the third to eight Pound, and in the last Pit which is always fresh. Mine to twelve Pound and so in Proportion ac - cording to the Goodnels of the Mine, and its be - ing well Calcin ’ d. For sometimes the Liquors palling the four several Pits, will not be increas ’ d to above fix or leven Pound Weight, and at other times above twelve Pound; seldom holding a con - stant Weight one Week together: Yet many times Liquor of seven or eight Pound Weight produces more Allum than that of ten or twelve Pound Weight, either thro ’ the badness of the Mine, or its being ill Calcin ’ d ', which is the usual Rea fon. And if by palling the Weak Liquor thro ’ ano - ther Pit of fresh, Mine, you bring it to be ten or twelve Pound Weight, yet you ( hall make Ids Allum with it, than when it was but eight Pound Weight. For what it gains from the last Pit of Mine will He most ' Nitre and Slam, which Poisons tlie good Liquors, and Diforders the whole House till the Slam be wrought off. That which they call Slam is first perceived by the Redness of the Liquor when it comes from the Pit, occasion ’ d either by the badness of; he Mine, or more usually its being oyer or under Calcin ’ d, which in the Setler finks to the bottom, and there becomes a muddy Substance, and of a dark Co - lour. That Liquor which conies Whiteft from the Pits is the best.,, When a Work is first begun, they make Allum of the Liquor only that comes from the Pits of Mine, without any other Ingredients: And io might continue, but that it would spend so much Liquor as not to quit Cost, Kelp is made of a See - weed call ’ d Tangle, such as comes to London on Oyster Barrels. It grows on Rocks by the Sea - side, between high and low Water Mark. Being dry ’ d ir will burn and run like Pitch i when, cold and hat'd, ’ tis beaten to Allies, steeped in Water, and the Lees drawn off to two Bound Weight of thereabouts. . Because the Country People who furnish the Work with Urine, do sometimes mingle it with Sea - Water, which cannot be discover ’ d by weight they try it by putting tome of ir to the boyling Li - quor: For, then if the Urine be Genuine it will. Work like Yeast put to Beer or Ale j but if min - g ’ ed. it will stir no more than so much Water. They observe that the best Urine for that pur - pose, is Inch as comes from Poor Labouring - Peo - ple who drink but little strong Drink. The Boiling Pans are made of Lead, nine Feet Long, five Broad, and two - i Deep, fet upon Iron Plates about two Inches Thick; which Pans are commonly new Cast, and the Plates Repair ’ d five times, in two Years. When the Work is begun and Allum once made, j then they lave the Liquor which comes from the A'lum, or wherein it shoots, which they call the Mothers, with this they fill f of the Boilers, arid put in f of the frefli Liquor which comes from the Pits. Being thus fill ’ d up with cold Liquor, the Fires having been never drawn out, it will Boil A L L A L T again in less than two Houss - time. And in every two Hours time the Liquor will waft four Inches, and the Boilers are sill'd ‘ up again with Green Li - H Trie Liquor if Good, in the Boiling, will be Greasy, as it were, at the op t If Nitrous, it will be Thick, Muddy and Red. In: Boiling i Hours it will be Pound Weight - Then is put int the Boiler about an Hogffiead of the Lees oi Kelp, of about two Penny Weight, which will re - dnee the whole Boiler to about Pound Weight. Tf t - Up Liquor be Good, as soon as the Kelp Lees are put into the Boiler, they will Work like Yeast put to Beer: But if it be Nitrous, the Kjlp Lees will stir it but very little; and in that Case the Work - men must put in more and stronger Lees. Presently after the K'lp Lees are Put lnco cc Boiler, all the Liquor together is drawn into a SHtler a big as the Boiler and trade of Lead, in which it stands about two Hours and uh that time most of the Nitre and Slam sink to the bot - C This Separation is made by the Help of tit Kelp Lees, for when the whole Boiler consists of Green Liquor drawn from the Pits, it is of Pow - strong enough to cast of the Slam and the Nfi - tre but when the Mothers are us ’ d, the Kelp Lees are needful to make the said Sepaiation. Next the said Liquor is Scooped out of the Settler into a Cooler, made of Deal Boards, and Ramm ’ d with Clay. Into this is put Gallons, or more of the Urine, according to the Goodness or Badnels of the Liquor, for when the Liquor is Red and Nitrous, the more Urine is requir ’ d. In the Cooler, the Liquor in Temperate Weather stands four Days; the second Day the Allum be - gins to Strike, gather and harden about the Sides, and at the bottom of the Cooler. If the Liquor should stand above four Days, then it would turn to Copperas. The Use of the Urine is as well to call oft the ' Slam, as to keep the K'P Lees from hafdning the Allum too much. In Hot Weather the Liquor will be a Day lon - ger in Cooling, and the All'um in gathering, than in Temperate Weather. But in Frost, the Allum shoots or strikes too soon, not giving Time for the Nitre and Slam to sink to the bottom, where - by they are mingid with the Allum. This produ - ces double the Quantity, but being foul cis confu - med in Waffling.;. “ When the Liquor Hath flood four Days in the Cooler, than that call ’ d Mother, is Scooped into a Cistern; the Allum remaining on the sides and bottom, and from thence the Mothers are Pumpt back into the Boilers again; So that every five Bays the Liquor is Boil ’ d again, until it evaporate or turn into Allum or Slam. The Allum taken from the sides and bottom of the Cooler; is put into a Cistern and Walhed with jiVater, that they use for the fame purpose; being about Pound Weight, after which it is poached as follows. Being Walhed it is put into another Ban with a Quantity of Water, where it Melts and Boils a little then tis Scooped into a great Cask, where it com -. xnonly stays o Days, and is then fit to take down lor the Market. The Liquors are Weigh ’ d by Troy Weight; so that half a Pint of Liquor must Weigh more than so much Water, by so many P any W eight. From Phil, Trans. N.. '

alanfurnaceoralmond.c: ALAN Furnace or Almond, as some Write it, is a Furnace us ’ d by Refiners, and by them call'd the Sweep; By it all fores of Metals are separated from Cinders, pales of Melting Pots,, Tefts, Bricks and all other harder Bodies; which must. first be beaten to Powder before they are put into the Furnace. This Furnace is about fix Foot High, four Wide and two Thick; made of Brick, having a Hole in the midst at the Top, eight Inches over, and growing narrow towards the Bottom, whereon the forepart ends in a small hole environed with a Semicircle of Iron, to keep the Melted Metal; about the middle of the back there is another hole to receive the Nose of a great pair of Bellows ! When the Furnace is Annealed, wits Charcoal and Hot, they throw two or three Snovelsof Co. il to one of the foremention ’ d Powder ’ d slusy, and so proceed during the wliole Work, which continued without intermission three Days and Nights. After eight or ten Hours the Metal begins to run, and when the Receiver below is pretty full, they Lade it out with an Iron Ladle, and cast it into Sows: in HolloWS, or Forms made with Ashes.

almoner.c: ALMONER, is an Officer in a King ’ s or Prin - ces House, whose Business is to Distribute Aims to the Poor; he hath Forfiture of all Deodands and the Goods of Felous de fe, which he is to Dispose off to the Poor Terms de lay.

alnageraulnager.c: ALNAGER, Aulnager; properly one thatMea - surety Cloth by the Ell, the doing of which is Alnage. He is a publick Sworp Officer of the King, who either by himself or his Deputy looks to the Assize of Woollen Cloth throughout the Kingdom, and to the Seals for that purpose or - main ’ d. Now there are three Officers belonging to this Affair, the Searcher, the Mcafurer, and the Alnager; which last is new become the CoHedlor of the Suhfidy granted to the Crown by several Statutes.,

aloof.c: ALOOF, is a Sea Term signifying as much as keep your Luff; being a Word of Command from him that Conns, to the Man at the Helm to keep the Ship near the Wind, when ( he Sails upon a Quarter Wind. - AjLOPEX, is by some Writers, a Term us ’ d ? for the Muscle Ffoas., A

amabyroramvahyf.c: AMABYR, or Amvahyf, was the Old Custom of the Pretium virginitatis Domino Solvendum. Henry Eajled Arundel, by Deed Dated Aug.,. of Phil, and Mar. releas ’ d this Custom to his Tenants by the Name of the Custom of Ama - her and Cherage.

amaasa.c: AMAASA, are such Pieces of Glass as are us ’ d in Ennammelling, and are sometimes call ’ d En - cautta j by some Smalt a and Terra Saracenica. Bruno.

amaracinon.c: AMARACINON, is a very precious Oyntment prepared with Rich Oyls and highly Aromatick Spices.

ambigenalhyperbola.c: AMBIGENAL Hyperbola, is an Hyperbola which hath one of its Infinite Legs inscribe ’ d in it and the other circumscribe ’ d about it.

amethyst.c: AMETHYST, are such Medicines as will prefer Men from being soon inebrias ’ d with Wine or strong Liquor, - Bruno, A NC

ammonium.c: AMMONIUM, is by some Writers us ’ d for Collyrium. Which See.

amphora.c: AMPHORA, was anciently a Measure of Ca - parity, sometimes call ’ d y dutov, and was of Sorts; the Italian Amphora, which Gallen faith, held Pound of Water: The Attisk, Amphora ? which was larger, and was call ’ d See Freights and Measures.

analysisofinfinites.c: ANALYSIS of Infinites. See Fluxions and Ge ometry.

ancestor.c: ANCESTOR. The Law distinguishes between Ancedor and Predecejfor; the former being applied to a Natural Person as A. B, and his Ancefier the A N G the latter to a Body Politick or Corporate; as a Bishop and his Predeceffors. Tho ’ the ' Word Antecessor, whence Ancejier is de - riv ’ d is not applied to the Anceflor of a Family, but to the Prepoffeffor of an Mate; or a Prede - cessor in Office. Ancefirel Homage, is such Ho - mage as hath been perform ’ d by our Ancejiors.

anchorsinarchitecture.c: ANCHORS, in Architecture, is a certain kind of Carving, in the Form of an Anchor or Arrow Head, which is placed by way of Ornament to the Boultins of Capitals of the Tuscan, Doricl (, and lonicli Orders; and also to the Boultins of Bed Mouldings, of the Doricl i, Ionic f and Corinthian Cornifties. The Anchors and Eggs being placed Alternately.

ancientdemesneordemdyn.c: ANCIENT Demesne or Demdyn, is a certain Tenure whereby all Mannors belonging to the Crown in St. Edwards or William the Conqueror s Time were held. The Numbers and Names, ( c. of such Mannors were entred by the Conqueror, in a Book call ’ d Dooms - day Book, and now remain - ing in the Exchequer, so that stich Lands as by that Book appear ’ d to have belong ’ d to the Crown at that Time, are call ’ d Ancient Demesne. The Tenants in Ancient Demesne are of two forts; one that hold their Lands frankly by Charter, the other by Copy of Court Roll, or by the Verge at the Will of the Lord.; according to the Custom of the Mannor. The Advantages of this Tenure; are i. That Tenants holding by Charter cannot be rightfully impleaded out of their Mannor; and when they are they may abate the Writ by Plea - ding the Tenure,. They are free from Toll for all things relating to their Lively - hood and Hus - bawdry i Nor can they be impahnelied upon any Inquest.... aNCONY, is the Term in the Iron Works for a Bloom, wrought into the Figure of a flat Iron Barr of about three Foot long, with two Square rough Knobs, one at each end j, which are after - wards to be wrought at the Chafery. See Iron.

angaria.c: ANGARIA, was formerly the Word for any troublesome or Vexatious Duty or Service paid by the Tenant to the Lord.

anguinealhyperbola.c: ANGUINEAL Hyperbola, is one of an Well - like Figure which cuts its Asymptote with contrary Flexions, and is produced both ways with contrary Legs. See CuroeL

angularmotion.c: ANGULAR Motion, in Autonomy, is the en - ereafe of the Distance between any two Planets &c. Revolving round any Body as the Center of A N G their Motion and is express ’ d by two Right Lines drawn from the laid Center to the Revolving Bo - dies, which will open wider, and consequently grow greater, as the Revolving Bodies part farther and farther from one another.

animalsecretion.c: ANIMAL Secretion, is that Adion in ah Ani - mal Body, whereby, by means of the Glands all proper Separations of Particles, proper to be Se - cerned or Separated from the Blood, are made, throughout its whole Course of Circulation. How these Secretions are every where made in the Body, ’ tis of very great Use to understand; and some of our Modern Physicians who have apply ’ d them - selves to confider the wonderful Machine of a Human Body Geometrically and Mechanically, have made great Advahces this way; such as Bo - belli, Bellini, Baglivi, Pitcairne, Cheyne, Wain - might, &c from whom you have the following Account of this Important Affair. The Nature of Secretions in general, depends up - on these Three Things. (. ) The Different Dia - meter of the Orifice of the Secretory Dull; for there - by all Particles whose Diameters are greater than those of the Duffs, must be excluded; and it may be concluded that any Peccant or Morbifick Matter may be Evacuated therefore by any of the Glands, provided that their Orifices be but fuffici - ently enlarge ’ d, ( together with the Diameters of the Secretory Duds. (. ) The Different Angle which the Secretory DuSt makes with the Trunks of the Artery,, For all Fluids press the Sides of the containing Vessels in a Di - region perpendicular to its Sides; and this is e - videntin the Pulsation of the Arteries, since ’ tis to that Pressure, that this Pulfarion is owing. It is likewise evident that the Blood is urg ’ d forward by the force of the Heart; So that this Motion of Se - creation must be Compounded of both these Mo - tions. Now this Lateral Pressure, is greater when the Velocity of the Longitudinal Motion is so too; but yet ’ tis not in the Proportion of this Velocity. For the Lateral Pressure is considerable, even when the Fluid is at reft; being then in proportion to the Specifick Gravity of the Fluid - And in a Fluid, like the Blood in the Arteries, which is urg ’ d by a Longitudinal Direction, this Lateral Pressure is in a Compound Proportion qf both: From whence it will follow, that if two Particles of equal Diameters, but of unequal Specifick Gra - city do arrive, with the fame Velocity; at in Ori - sice capable of admitting them, yet they will hot both enter it and pass, because their Motion of Di - section is different. that this Diversity in the Angles, which these Duds make with the Trunk of the Artery, seems altogether necessary to ac - count lor the possible Diversities of Secerned Fluids, even supposing their Diameters and Figures to be the fame: For no doubt the Blood is a Heterogene - ous Fluid, and contains parts of very different Speci - sick Gravities,, Cohariions and Denfities. - Whereas the Separated Fluid must be Homogeneous, in order tc perform the uniform FnUdions of Life. (. ) The different Velocities with which the Blood drives at the Orifices of these Secretory DuCls. For since the Secretions are made in form of a Fluid, no possible Reason can be assign ’ d, why since Ani - mals have a soft loose Texture and Union of the Solid Parts, and wily one part of the Body is of a Tender, Loose, easily Separable Texture, and Others of ah Harder, Former and more fe Co hariion; but this different Velocity of the Blood, at the Orifices of the Secretory Duds And tho ’ the Diversity Diversity of the Diameters of these DuCts, is cer - tainly that which is of the greatest Moment in this Affair of Secretion; yet ' tis impossible to account for the Similarity of the Secerned Fluids from one so Heterogeneous, as the Blood is from this alone: Since all Particles of never so different Kinds and Natures will be indifferently separated there, if their Diameters are less than thole of the Secretory Duds and their Direllion right. Again, more particularly from what the above mention'd Authors have deliver'd, such Propofici ons as these may be Establish'd. I. That of an Heterogeneous Fluid at reft in the Body, and equally prest the most Liquid Part, must be forc'd out first. II. That of such an Heterogeneous Fluid, as the Blood, when it Stagnates its heavy Parts will precipitate, and its Light be Elevated, and all will take place according to their Specifick Gravities. And when it doth not Stagnate, the Se - operation of the Heavy Parts from the Light, will be in proportion to the Slowness of the Motion of the Fluid. III. The Red Fibrous part of the Blood on its Stagnation, retires to its Center and forces the Serum to the Sides of the Vessel, which contains them, and from these z Propositions it will follow, that the Slower the Bloods Motion is, the more Serum will be separated from it, cateris paribus. IV. The most viscid Parts of the Serum are the highest, Vis ', such as are separated in the Glands of the Nose, Mouth, Palate, Windpipe, Stomach, Guts, & e. because these Swim in Water which is lighter than Serum. V. Fluids resist the Motion of such Bodies most, whose Surfaces are greater in Proportion to their Solidities; or whose Speci - sick Gravities are the Ieaft. Wherefore the most Vifeid part of the Serum must be the least Sufcep - table of Motion, or must be moved with the great - test Difficulty thro ' the Arteries. VI. A Fluid forc'd thro ’ a Concave Cylinder ( and much more so, thro a Concave Cone ) moves with greater Ce - levity at the Axis than at the Sides. This Baglivi faith he hath observ'd in the Arteries of Frog. Wherefore the lighteft Parts being least Susceptible of Motion, will be forc ’ d to the Sides of the Ar - teries where there is the least Motion: So that where there is the least Motion, there will the Lighteft or most Vifeid part of the Sarum be sea - rated, and from hence it will follow also, That the Viscidity of the Separated Fluid will be Reciprocally, as the Celerity of the Blood at the Orifice of the Se - parting Can ’. Again, Since Bellini hath prov ’ d that the Velocity of the Blood, at the Orifice of the Secretory Dud, is as the Number of Plications, Folds or Turns in the Complicated Artery ( Prop.. de Motu Cordis. ) Therefore the Viscidity of the Secerned Matter, will be also as the Number of Pli - cations in the Complicated Artery. VII. When the Motion of the Blood is too Slow, the most Serous - part is thrown on those Arteries, which are the Smallest, most Complicated, or at the Greatest Distance from the Heart. VIII. The Intestines in an Animal, are a Gland, and the Lafteals are the Secretory Vessels. IX. The Orifices of the Execu - tory Vessels of any Gland are Circular, because all the Vessels of the Body, in which the Blood or o - ther Fluids move, are either Hollow Cylinders or Cones: for the Pressure of a Fluid, being always Normal to the Sides of the containing Vessel, and being at equal Distances from the Center, the J Sides must be every where equally Diftraded, ’ t tig a Section perpendicular to the Axis of the Vessel must be a Circle, and therefore the Vessel must be either of a Cyliridrick. or Conical Figure. Now from hence it will follow, that the Orifices of Secretory Duds of different Glands, differing not in Figure but only in Magnitude, The Fluids Sea - rated in Different Glands will differ only in Degrees of Cohffion and Fluidity. X. The Relaxed Coat of any Gland encreases the Viscidity of the Secerned Mat - l ter. Vice versa. The reason of which is, that the Matter will grow much more Vifeid, by flaying longer in the Gland, the thin Parts being Evapo - rated by the Heat of the Body. XI. Such Glands whose Compounding Arteries are most Complicated, Secerne the most Vifeid Matter from the Blood for in these Arteries, the Resistance being greater than in Strait ones, the Motion of the Blood must be Slower in Proportion to the Number of their Plica - tions and where the Blood runs Slaweft, its Vifcidi - ty will be Greatest, cc. XII. The Quantity of Fluid Matter Sc / crated in any Gland, is in Compound Pro - portion of the Quantity of the Blood; its Celerity at the Orifices of the Excretory Vessels, and the wideness of those Orifices direBly, and the Viscidity of the Blood Reciprocally. XIII. An encreas'd Quantity of Blood encreases the Fluid Secretions, in a Proportion greater than the Vifeid; and a decreas'd Quantity will lessen the Fluid Secretions more than the Vifeid. XIV. An encreas'd Celerity of the Bloods Motion encreases the Fluid Secretion, more than the Vifeid, & vice versa. XV. An Universal Enlargement of the Orifices of all the Glands, encreases the Fluid Secre - tions, &c. & vice versa. XVI. An encreas ’ d Vilci - city of the Blood, decreafeth the Fluid Secretions more than the Vifeid, & vice versa, an encreas ’ d Fluidity encreafeth the Fluid Secretion more than the Vis - seid ones. See Dr. Moreland's Letter to Dr. Mead about the Secrerionsin an Animal Body. Philo f Trans. N.. See also an Account of the Na - ture of Animal Secretion by Franfcifcut Spolatus in the Leipfid A bis of Nov..

anniversary.c: ANNIVERSARY, was called by our Fore fathers a Tear - Day and a Mind - Day, i. e. a Memo - rial - Day; and is properly the Yearly return of the Day of the Death of any Person: And this Day the Religious regiftred in their Obitual or Mar - pyrology, and Annually observed in Gratitude to their Founders and Benefactors.

ante.c: ANTE, the fame with Antes. ANTIPjEGMENTS, in Architecture, are the Ornaments op Garnifhings in Carved Work which are fee on Architraves, whether of Wood or Stone.

antipathy.c: ANTIPATHY, is properly an AffeCtion of a contrary Nature to another; and therefore what we do in a very high Degree dislike or have an Aver - A R C Aver So; against, we fay we have an Antipathy to. ‘ Tis easy to fee that this ifiay have place in the Arise & ions - and Passions of Mankind but whether there be any fitch thing in the Properties of Natu - ral Bodies, ' hath been e [ questioned; and I think, as Dr. Hock hath long since observed, the EfFeCts which Cine have thought - owing to some secret Antipathies in the Natures of things, ought rather to be ascribed to an Incongruity: See Congruity.

antique.c: ANTIQUE, is a Word much u fed by Archi - tects, Sculptors, and Painters; and by it they mean ass the Ancient Pieces of Architecture, Sculpture, and Painting from the Time of Alexander the Great to the Irruption of the Goths; as also Intaglias within that Time: All w hich they call Antique; and whatever is done in - Imitation of the Great Masters of that Age, they fay is after the Antique Manner.

apertionsinarchitecture.c: APERTIONS, in Architecture, are the Open - ings in any Buildings such as Doors, Windows, Stair - cafes, Chimneys, Outlets or Inlets for Light, Smoakf &c.

aphroditarium.c: APHRODITARIUM, is a dry Medicine made of an equal Weight of Frankincense, Pomegra - name, Cerufs, Meal, and Scales of Brass; and Ga - len calls a kind of Collyriutn by this Name.

aphrogeda.c: APHROGEDA, is Milk beat into an entire Froth, and was a Medicine used by Galen.

apron.c: APRON, is a piece of - Lead which laps over or covers the Vent or Touch - hole of a great Gun.

appetituscaninus.c: APPETITUS Caninus, is an Inordinate extra -, vagant Hunger, to the Degree of a Disease, lb that Men come to Devour every Thing like Dogs. ’ Tis attended with a Lienteria usually, or some such Cceliacal Flux, by which it is distinguish ’ d from fi ? ’ tis call ’ d sometimes Phagedana.

Others think he was first call ’ d the Dean of the Arches, because the Official to the Archbishop being many times employ d a - broad in Embalfies for the King and Realm, the Dean of the Arches was his Substitute in this Court, and by that means the Names became confounded The Jurifdidtion of this Judge is ordinary and ex - tended ! it felt thro ’ the whole Province of Can terbury j so that on any Appeal made, he forthwith, and without any farther Examination of the Ca'ufe, fends out his Citation to the Appellee, and his In - hibition to the Judge from whom the Appeal was made. asaphatum.c: ASAPHATUM, a kind of Impetigo, Serpigo. or running Itch.

ashlar.c: ASHLAR, is the Work - mens Term for Com - mon or Free - stone, as it comes out of the Quar - ry.

aspectdouble.c: ASPECT Double, is a Term in Painting, us'd for a single Figure representing two or more dise - rent Objects; which is caused either by a change of the Position of the Eye, or by Angular Giaifes, ( c. '

assembly.c: ASSEMBLY, in the Military Art, is the second Beat of a Drum before a March on hearing this the Soldiers strike their Tents, and roll them up; and then hand to their Arms. The third Beat - ting is called the March, as the first is called the General.

assistjudicium.c: ASSIST Judicium, is the Judgment of the Court given against the Plaintiff or Defendant for Default.

astrolabe.c: ASTROLABE, this Planisphere considered as a Projection of the Sphere, is of two Kinds. The first is a Projection of the Sphere on the Plane of the Equinoctial in the Stereographick Way, the Eye being supposed to be placed in the Pole of the World. The other Astrolabe is that of Gemma Fri - fius; which supposes the Eye in the Point of the Intersection of the Equator and Horizon, Project - ing the Sphere on the Plane of the opposite Meri - dian.

attendantinlaw.c: ATTENDANT, in Law is used in this Sense, for one that oweth a Duty or Service to another; or after a fort dependeth upon another, v. gr. There is a Lord, Mesne and Tenant. The Tenant holdeth of the Mesne by a Penny, the Mesne hol doth over by two Pence. The Mesne releafeth to the Tenant all the Right he hath in the Land, and the Tenant Dies: Then shall his Wife be endowed of the Land and be Attendant to the Heir of the third part of the Penny, and the third part of the two Pence, forfhe shall be endued of the best part of the Possession of her Husband. They fay also, that where the Wife is endowed by the Guardi - an, she hall bsc Attendant to her Heir at his full Age.
